file: 2014/2014-05-26_business ethics_crimes_mobile (cell) phones_large screen smartphone_stealing_life of crime_chosen lifestyle.gif
title: Not Working While Walking Is Theft

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have a large-screen smartphone, and yet you don't work while walking from one place to another.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's like stealing from the company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't realize I had chosen a life of crime.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And you're not even doing it right.

setting: Conference room table, then a hallway or office
situation: The Boss scolds Dilbert for owning a large-screen smartphone yet not working while he walks between locations, calling it stealing from the company. Dilbert sarcastically remarks that he didn't know he had become a criminal. Dogbert, sitting nearby, adds that he isn't even a good criminal.
punchline: Dogbert mocks Dilbert by suggesting that if he is going to be accused of stealing from the company, he should at least be doing it effectively.
summary: A manager equates unproductive walking time with theft, and Dilbert's sarcastic reaction earns him a dig from Dogbert about being an inept criminal.

file: 2014/2014-04-07_anger_interrupting work_jargon_meeting with boss_not enough passion_stupid trendy_performance evaluation.gif
title: Boss Demands Passion, Gets Fury

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't show enough passion for your job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop interrupting my work with your stupid, trendy management jargon!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Was that better or worse? I don't know how to tell.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert during a one-on-one that he doesn't show enough passion for his job. Dilbert explodes in an angry, flailing outburst at the Boss for interrupting his work with trendy management jargon. The Boss calmly asks whether that outburst counted as an improvement.
punchline: Dilbert's furious rant is exactly the passion the Boss asked for, but the clueless Boss can't tell whether it's good or bad, which shows how meaningless his jargon-driven evaluation is.
summary: After being told he lacks passion, an employee loses his temper at his manager, who is unable to judge whether the outburst is progress.

title: AI As Smart As The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to create artificial intelligence that is as smart as me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. I should have that by lunchtime.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because you're a fast worker?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure.

setting: Office, in conversation while Dilbert holds a coffee mug
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to build an artificial intelligence that is as smart as he is. Dilbert promises to deliver it by lunchtime, and the Boss assumes it's because Dilbert works quickly. Dilbert goes along with that explanation.
punchline: Dilbert implies that matching the Boss's intelligence is so easy it can be done in a morning, while the Boss obliviously credits Dilbert's speed instead of realizing he's being insulted.
summary: A manager requests a machine mind equal to his own, and his engineer cheerfully promises it within hours, leaving the manager to misread the reason.

title: Telecommuting Was Too Exhausting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought you were telecommuting this week.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It was too exhausting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have no follow-up questions.

situation: Dilbert runs into a coworker holding a coffee mug and asks why he is at the office when he was supposed to be telecommuting this week. The coworker says working from home was too exhausting, then sips his coffee. Dilbert, stunned, declines to ask anything further.
punchline: The coworker finds working from home more tiring than commuting to the office, an absurd claim that leaves Dilbert speechless and unwilling to probe further.
summary: A man who was meant to work remotely turns up at the office anyway, claiming that staying home wore him out, and his baffled colleague lets it drop.

title: Co-CEO's Death Isn't Bad News

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Co-CEO

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have bad news.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your co-CEO died trying to kitesurf some class 6 rapids for a publicity stunt.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Get to the bad part. Is it margins?

situation: Dilbert, speaking to Dogbert in his role as Co-CEO, announces that he has bad news and then reports that Dogbert's fellow co-CEO died kitesurfing dangerous rapids as a publicity stunt. Dogbert is unmoved and asks Dilbert to get to the actual bad part, guessing that it concerns profit margins.
punchline: Dogbert is so callous and finance-obsessed that the death of his co-CEO doesn't register as bad news; only a threat to profit margins would.
summary: An executive hears that his business partner has perished in a reckless stunt and shrugs it off, waiting to hear about something that actually matters, the finances.

title: Bubble of Optimism Never Happened Before

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Happy, happy, happy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm enjoying a bubble of optimism because I'm feeling rested and no one has been awful to me all day!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How long does it usually last?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know. It's never happened before!

situation: Dilbert strolls through the office humming and thinking happy thoughts, with music notes floating around him. He stops to explain to a coworker holding a coffee mug that he's in a bubble of optimism because he's rested and nobody has been awful to him. When asked how long the feeling usually lasts, he admits he has no idea since it has never happened before.
punchline: Dilbert's good mood is so unprecedented that he can't say how long it lasts, implying that being well rested and treated decently at work is a rare event for him.
summary: A rare burst of cheerfulness leaves an office worker unable to say how long it will last, since he has never felt it before.

file: 2014/2014-10-01_drinking_hiring_personality tests_sales_sales personnel_sociopaths_storytelling skills_morgue_selfie_dead guy_super drunk_hired_sales person_new hire_business.gif
title: Morgue Selfie Wins Sales Job

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can tell a lot from an applicant's storytelling skills. So tell me a story.

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: Last week, I broke into a morgue and took a selfie with a dead guy. But in my defense, I was super drunk.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a new salesperson.

situation: The Boss interviews a sales applicant and asks him to tell a story to show off his storytelling skills. The applicant cheerfully confesses to breaking into a morgue and taking a selfie with a corpse while drunk. In the last panel the Boss, holding a coffee mug, announces he has hired a new salesperson.
punchline: The Boss hires the applicant because his shameless, antisocial story makes him seem like a natural salesperson, implying that sales rewards a lack of ethics or conscience.
summary: A job candidate admits to a bizarre and illegal drunken escapade, and the interviewer is so impressed that he gives him a sales position.

file: 2014/2014-02-12_conversation_executives_leadership_acceptable behavior_alight goals_company objectives_deal directly_conflict_maintain positive attitude_impressive.gif
title: Boss Boasts Leadership, Gets Mocked

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who's up for some leadership?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Watch me define acceptable behavior, align your goals with company objectives, prioritize respect, deal directly with conflict, maintain a positive attitude and pretend to care!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That would be impressive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Settle down, Bilbo.

situation: The Boss announces he is about to show off some leadership while Dilbert and a coworker with a coffee mug look on. He then rattles off a list of management clichés, ending with 'pretend to care'. The coworker says it would be impressive, and the Boss tells him to settle down.
punchline: The Boss's own list of leadership skills ends with 'pretend to care', and a coworker's deadpan 'that would be impressive' is brushed off with a curt rebuke that shows the Boss has no real leadership at all.
summary: A manager promises a display of leadership, recites a buzzword checklist, and snaps at the one colleague who quietly doubts he can pull it off.

title: Robots Turn Employees Into Meat

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: The company has two exciting announcements.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: We are launching a new artificial meat product.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Clap clap clap clap clap clap

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: In unrelated news, our manufacturing plant is now fully automated by robots.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Wow. It got quiet in here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't want to say we have no trust in senior management, but. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you order the robots to kill all of the manufacturing employees and turn them into a meat product?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Before I answer that, can we agree that capitalism has some rough edges?

setting: Conference room during a company announcement meeting
situation: A senior executive announces a new artificial meat product and, in the next breath, that the manufacturing plant is now fully automated by robots. The room goes silent, and Dilbert asks whether the robots were ordered to kill the factory workers and turn them into the meat product. The executive dodges the question by asking everyone to agree that capitalism has some rough edges.
punchline: The executive's evasive request to acknowledge capitalism's 'rough edges' effectively admits that the workers were turned into meat.
summary: A manager's two cheerful announcements about fake meat and robot factories lead a wary employee to suspect something grisly, and the evasive reply confirms it.

title: Paying Consultants To Go Away

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: On the advice of our consultant, we're going to rewrite the CMS from scratch.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How much did you pay the consultant for the same advice your employees gave you for free?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't pay consultants for advice. I pay them to leave.

situation: The Boss announces at a meeting that the company will rewrite its content management system from scratch because a consultant recommended it. Alice points out that employees had already given the same advice for free and asks how much the consultant was paid. The Boss replies that he pays consultants to leave, not to advise, leaving Dilbert confused.
punchline: The Boss admits he pays consultants only to go away, and ignores his own employees' free advice until an outsider repeats it for a fee.
summary: A manager follows a paid consultant's recommendation that his own staff had already made, then explains that the fee is really a price for getting rid of the consultant.

file: 2014/2014-05-23_gadgets_wearable tech prodcuts_looking cool_feeling cool_hit clubs_early adopter problem.gif
title: Wearable Tech Nobody Wants First

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're having an early adopter problem with our wearable tech products.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Executive
transcript.text: No one wants to go first?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wish we had that problem.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder if we look as cool as we feel.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let's hit the clubs and find out.

setting: Boss's office, an office building exterior, and a workplace area
situation: The Boss complains to a subordinate that customers are not adopting the company's wearable tech products. The subordinate assumes nobody wants to be first, but the Boss says he wishes that were the problem, implying no one wants the products at all. Meanwhile Dilbert and Wally, wearing the gadgets, wonder whether they look as cool as they feel and plan to test it at nightclubs.
punchline: The product's problem is not that people are hesitant to be first but that nobody wants it at all, while the employees wearing the gadgets are blissfully unaware of how dorky they look.
summary: A company blames hesitant early adopters for sluggish wearable gadget sales, though the real issue is that no one wants them and the gadget-clad employees only imagine they look cool.

title: Boss Blames Personal Problems, Not Overwork

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder why everyone is in a bad mood lately.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Maybe they have personal problems.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How could they have time for personal problems when I work them 70 hours a week?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Then I don't know what it is.

setting: The Boss's office, with Catbert sitting on the desk
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, wonders aloud why everyone at work is in a bad mood. Catbert, the evil HR director, suggests personal problems, but the Boss dismisses that because he works his staff 70 hours a week. Catbert then says he has no idea what the cause could be.
punchline: The Boss cannot see that making his employees work 70-hour weeks is the obvious cause of their bad mood, and Catbert sarcastically feigns ignorance rather than say so.
summary: A clueless manager puzzles over his team's sour attitude while casually admitting to the punishing schedule he imposes on them.

file: 2014/2014-11-02_obliviousness_time management_touch_touching_touching paper_turn off phone_ignore email_one touch_salad tongs_on etouch_interupted.gif
title: Touch Each Paper Only Once

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The key to good time management is touching each piece of paper once.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I can only touch it once, I'd better do it right.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll need to make sure I don't get interrupted after the first touch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Turn off my phone, close my door, and ignore email.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, here goes one touch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ugh. This will take an hour and I only have ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make a copy, throw away the original, and don't let me touch the copy until I have an hour in my schedule.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder if I'm allowed to use salad tongs.

situation: The Boss adopts a rule that he may touch each piece of paper only once, so he obsessively plans how to protect that single touch from interruptions. When he finally picks up a document and realizes it will take an hour to deal with, he has an assistant copy it and hide the copy from him until his schedule opens up. He ends by wondering whether handling paper with salad tongs would count as not touching it.
punchline: The Boss takes a time-management slogan so literally that he invents absurd workarounds, like salad tongs, to avoid ever doing the work.
summary: A manager misreads a productivity tip so literally that he builds elaborate rituals and loopholes around a single touch of paper instead of getting anything done.

file: 2014/2014-09-14_bad psoture_body language_comaplints_communication style_contact the dead_criticism_fear_fengshui_gut feeling_job review_psychic_rationality_threatening_whiny babies.gif
title: Alice Mocks Vague Communication Complaints

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, people are uncomfortable with your communication style.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did someone complain?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. I'm picking it up in their body language.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So... People have bad posture and that means I don't say things right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Call it a gut feeling.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ohhhh. That sounds rational.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let's toss some feng shui into the equation and maybe get a psychic to contact the dead to see what they say about me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Or maybe everyone could stop being whiny babies!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, wait, I see it now.

situation: The Boss tells Alice during a review that people are uncomfortable with her communication style, but admits no one actually complained. He is only inferring it from body language and a gut feeling. Alice sarcastically suggests adding feng shui and a psychic, then shouts at him, which makes him suddenly agree with the criticism.
punchline: Alice's outburst at the end proves the Boss's baseless criticism right, so he claims to see the problem only after she yells at him.
summary: A manager criticizes an employee based on nothing but a hunch, and her furious rant gives him the evidence he lacked.

title: Driven Google Hire Telecommuting Pun

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a guy who worked at Google because he said he was driven.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because they have free bus service?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Has he shown up for work yet?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I thought he was telecom-muting.

situation: The Boss explains that he hired a former Google employee because the man claimed to be driven. Dilbert sarcastically guesses the man only means Google's free commuter bus service, then asks whether the new hire has actually shown up. The Boss, unaware of the problem, says he thought the man was telecommuting.
punchline: The Boss mistook a claim of being 'driven' for ambition when it only meant being bussed to work, and he is so clueless that he doesn't notice the new hire has never turned up.
summary: A gullible manager hires someone on the strength of a Google resume and a vague boast, then cannot say whether the new employee has ever arrived.

file: 2014/2014-05-24_customer survey_flying car_idiots_new software_people who buy_survey_cafe_coffee cup.gif
title: Customers Want a Flying Car

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have the results of our customer survey.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The new software feature they want most is "flying car."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you survey any people who aren't idiots?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I only surveyed people who buy from us.

situation: Dilbert brings the Boss the results of a customer survey. The most requested new software feature turns out to be a flying car, so the Boss asks whether any non-idiots were surveyed. Dilbert replies that he only surveyed people who buy from the company.
punchline: By saying he only surveyed people who buy from the company, Dilbert implies that the company's customers are idiots.
summary: A survey of paying customers produces an absurd feature request, prompting a deadpan insult at the people who keep the business running.

title: Faking Workaholism for Company-Paid Rehab

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm pretending to be a workaholic so the company will pay for rehab.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Waaaa!!! I am working too hard! It is starting to affect my health!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That seemed a bit dramatic.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Here we go with blaming the victim.

setting: Office break area, with employees holding coffee mugs
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert he is pretending to be a workaholic so the company will pay for his rehab. He then loudly wails about working too hard and harming his health, drawing the attention of The Boss. The Boss says the outburst seemed overly dramatic, and the coworker accuses him of blaming the victim.
punchline: The coworker is staging a fake workaholic breakdown to get free rehab, and when the boss doubts him he indignantly plays the victim card, proving the act works.
summary: An employee stages a theatrical complaint about overwork to get his employer to fund treatment, then acts wounded when his boss is skeptical.

title: Rat Hugs Without Relationship Hassle

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I want the health benefits of hugging without the hassle of a relationship.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This rat is like a patch that increases my oxytocin levels.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought we were in love.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's your oxytocin talking.

situation: Wally stands holding a coffee mug with Ratbert clinging to his shoulder, explaining that he wants the health benefits of hugging without having to be in a relationship. He describes the rat as a patch that boosts his oxytocin. Dilbert, apparently hugged by the rat too, says he thought they were in love, and Wally dismisses it as just the hormone.
punchline: Wally treats affection as a purely chemical dose, so when Dilbert mistakes the oxytocin rush for real love, Wally coldly dismisses it as just hormones talking.
summary: Wally uses a clingy rat as a low-commitment source of hugging benefits and brushes off Dilbert's sudden feelings as a hormone effect.

file: 2014/2014-10-23_blackmail_morality_morals_angel investor_pantless_drunk_photos_phone camera_million dollar seed investment_tie score.gif
title: Blackmailing the Pantless Angel Investor

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I met with that angel investor at his house and he answered the door pantless and drunk.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: So I snapped a few photos with my phone and secured a million-dollar seed investment.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Was that wrong?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's call it a tie.

situation: Tina tells Dilbert that she visited an angel investor at his home and found him pantless and drunk. She took photos with her phone and used them to secure a million-dollar seed investment. She asks whether that was wrong, and Dilbert gives a noncommittal answer.
punchline: Dilbert's 'let's call it a tie' implies that the investor's behavior and Tina's blackmail are equally unethical, so neither side is morally better.
summary: A coworker admits she funded her startup by photographing a drunken, trouserless investor, and her colleague declares the ethics a draw.

title: Puppet That Ate a Dictionary

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What can I do to help you operationalize our strategy?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could stop talking like a puppet that ate a dictionary.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know how analogies work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm counting on that.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert what he can do to help operationalize the strategy. Dilbert tells him he could stop talking like a puppet that ate a dictionary, an insult built on an analogy. The Boss responds that he doesn't know how analogies work, and Dilbert says he is counting on that.
punchline: Dilbert insults the Boss's jargon-heavy speech with an analogy, and the Boss's confusion about analogies means he doesn't realise he has just been insulted.
summary: A manager's buzzword-laden offer of help draws a sarcastic comparison from an employee who is relying on his boss being too clueless to catch it.

file: 2014/2014-09-22_cognitive control_hiring_job interview_self control_temptation_prediction of success_donut_laptop_bottle vodka_resist.gif
title: Interview Temptation Test With Vodka

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your experience is impressive, but a better predictor of success is your cognitive control.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I will leave you for ten minutes with a donut, a laptop full of inappropriate videos, and a bottle of vodka. Try to resist them.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Yee-ha! Mmm-mm!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Do not go in there.

setting: Human resources interview room and the hallway outside it
situation: Catbert, acting as an HR interviewer, tells a job candidate that cognitive control predicts success better than experience. He leaves the candidate alone with a donut, a laptop of inappropriate videos, and a bottle of vodka to test his self-restraint. The candidate is heard whooping and enjoying himself, and Catbert warns Dilbert not to go into the room.
punchline: The candidate failed the self-control test spectacularly, and the cheerful sounds from the room show he gave in to every temptation, so Catbert warns others away.
summary: An HR cat sets up a temptation trap for a job applicant, who clearly fails it in riotous fashion.

file: 2014/2014-11-16_criticism_frankness_goals_honesty_managers_root cause_bad parenting_pointy headed boos_underlings_rapidly evolving nature_talented employee_boss life story.gif
title: Dilbert Traces Boss's Root Cause

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You haven't achieved any of your goals for the year. What is up with that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want an explanation that goes back to the root cause?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Of course.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The problem started years ago, when two idiots unwisely created a third, smaller idiot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They compounded their mistake with bad parenting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The toddler ate candy and sniffed wet paint until he became a Pointy-Headed Boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The Pointy-Headed Boss set goals for his underlings that ignored the rapidly evolving nature of the industry.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then he got angry at his most talented employee for giving an accurate answer to a question.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hate you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nothing could halt the downward spiral.

situation: The Boss scolds Dilbert for missing all his yearly goals. When the Boss asks for an explanation that goes back to the root cause, Dilbert narrates the Boss's own life story, from his parents to his childhood to his bad management and his anger at honest answers.
punchline: Dilbert uses the requested root-cause analysis to reveal that the real cause of the failure is the Boss himself, and the Boss reacts by getting angry, proving Dilbert's point.
summary: Invited to dig into why goals were missed, an employee traces the whole problem back to his manager's upbringing and bad decisions.

title: Vacation Request Backfires Into Overwork

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I take my vacation next week?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fine. Just work twice as hard this week to get everything done before you leave.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In that case, I prefer not taking a vacation at all.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's starting to look as if nothing can make you happy.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for permission to take a vacation next week. The boss agrees only on the condition that Dilbert work twice as hard this week to finish everything before leaving. Dilbert decides he would rather skip the vacation, and the boss concludes that Dilbert simply can't be pleased.
punchline: The boss turns a granted vacation into a burden and then blames the employee for being unhappy, ignoring that his own unreasonable condition caused the problem.
summary: A manager approves time off but attaches a punishing workload, then complains that his employee is impossible to satisfy when the offer is declined.

file: 2014/2014-03-27_efficiency experts_stress_consultant_booze muhkidney_travel work_unhealthy food_total failure_sleepless nights_power point slides_business.gif
title: Sleepless Consultant Admits Own Failure

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Consultant from Booze Muhkidney

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: All I do is travel, work, and eat unhealthy food.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I'm a total failure at managing my own life, and yet people hire me for business advice.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I haven't slept since October.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was told there would be PowerPoint slides.

setting: Conference room with a long table
situation: A consultant from the firm Booze Muhkidney sits across the table from Dilbert and confesses that his own life is a mess: constant travel, overwork, bad food, and no sleep since October. Dilbert, unmoved by the confession, only wants to know where the promised PowerPoint slides are.
punchline: Dilbert ignores the consultant's obvious breakdown and cares only about getting the standard consultant deliverable, showing how little anyone values the actual advice.
summary: A worn-out consultant unloads his personal troubles on a client who simply wants the slide deck he was promised.

file: 2014/2014-08-24_programming skills_next hire_python_java_php_solve_ignorance problems_gap in knowledge_string theory_graviton.gif
title: Boss Thinks Lists Equal Knowledge

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What programming skills should I be looking for in our next hire?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: jQuery, Ruby, HTML5, Python, Java, PHP, and, of course, C++.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you could write those down.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That should totally solve your ignorance problem.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are there any other gaps in your knowledge that I can fix by writing things down?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How about string theory? I can explain that in a few words.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Graviton... supersymmetry... perturbation... M-theory.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know string theory now.

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert which programming skills to look for in a new hire, then thinks that having them written down fixes his own ignorance. Dilbert sarcastically asks what other knowledge gaps can be fixed by writing things down, and recites a handful of string theory buzzwords, after which the Boss believes he now understands string theory.
punchline: The Boss believes a list of buzzwords is the same as understanding a subject, so Dilbert's sarcastic offer to 'fix' his ignorance with keywords convinces him he has mastered string theory.
summary: A manager who knows nothing about technical hiring thinks a written list of terms equals expertise, and walks away convinced he has learned physics after hearing four jargon words.

title: Nobody Praises the Previous Engineer's Code

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The project I inherited has weak code. I need to rewrite it from scratch.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Will there ever be an engineer who says, "That last guy did a great job. Let's keep all of it"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm hoping the idiot you hire to replace me says that.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the project he inherited has weak code and that he wants to rewrite it from scratch. The Boss wonders aloud whether any engineer will ever praise their predecessor's work and keep it. Dilbert replies that he hopes his own eventual replacement, whom he calls an idiot, will say exactly that about his code.
punchline: Dilbert admits that the only engineer who would approve of his code is one he considers an idiot, revealing that every engineer disparages predecessors' work and expects the same fate.
summary: An engineer who wants to scrap his predecessor's code is asked by his manager why nobody ever approves of earlier work, and he answers that only a fool would admire his own.

title: Everyone Is a Team Member, Except

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I dislike the words "boss" and "employee." From now on, we are all "team members."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll be the team member that makes the decisions and gets paid the most. You'll be the team members I punish when things go wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But otherwise we are all equal?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whoa! Calm down, Spartacus.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss announces at a meeting that the terms "boss" and "employee" are being abandoned in favor of "team members." He then clarifies that he will still make all decisions, earn the most money, and punish the others when things go wrong. When Dilbert asks whether they are otherwise equal, the Boss mocks him for getting carried away.
punchline: Renaming bosses and employees as "team members" changes nothing about the power and pay imbalance, and the Boss ridicules anyone who expects real equality.
summary: A manager rebrands his staff as equals in name only while keeping all authority, money, and blame-assigning for himself.

title: Consultant Recommends Most Profitable Solution

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our consultant has recommended a company-wide transformation to make us more competitive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it a coincidence that consultants always recommend solutions that pay their firms the most?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How would I know?

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I'll look into that for you.

situation: The Boss announces that a consultant has recommended a company-wide transformation. Dilbert asks whether it is a coincidence that consultants always recommend whatever pays their own firms the most. The Boss shrugs it off, and the consultant, who is sitting right there, offers to investigate the question himself.
punchline: Asking the consultant to investigate his own conflict of interest guarantees the conflict will never be examined honestly.
summary: A manager's pricey overhaul plan draws a pointed question about consultant motives, and the consultant in question volunteers to look into it himself.

title: Mourning the Wrong Dead Colleague

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We mourn the untimely passing of our beloved colleague, Fred. We will never forget him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was Ted, not Fred.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Was he beloved?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't remember. It was like a week ago.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss, seen from behind in the foreground, solemnly announces the death of a colleague and promises everyone will never forget him. Dilbert corrects him that the deceased was named Ted, not Fred. The Boss asks if Ted was even beloved, and Wally says he can't remember because Ted died about a week ago.
punchline: The company's tribute claims they will never forget the dead colleague, yet within a week nobody even remembers his name or whether anyone liked him.
summary: A boss gives a heartfelt eulogy for a deceased coworker but gets his name wrong, and the staff admit they have already forgotten the man.

title: Exit Interview Victory Lap Denied

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Exit interview

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Heh-heh. I am going to speak my mind and dump on everyone.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give me your I.D. and get out. If anyone wanted your opinion I would have paid you enough to stay.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: So much for my victory lap.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You forgot your mug!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Zip!

setting: Conference room during an exit interview
situation: A departing employee sits down for his exit interview, smugly planning to unload all his criticisms on the company. The boss cuts him off immediately, demands his ID and tells him to leave. The boss then throws the employee's forgotten coffee mug after him as he walks out.
punchline: The employee's plan to vent his grievances is shot down because the company never valued his opinion enough to pay him well, and he gets no dramatic exit, just a mug thrown at him.
summary: A quitting worker eager to air his grievances is instantly dismissed by a boss who has no interest in hearing them.

file: 2014/2014-10-12_budgets_deadlines_logic_obliviousness_projects_reasoning_software upgrade_rolled out_estimated finish date_same way_failure_on budget.gif
title: Repeating Failed Methods, Expecting Success

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: The software upgrade will be written and rolled out in three months.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Has any project of this complexity ever been completed by the estimated finish date?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Not yet. We're confident we'll be the first.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that because you're doing things differently from all of those who went before and failed?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: No. We're doing things exactly the same way as the people who failed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you see what I'm getting at?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: No, not really.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: And we expect to be on budget.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Snork!

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: A manager announces a software upgrade will be finished in three months. Dilbert asks whether any similar project has ever finished on time, and the manager admits none has but insists his team will be the first, even though they are using the same methods as those who failed. Dilbert tries to point out the flaw and the manager doesn't get it.
punchline: The manager confidently expects success and on-budget delivery while using the same approach that failed for everyone else, and he is completely oblivious to the contradiction, even as a coworker snorts with laughter.
summary: A confident manager promises a quick, on-budget software rollout using the very same methods that doomed every earlier attempt, and he can't see the flaw in his reasoning.

title: Dilbert Out-Learns His Financial Advisor

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Financial advisor

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You kept me waiting in the lobby for five minutes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I used that time to learn everything that matters in the field of personal investing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you know that you don't know much?

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: I did not know that.

situation: Dilbert arrives for an appointment and complains that the financial advisor kept him waiting in the lobby for five minutes. He says he used the time to learn everything that matters about personal investing on his phone. He then tells the advisor that the advisor doesn't know much, and the advisor admits he didn't know that.
punchline: Dilbert learned more about investing from a five-minute phone search than the supposed professional knows, exposing the advisor's ignorance, and the advisor can only admit it.
summary: A client uses a short wait to research investing on his phone and discovers he knows more than the professional he came to hire.

file: 2014/2014-01-05_happiness_new philosophy_live for today_motto_avoid starving tomorrow_ruin every minute_living in past_gustave_traded beaver pelts_psychology.gif
title: Wally Dismantles Asok's Life Philosophy

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm trying out a new philosophy for my life.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My new motto is "Live for today."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you live for today, how do you avoid starving tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you do one little thing wrong today, it could ruin every minute of the rest of your life.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: So... I should live for the future?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, that would ruin today.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I recommend living for the past.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My past was no fun.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Pretend you were someone else.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My philosophy is that my name was Gustav and I traded beaver pelts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop ruining my present.

situation: Asok announces he is adopting a new life philosophy of living for today. Wally, coffee mug in hand, picks apart each time frame, saying that today, the future and the past could all be ruined, then suggests Asok pretend to be someone else. Asok adopts a fantasy past as a fur trader named Gustav, which annoys Dilbert.
punchline: Wally's cynical advice leads Asok to invent an absurd past life as Gustav the beaver pelt trader, which just irritates Dilbert and ruins his present.
summary: A young employee's search for a life motto is deflated by a coworker who finds fault with the present, future and past alike, ending with an absurd invented identity.

title: Learning to Look Busy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now that we're organized as a holacracy, I need to learn how to look busy like the rest of you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Try walking into people's cubicles without an invitation and babbling about things they don't care about.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I should write this down.

situation: The Boss stands beside a seated coworker's desk and says that, now the company is organized as a holacracy, he needs to learn how to look busy. The coworker, holding a coffee mug, advises him to barge into cubicles uninvited and babble about irrelevant things. The Boss earnestly decides to write the advice down.
punchline: The Boss's habit of interrupting people and rambling pointlessly is described as the way to look busy, and he fails to realize he already does it and treats it as new advice.
summary: A manager asks a worker how to appear busy under a new flat organizational structure and is told to do exactly what he already does to everyone.

title: Reinstall Everything to Read Document

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I couldn't open the document you sent with your project update.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Try erasing your hard disk and reinstalling the operating system.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I guess I don't need it that badly.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: After all the work I put into making that document?

situation: The Boss complains that he couldn't open the document Wally attached to his project update. Wally, holding his coffee mug, deadpans that the fix is to wipe his hard disk and reinstall the operating system. The Boss gives up on reading it, and Wally acts offended that his hard work will go unread.
punchline: Wally offers an absurdly extreme tech-support fix as a way to avoid helping, then feigns hurt feelings when the Boss reasonably abandons the document.
summary: A manager can't open an attached file, and his lazy employee suggests a ridiculously drastic remedy before sulking that his effort is being ignored.

title: Can't Shake Hands and Remember Names

transcript.speaker: Randy
transcript.text: Hi. I'm Randy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't memorize names and shake hands at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Randy
transcript.text: It's Randy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't even bother. Seriously.

situation: A coworker named Randy introduces himself to Dilbert and offers a handshake. Dilbert claims he can't memorize a name while shaking hands, then shakes anyway as Randy repeats his name. Dilbert tells him not to bother, since the name won't be retained.
punchline: Dilbert's absurd excuse for forgetting names is undercut by the fact that he has no intention of remembering Randy's name at all, and he says so bluntly.
summary: A man introduces himself and tries a handshake, but Dilbert says his brain can't handle both tasks and tells him not to waste his breath.

title: Too Many Projects To Work

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Three months. That's how long I have been waiting for you to do your part of the project.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Perhaps you don't realize how many projects I'm on.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Have you done any work for the other projects?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: That would defeat the point of having multiple projects.

situation: A woman complains that she has waited three months for her colleague to finish his part of a shared project. He holds a coffee mug and says she doesn't realize how many projects he is on. She asks whether he has done any work on the other projects, and he replies that doing so would defeat the point of having multiple projects.
punchline: The man treats being assigned to many projects as a way to avoid doing any work on any of them, so actually doing work would ruin the purpose.
summary: A coworker uses an overloaded project list as cover for never delivering anything, and admits that working on them would spoil the arrangement.

file: 2014/2014-07-12_competition (psychology)_embarrassed_dress the same_everyday_reserve of willpower_fashion decisions_work_wrote and app_importance of routine.gif
title: Dilbert Out-Routines Fashion-Conscious Coworker

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you ever feel embarrassed that you dress the same way every day?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you ever feel embarrassed that you don't understand the importance of routine in managing your limited reserve of willpower?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I made 75 fashion decisions before breakfast.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wrote an app.

situation: A female coworker with a bob haircut mocks Dilbert for wearing the same outfit every day. Dilbert shrugs it off, and she then lectures him about routines conserving willpower. She reveals she spent her morning making dozens of fashion choices, while Dilbert counters that he used his saved energy to write an app.
punchline: By not wasting willpower on clothing choices, Dilbert accomplished something productive while his critic exhausted her mental energy on outfits, proving her own argument against her.
summary: A coworker who agonizes over her wardrobe is outdone by Dilbert, whose uniform routine left him energy to build software.

file: 2014/2014-08-03_venture capitalists_reputation of the angel_angel investors_skill of engineers_huge raise_big chicken.gif
title: Dilbert's Bluff Gets Called

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you know what venture capitalists care about when they make investment decisions?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They care about the reputation of the angel investors who already put money in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you know what the angel investors care about?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They care about the skill of the engineers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Therefore, you should give me a huge raise or else I'll quit and do my own start-up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go ahead, you big chicken.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're going to die poor! Ha ha ha!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was harsh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And yet you didn't resign. Any more questions?

setting: Office, Dilbert and the Boss talking in the Boss's workspace
situation: Dilbert walks the Boss through a chain of logic about how venture capitalists and angel investors value engineering skill, then demands a huge raise or he'll quit and found a start-up. The Boss calls his bluff and mocks him, predicting he'll die poor.
punchline: Dilbert's threat to quit is empty because he clearly won't leave his safe job, and the Boss knows it and uses that to shut down the negotiation.
summary: An engineer's carefully argued raise demand collapses when his manager dares him to quit and he doesn't.

file: 2014/2014-05-06_charitable organizations_corporate charity_deception_no boss fooled_teaching interview techniques_trained umemployed_work ethic_job skill.gif
title: Charity Teaches Unemployed to Look Busy

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Last week, I did my corporate charity work by teaching unemployed people how to interview for jobs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't they also need job skills?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Nah. I taught them how to look busy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No boss will be fooled by that.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you believe I trained unemployed people last week?

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Wally tells his colleagues that his corporate charity work involved coaching unemployed people on interviewing. When the Boss asks about job skills, Wally reveals he only taught them to look busy. The Boss says no boss would be fooled, and Wally slyly asks whether the Boss even believes he did any training at all.
punchline: Wally's charity work is itself a fake: he has fooled the Boss with the very trick of appearing productive that he claims to have taught.
summary: A slacker's account of his volunteer work turns out to be an elaborate demonstration of the deception he supposedly taught.

title: Fattening Coworkers With Muffins Scheme

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I brought you some muffins so I won't need to watch my weight.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: If I fatten up the people around me, I'll look good even if I gain a few pounds.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Won't that make you look mean?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: In phase two, I'll also make you angrier than me.

situation: Carol offers her coworkers a box of muffins, including Dilbert and Wally, who are holding coffee mugs. She explains that she is deliberately fattening up the people around her so she will look slim by comparison. When Dilbert points out this might make her seem mean, she reveals a second phase of making them angrier than she is.
punchline: Carol's scheme to look better by comparison is so petty and calculating that she plans to also relativize her bad temper by making everyone else angrier.
summary: A coworker hands out baked treats as part of a scheme to make herself look better compared with everyone nearby, and her plan has a further sinister stage.

title: Lying By Omission About Bugs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When you talk to customers, stop mentioning our software bugs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I lie?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, no. I just need you to present the information that is good for us and leave out the rest.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lie by omission?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's better if we don't label it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I use my real name?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to stop telling customers about the software's bugs. When Dilbert asks if he's being told to lie, the Boss rephrases it as presenting only favorable information. Dilbert calls it lying by omission, and the Boss says it's better not to label it.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that if he is being asked to deceive customers without admitting it, he might as well do it under a fake name since the Boss wants no accountability for the dishonesty.
summary: A manager wants his employee to hide product defects from buyers while refusing to call it deception, and the employee wryly asks whether he should also hide his identity.

title: Strangling Over Product Prototype Questions

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Inexperienced guy

transcript.speaker: Inexperienced Guy
transcript.text: Can you answer some questions about our product prototype?

transcript.speaker: Woman with Big Hair
transcript.text: No, but I would be happy to strangle you with your own lanyard and put your corpse in my boss's Escalade to frame him for the crime.

transcript.speaker: Inexperienced Guy
transcript.text: That scenario is alarmingly specific.

transcript.speaker: Woman with Big Hair
transcript.text: For this sort of thing, premeditated is the way to go.

situation: A junior employee approaches a coworker with big hair to ask questions about a product prototype. She responds by calmly describing how she would strangle him with his lanyard and frame her boss for the murder. The young man is unnerved by how detailed the plan is, and she explains that careful planning is the way to go.
punchline: Her annoyance at being interrupted is so intense that she has already worked out a detailed, premeditated murder plan, and she is matter-of-fact about it.
summary: A coworker responds to a newbie's request for help by calmly outlining an elaborate plot to kill him and pin it on her boss.

title: Tube Clothes Simplify Daily Decisions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I only wear tube clothes now because it reduces my number of daily decisions.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You mean decisions such as... where to go on a date?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because I don't see that coming up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm still fine-tuning the system.

situation: Dilbert, wearing a shapeless tube-like garment, tells a female coworker holding a coffee cup that he wears tube clothes to reduce his daily decisions. She asks whether that includes deciding where to go on a date. He replies that the question never comes up, then says he is still fine-tuning his system.
punchline: Dilbert's wardrobe 'system' eliminates decisions, including dating, because his unflattering outfit guarantees he will never get a date, which he awkwardly passes off as a work in progress.
summary: A man in a shapeless garment boasts of streamlined choices, only to be reminded that his look has also eliminated his love life.

title: Daddy's Advice: Pass the Problem Along

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm hitting a snag with this RFP because our products don't do what they need.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Should I give up and accept failure or lie about our features and transfer the problem to them?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My daddy used to say it isn't a problem if you can give it to someone else.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then he drove you to school?

situation: Asok tells Dilbert he is stuck on a request for proposal because his company's products can't meet the customer's needs. He considers either admitting failure or lying about the features so the customer inherits the problem. He cites his father's saying that a problem disappears if you hand it to someone else, and Dilbert replies by asking if his father then drove him to school.
punchline: Dilbert's question implies that the father's attitude of passing off problems extended even to the job of driving his child to school, which exposes how selfish and irresponsible the philosophy is.
summary: A junior employee ponders lying to win a bid and quotes his father's philosophy of offloading problems, and a coworker mockingly turns that philosophy on the father's parenting.

file: 2014/2014-02-25_business ethics_obliviousness_million units_customers happy_our goals_their goals_this quarter.gif
title: Our Goals Versus Customer Goals

transcript.text: Our goal is to ship a million units this quarter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do we have any goals that involve making customers happy?

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: I'm talking about OUR goals, not THEIR goals.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Totally different.

situation: At a meeting, a manager announces the goal of shipping a million units this quarter. Dilbert asks whether any goals involve making customers happy. The manager dismisses the question, saying he means the company's goals, not the customers' goals, and the Boss agrees that they are totally different.
punchline: Management treats customer happiness as a completely separate matter from the company's goals, revealing that customer satisfaction is not a priority at all.
summary: A sales target is announced, and when someone raises customer happiness, management waves it off as belonging to someone else's agenda.

file: 2014/2014-10-27_advertising_deception_graphic design_graphic designers_marketing_a_b testing_design options_skill set_random behavior_talent_secrets_business.gif
title: A-B Testing Exposes Designer's Random Talent

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Graphic Designer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll do some A-B testing with the design options you provided.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Interestingly, the fact that you can't predict which design will perform best means your skill set is mostly random behavior that you package as talent.

transcript.speaker: Graphic Designer
transcript.text: This works better if I'm the only one who knows that.

He then points out that because the designer cannot predict which design will win, the designer's skill is really just random output presented as talent. The designer responds that this only works if nobody else realizes it.
punchline: The designer admits his expertise is essentially luck, and that the illusion of talent only holds up while nobody examines it closely.
summary: A designer is bluntly told that his inability to forecast winning designs reveals his craft to be mostly chance dressed up as skill.

file: 2014/2014-03-30_gut in charge_gut instinct_ignoring certain people_key to success_morse code_never right_thinking_wants a sandwhich.gif

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if they're right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They aren't right!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really? Other people are never right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have to trust your gut!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

file: 2014/2014-01-15_competition (psychology)_inventions_space flight_elon musk_space hsips_electric cars_electric rocket_robots_colonize_planet_power cord.gif
title: Electric Rocket Needs a Power Cord

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.text: Which planet should we do first?

situation: The Boss announces he wants to outdo Elon Musk in vision and orders Dilbert to build an electric rocket ship full of robots to colonize other worlds. Dilbert asks which planet to target first, and the Boss answers that it depends on the length of the power cord.
punchline: The Boss's supposedly visionary plan is undermined by his naive assumption that an electric rocket would be plugged in with a cord, so its range is limited by the cable length.
summary: A boss determined to out-dream a famous tech billionaire demands an electric spaceship, then reveals he expects it to run on an extension cord.

transcript.text: Is there a budget for this impossible project?

transcript.speaker: The Boss

When Dilbert asks a basic question about the budget, the Boss accuses him of needing micromanagement and complains that Dilbert has ruined his hands-off leadership.
punchline: The Boss claims to be a hands-off leader but treats any reasonable question about an impossible assignment as neediness that forces him to get involved.
summary: A manager who prides himself on staying out of the way blames his employee for dragging him back in after assigning a physically impossible task.

file: 2014/2014-06-09_deception_work ethic_huge losses_stock up_big raise_similar system_lowering expectations_employee of the year_job perfromance.gif
title: Lowering Expectations to Win Raise

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We announced huge losses, but analysts thought it would be even worse, so our stock went up.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm using a similar system to get a big raise. For years I've been lowering everyone's expectations of my performance.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Next I'll...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I made a phone call today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Employee of the year!

setting: Office break area and the boss's office
situation: Dilbert holds a coffee mug while a balding coworker explains that a company's stock rose despite announced losses because analysts expected worse. The coworker says he is using the same trick for a raise by steadily lowering everyone's expectations of his performance over many years. In the final panel he reports that he made a phone call, and the boss, thrilled, declares him employee of the year.
punchline: The coworker's long campaign of being useless has set the bar so low that a single phone call looks like heroic achievement.
summary: A slacker reveals he has spent years making everyone expect nothing from him so that the smallest effort will look like outstanding work.

file: 2014/2014-04-22_managers & supervisors_travel budget freeze_technical problems_fiancail targets_satisfying customers_sounds bad_said outloud_business.gif
title: Budget Targets Beat Customer Satisfaction

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need an exception to the travel budget freeze so I can fix an important customer's technical problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, because arbitrary financial targets are more important than satisfying customers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wait... Why does that sound bad when I say it out loud?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If it makes you feel better, I wasn't listening.

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss for an exception to the travel budget freeze so he can go fix an important customer's technical problem. The Boss refuses, stating that arbitrary financial targets matter more than customer satisfaction, then belatedly realizes how that sounds. Dilbert deadpans that he wasn't listening.
punchline: The Boss blurts out his twisted priorities and only realizes how bad they sound after saying them aloud, and Dilbert's sarcastic reply offers him no real comfort.
summary: A manager denies a travel request to help a customer, then stumbles over the absurdity of his own reasoning when he hears it spoken.

title: Robot Boss Threatens Replacement, Communicates Well

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Temporary robot boss

transcript.speaker: Robot Boss
transcript.text: I have come to micromanage you.

transcript.speaker: Robot Boss
transcript.text: But only until I replace you with a robot and turn you into furniture.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: On the plus side, he has a plan and he communicates well.

situation: A temporary robot boss, holding a coffee mug, announces to Dilbert that he has come to micromanage him. He then adds that he will eventually replace Dilbert with a robot and turn him into furniture. Dilbert later tells a bald coworker that, on the plus side, the robot boss has a plan and communicates well.
punchline: Dilbert is so used to incompetent human managers that a boss who threatens to turn him into furniture still seems like an improvement because he has a plan and communicates clearly.
summary: A menacing mechanical supervisor lays out his grim intentions, and the employee finds the clarity oddly refreshing compared with usual management.

file: 2014/2014-02-18_ignorance (knowledge)_sleeping & waking up_five hours of sleep_sleep deprivation_lowers intelligence_1000% raise.gif
title: Sleep-Deprived Boss Requests Thousand Percent Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm training myself to get by on five hours of sleep per night.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Studies show that sleep deprivation lowers your functional intelligence.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No it not be doesn't.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can I have a thousand percent raise?

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, brags to Alice that he is training himself to live on five hours of sleep a night. Alice calmly points out that studies show sleep deprivation lowers intelligence. He garbles his denial, and she takes advantage by asking for a thousand percent raise.
punchline: The Boss's garbled, nonsensical denial proves Alice's point about sleep deprivation, and she exploits his impaired state to ask for an absurd raise.
summary: A boss proudly cuts back on sleep, and his coworker uses his scrambled thinking to try to extract an outrageous pay increase.

file: 2014/2014-01-02_managers & supervisors_public speaking_heros journey_power point_pointed haired monster_business.gif
title: Hero's Journey PowerPoint, Boss as Monster

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Experts say you should format your presentation like a "hero's journey."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Eventually, the plucky engineer finished his PowerPoint slides despite interference from a pointy-haired monster."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Experts never warn you about that part.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that experts recommend structuring a presentation like a hero's journey. Dilbert starts writing his slides as a story, narrating a plucky engineer whose work is hindered by a pointy-haired monster, while the Boss hovers over his shoulder. The Boss walks away, oblivious that he is the monster in the story.
punchline: The Boss fails to recognize that he himself is the pointy-haired monster in Dilbert's hero's journey, and complains that experts never mention that hurdle.
summary: Asked to structure a presentation as an epic quest, an engineer casts his meddling manager as the villain, and the manager misses the point entirely.

file: 2014/2014-02-21_balanced_hiding in plain sight_life balance_rewarding work_so genius_work ethic_secret to rewarding life_learning secrets.gif
title: Work-Life Balance Through Nothing

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The secret to having a rewarding work-life balance is to have no life.

transcript.text: Then it's easy to keep things balanced by doing no work.

transcript.text: So simple, and yet, so genius.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It was hiding in plain sight.

setting: Office, with Wally holding his coffee mug
situation: Wally, coffee mug in hand, explains to Dilbert his secret for a rewarding work-life balance. He says you should have no life, and then you can balance that by doing no work. Dilbert is impressed and calls the idea genius, while Wally calmly sips his coffee.
punchline: Wally's 'balance' is achieved by zeroing out both sides of the equation, which neatly justifies his laziness as a clever life philosophy.
summary: A coffee-sipping slacker presents his own twisted formula for harmony between career and personal life, and a coworker admires it.

title: Distracted By Phones Mid-Conversation

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Studies say people are losing their ability to focus because of all the digital distractions.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Sorry, what?

transcript.text: Hold on...

transcript.text: What were you saying?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: Two coworkers stand talking while holding coffee mugs and phones. One mentions studies about people losing focus due to digital distractions, but gets sidetracked by his phone beeping. When asked to repeat himself, he has already forgotten what he was saying.
punchline: The man lecturing about lost focus gets distracted by his own phone mid-sentence and forgets his point, proving the study right.
summary: A man cites research on shrinking attention spans, then illustrates it perfectly when his phone chimes and he loses his train of thought.

file: 2014/2014-05-04_inventions_thinking_product ideas_billion dollar ideas_unwilling_corporation_dumb person idea_pretend_drone that attacks_wooden screen phone.gif
title: Billion-Dollar Ideas Not for Free

transcript.text: Does anyone have any billion-dollar product ideas?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I had a billion-dollar idea, I would quit this job and start my own company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Only a dumb person would give you his best idea for free.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And the best idea from a dumb person is still dumb.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I am willing to give you some ideas that are too lame for my own use.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you at least pretend to suggest good ideas?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about a phone with a wooden screen?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How about a drone that attacks anyone who looks at it?

situation: The Boss asks a meeting for billion-dollar product ideas. Dilbert points out that anyone with such an idea would quit and start their own company rather than give it away for free, though he offers to share ideas too lame for his own use. When the Boss asks him to at least pretend to suggest good ideas, Dilbert and Wally offer absurd product concepts.
punchline: Having reasoned that any genuinely good idea would never be shared with the company, Dilbert and Wally respond to the Boss's request for pretend-good ideas with deliberately ridiculous inventions like a wooden-screen phone and an attack drone.
summary: A manager fishing for million-dollar inspiration gets a lecture on incentives and then a pair of intentionally worthless gadget proposals.

title: Boss Pre-Judges Dilbert's Great Idea

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a great idea!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What kind?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it the kind I scoff at, the kind I steal, or the kind that makes me double your workload?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It might be all of those.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sounds good so far.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he has a great idea. The boss asks which of three outcomes it will lead to: being scoffed at, being stolen, or increasing Dilbert's workload. Dilbert admits it could be all three, and the boss cheerfully says that sounds good.
punchline: The boss's only interest in an employee's idea is how it can be dismissed, taken as his own, or used to pile more work on the employee, so a guaranteed combination of all three is exactly what he wants.
summary: A manager sizes up an employee's brainstorm purely by the ways he can exploit it, and is delighted to learn it qualifies for every one.

file: 2014/2014-11-23_deception_holidays_laziness_trust_work ethic_telecommute_bring kid to work_work from home_distrust_corrodes motivation_toxic environment_ruin naps.gif
title: Telecommuting on Bring Your Kid Day

situation: Wally asks his boss for permission to telecommute on Bring Your Kid to Work day. summary: A lazy employee guilt-trips his manager into letting him skip the office for a family event, though he has no child and just wants undisturbed sleep.

title: Irrational Humans, Instantly Proven Right

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.text: Da-dee da-dum

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Dilbert sits at a table with Alice and announces that his stress has dropped since he realized all humans are irrational. Alice takes the remark as a personal insult and furiously declares she will hate him forever. Dilbert, now alone at the table, hums cheerfully, unbothered.
punchline: Alice's instant, over-the-top reaction proves Dilbert's point about human irrationality, and he stays happily calm because he expected it.
summary: A man's calming theory about human irrationality is confirmed on the spot by a colleague's furious overreaction.

punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that he ignores clear signs the 'package delivery' drones are really intended as weapons for extremists.
summary: A clueless manager hands off a drone project while brushing aside every sign that the client may be a terrorist group.

punchline: Dilbert's quip implies the Boss only sounds dumb when people actually understand what he means, and he claims that happens just once a week, a jab at how routinely foolish the Boss is.

title: Please Kill Me, Boss Wants Updates

situation: Dilbert tells Wally over coffee that he plans to have his brain preserved through cryonics so he can live forever in a robot body. The Boss interrupts to demand a status update about why Dilbert's previous status report was not updated. Dilbert, in despair, begs Wally to kill him, and Wally declines because a dead person could never repay the favor.
punchline: Dilbert is so miserable at the prospect of endless status updates that he begs to be killed, and Wally refuses on the cynical grounds that a favor to a dead man can never be repaid.
summary: A man dreaming of immortality as a robot is crushed by a bureaucratic demand for paperwork, only to be refused a mercy killing by a coworker who is strictly transactional.

file: 2014/2014-04-21_big business_money_obliviousness_travel budget_business travel_long term profitability_budget frozen.gif

transcript.text: Um...

situation: At a meeting, Dilbert announces that the travel budget has been frozen to hit this quarter's income estimates. Phil sarcastically asks whether the reason is that travel is worthless or that the company has stopped caring about long-term profitability. Dilbert answers by telling him to take as long as he needs to think, which leaves Phil at a loss.
punchline: Phil offers two damning explanations for the cut, and the speaker responds as if he had asked a sincere question, giving him time to answer instead of acknowledging that short-term earnings are being put ahead of the company's future.
summary: A sharp question about why travel spending was cut gets met with an offer of unlimited thinking time rather than any real answer.

title: Years of Bad Data, Finally Questioned

transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I said the data is totally accurate.

situation: The Boss, seated at his desk, asks Dilbert whether the data he supplied is correct. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, candidly admits he has been feeding the Boss wrong data for years because nobody ever asked. When the Boss reacts with 'What?', Dilbert quickly reverses and claims the data is totally accurate.
punchline: Dilbert reveals the Boss has never verified anything he's been given, then retreats to a blandly reassuring lie the moment the Boss reacts, showing how little scrutiny management applies to the data it relies on.
summary: After finally being questioned about his figures, an employee confesses years of bad reports, then smoothly pretends he said the opposite.

summary: A manager uses a wearable gadget to dissect every detail of an employee's behavior, right down to his urge to attack the manager.

summary: A lazy coworker dodges a request by blaming a colleague's criticism, then reacts to a gruesome threat purely in terms of his own sleep schedule.
