file: 2014/2014-05-30_efficiency experts_medicines_more motivated_competetive_safe and natural_side effects_psychopathy_improved dating life_needle_injection.gif
title: Boss Injects Dilbert With Motivation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I found a quick way to make you more motivated and competitive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know it's safe because it's all natural.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The only known side effects are psychopathy and an improved dating life.

situation: The Boss approaches Dilbert at his desk holding a syringe and announces he has found a quick way to make him more motivated and competitive. He injects Dilbert, claiming it is safe because it is natural. Dilbert is then transformed into a muscular, horned, devil-like figure, and the Boss cheerfully lists the side effects.
punchline: The Boss casually treats psychopathy as an acceptable side effect, offset by a better dating life, showing how management will pursue competitiveness at any human cost.
summary: A manager injects an employee with a so-called natural serum that turns him into a monstrous, cutthroat version of himself, and brushes off the side effects as trivial.

title: Co-CEO Duties Split Dangerously

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Co-CEOs

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's split the duties this way...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will be the CEO who attends boring meetings, and you can be more of a Richard Branson type who does dangerous publicity stunts.

transcript.speaker: Co-CEO
transcript.text: I love that idea.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And then there was one.

setting: Executive office, sitting across a desk
situation: Dogbert and a human executive are co-CEOs, and Dogbert proposes dividing the work. Dogbert takes the boring meetings while the other CEO gets the dangerous publicity stunts. The executive happily agrees, while Dogbert privately thinks that soon only one CEO will remain.
punchline: Dogbert is deliberately assigning the other co-CEO deadly stunts so he will die and Dogbert can become the sole CEO.
summary: A scheming dog arranges a job split that quietly sets his human partner up to be killed, leaving him in sole charge.

file: 2014/2014-02-08_discrimination_gays_ignorance (knowledge)_india_supreme court_nuclear arsenal_scientific knowledge_illegal to be gay_nuke_taj mahal_so gay.gif
title: Asok Misunderstands the Word Gay

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I can never return to India because the Supreme Court made it illegal to be gay there.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does it worry you that they have a nuclear arsenal and the scientific knowledge of inebriated astrologists?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They might nuke the Taj Mahal.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I know! That place is so gay, right?

setting: Office break area, both holding coffee mugs
situation: Asok tells Dilbert he can't go back to India because its Supreme Court has made being gay illegal. Dilbert responds by raising concerns about India's nuclear weapons and the shaky science behind its leaders. Asok agrees about the threat to the Taj Mahal, but uses 'gay' as a slang insult for the monument.
punchline: Asok, who just complained about anti-gay laws, immediately uses 'gay' as a slur for the Taj Mahal, showing he is oblivious to his own casual prejudice.
summary: A man laments a ruling criminalizing homosexuality in his homeland, then casually uses the word as a put-down for its most famous landmark.

title: Rewarding Employees Randomly Works

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you have any problems filling in for me while I was on vacation?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: It was hard at first. I couldn't tell who was lying about doing a spectacular job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why I reward them randomly.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I tried that and it did seem to settle them down.

situation: The Boss returns from vacation and asks the robot who filled in for him whether there were any problems. The robot says it was hard to tell which employees were lying about doing spectacular work. The Boss reveals he simply rewards people randomly, and the robot confirms it tried the same approach and it calmed the staff.
punchline: Management rewards are so disconnected from actual performance that a robot's random handouts work just as well as the boss's own approach, implying that merit-based recognition is meaningless.
summary: A boss and his robot stand-in agree that handing out rewards at random is the easiest way to keep unverifiable employee claims from causing trouble.

file: 2014/2014-02-27_cruelty_frustration_achieved golas_secret goals_set for you_failed to achieve_anger_exact situation.gif
title: Secret Goals Guarantee Failed Review

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm happy to report that I achieved every goal you set for me last year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But you failed to achieve the secret goals I set for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would you have secret goals for me?!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For this exact situation.

setting: The Boss's office during an annual performance review
situation: Dilbert proudly tells his boss that he met every goal assigned to him for the year. The boss replies that Dilbert missed the secret goals he was never told about. When Dilbert angrily asks why secret goals exist, the boss admits they exist precisely so he can deny a good review.
punchline: The boss invents undisclosed goals so that no employee can ever fully succeed, giving him a guaranteed excuse to withhold praise or raises.
summary: A worker who ticked off all his assigned objectives learns his manager keeps hidden ones in reserve to justify a poor evaluation.

title: Asok Declared Officially Gay

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Supreme Court of India recently voted to uphold a law making it a crime to be born gay.*

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: *Essentially.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: To commemorate that hopelessly ignorant decision, Asok the intern is now officially gay.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay, we're done here.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Good, because I have a lot of gay stuff to do.

situation: Dogbert, seated behind his desk, comments on a ruling by India's Supreme Court that upheld a law criminalizing homosexuality, with a footnote admitting the description is a simplification. To mark the occasion he arbitrarily declares Asok, the intern, officially gay. Asok accepts the new status immediately and leaves, saying he has plenty of gay things to do.
punchline: Asok's cheerful, instant acceptance of an arbitrary official declaration mocks the absurdity of laws that dictate a person's sexual identity, with Dogbert's decree mirroring the ignorance of the court.
summary: To protest a court ruling criminalizing homosexuality, Dogbert bureaucratically decrees his intern gay, and the intern happily gets on with his new agenda.

file: 2014/2014-09-03_apathy_dangerously incompetent_last day of work_lazy_software_tell everyone_train_unwarranted confidence_engineering.gif
title: Last Day Training Gives False Confidence

transcript.speaker: Departing Employee
transcript.text: This is my last day of work, so I won't have time to completely train you on the software.

transcript.speaker: Departing Employee
transcript.text: But I can show you enough to give you unwarranted confidence, when you should be feeling dangerously incompetent.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds worse than doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: Departing Employee
transcript.text: Before I leave, I'll tell everyone you're lazy.

situation: A coworker on his last day of work sits at the computer with Dilbert to hand over the software. He explains he can only give a partial training that will leave Dilbert overconfident but unprepared. When Dilbert objects that this is worse than nothing, the coworker threatens to tell everyone Dilbert is lazy before he leaves.
punchline: The departing employee, with nothing left to lose, offers a deliberately harmful half-training and then blackmails Dilbert into accepting it by threatening his reputation.
summary: A soon-to-be-gone coworker offers a hazardously incomplete software handoff and backs it up with a reputational threat when Dilbert pushes back.

title: Angry Nominee for Good Attitude Award

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you've been nominated by your peers for the "Good Attitude Award."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Get out of here with your stupid, useless award!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I shouldn't let peers do the voting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like her odds to win again next month.

situation: The Boss approaches Alice at her desk and tells her that her peers nominated her for the Good Attitude Award. Alice screams at him to get out with his stupid, useless award. Afterward, the Boss wonders aloud about the voting process while Dilbert, standing with Wally, says he likes her chances of winning again.
punchline: Alice's furious outburst shows she has the worst attitude imaginable, yet her coworkers keep nominating her, apparently as a joke or out of fear, and Dilbert sarcastically predicts she will win again.
summary: A manager tells the notoriously furious Alice she is up for a positivity prize, and her explosive reaction proves how absurd the peer-voted honor is.

title: Smart or Leader, Boss Wants Both

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You didn't show leadership on your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying I didn't do things in a smart way?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Leading is different from acting in the smartest way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... either I can do things the smart way or I can be a leader like you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop twisting things around!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to be smart and you need to show leadership!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't expect your team to do what you want just because it's the smartest path.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Remind me which one of us hired those idiots.

situation: The Boss criticizes Dilbert for not showing leadership on his project, insisting that leading is different from doing things the smartest way. Dilbert points out that this makes it sound like he must choose between being smart and being a leader like the Boss, which the Boss dismisses as twisting words. The Boss then says Dilbert's team won't follow him just because his plan is smart, prompting Dilbert to ask who hired such unreasonable people.
punchline: Dilbert implies that the Boss is the one who hired the idiot team members who won't follow a smart plan, turning the Boss's complaint about leadership back on him.
summary: A manager faults his employee for lacking leadership while implying that smart decisions alone are not enough to win over a team, and the employee sarcastically blames management for the team's quality.

title: Robot Boss Interrupts Five-Year Engineering Problem

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Temporary robot boss

transcript.speaker: Robot Boss
transcript.text: My sensors detect no work coming from this cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: That's because I have been working on an engineering problem in my head for five years.

transcript.speaker: Robot Boss
transcript.text: Are you almost done?

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I was, but you just made me forget all of it.

situation: A temporary robot boss approaches a seated engineer's cubicle and says its sensors detect no work being done. The engineer claims he has been solving an engineering problem in his head for five years. When the robot asks if he is almost done, the engineer says the interruption made him forget everything.
punchline: The engineer uses an unverifiable 'thinking' excuse to cover for idleness, then blames the boss's interruption for erasing five years of supposed progress.
summary: Caught idling by an automated supervisor, a worker claims years of silent mental effort and then pins the loss of it on the interruption.

file: 2014/2014-05-03_magician_press agents_pubilcity_famous magician_fired_stayed in swear_rats for month.gif
title: Publicist Forgot To Publicize Stunt

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your last job was doing publicity for a famous magician. Why did you leave?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: My boss fired me after the trick where he stayed in a sewer full of rats for a month.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't hear about that.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I forgot to tell anyone it was happening.

situation: Dilbert interviews a candidate whose previous job was doing publicity for a famous magician. The candidate explains he was fired after the magician's stunt of living in a rat-filled sewer for a month. Dilbert says he never heard about it, and the candidate admits he forgot to tell anyone it was happening.
punchline: A publicist was so negligent that he never publicized a month-long public stunt, making the magician's ordeal pointless and the firing entirely deserved.
summary: A job applicant reveals that his stint as a magician's publicity agent ended because he neglected to announce an extreme month-long stunt to anybody.

title: Blaming Followers Instead of Leadership

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to show more leadership on your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you know my leadership is the problem? Maybe the team members are bad followers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's your job to fix it either way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The way you just fixed me with your leadership?

situation: The boss tells Dilbert that his project needs more leadership from him. Dilbert counters that the real problem might be the team members being bad followers. The boss insists it is Dilbert's job to fix it either way, and Dilbert points out how ineffective the boss's own leadership has just been.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically notes that the boss's attempt to 'fix' him with criticism is itself a demonstration of poor leadership, undermining the boss's advice.
summary: A manager lectures an engineer about leadership, and the engineer turns the manager's own heavy-handed approach against him.

title: Vacation Afterglow Ends Instantly

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I feel so rested and relaxed after my vacation.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I wonder how long the afterglow will last because. . . Excuse me while I check this text message. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it too late to start timing it?

situation: Alice walks through the office with her arms outstretched, declaring how rested and relaxed her vacation has left her. She wonders aloud how long the feeling will last, then checks a text message. She instantly erupts into a fiery rage while Dilbert, holding his coffee mug, asks if it's too late to start timing it.
punchline: Alice's post-vacation calm is destroyed within seconds by a single work text message, making the afterglow almost immeasurably short.
summary: A freshly relaxed coworker's vacation serenity goes up in flames the moment she reads a message from work.

title: Comparing Apples, Oranges, and Wives

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't compare apples and oranges.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's clearly wrong because you just compared them and declared them different.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Apples and oranges are both foods that grow on trees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It would be totally valid to compare them nutritionally.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've noticed that a lot of what comes out of your mouth makes no sense.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You sound like my wife.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You can't compare your wife to your subordinate. That's apples and oranges.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What is happening here?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't know, but I wouldn't compare it to work.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss declares that you can't compare apples and oranges, and Dilbert points out that he just did exactly that. A coworker chimes in with a pedantic nutritional comparison, Dilbert says the boss makes no sense, and the boss says Dilbert sounds like his wife. The coworker then objects that comparing a wife to a subordinate is apples and oranges.
punchline: The idiom about not comparing apples and oranges gets dissected and then misapplied in a tangle of illogic, ending with the coworker saying the confusing scene is unlike anything at work, which ironically implies work is usually just as nonsensical.
summary: A meeting derails into a muddled argument over a fruit cliché that ends with a spouse-versus-employee comparison nobody can make sense of.

title: Rumor Spreader Feels Slightly Guilty

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I heard you had a freak accident while vacuuming your house naked.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a rumor. I don't know how that stuff spreads.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: (thought) Now I feel a little bad that I told thirty people.

setting: Office break area by the coffee machine
situation: A coworker with a big black bob haircut approaches Dilbert at the coffee maker and says she heard he had an embarrassing accident while vacuuming naked at home. Dilbert dismisses it as a rumor and wonders aloud how such things spread. In the last panel, her thought bubble reveals she is the one who spread it to thirty people.
punchline: Dilbert wonders how rumors spread while standing in front of the person who told thirty people, and she only feels 'a little bad' about it.
summary: A gossiping coworker quietly admits she is the source of an embarrassing story that Dilbert is baffled to find circulating.

title: Graphic Designer Admits Secret Outsourcing Plan

transcript.speaker: Coworker in Blue
transcript.text: Dilbert, meet our new graphic designer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I had your job, I would secretly sub it out to strangers on the Internet and pay them 5% of my salary while I did nothing all day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oops. Sorry. I didn't know you were already there.

situation: A coworker introduces Dilbert to the company's new graphic designer. Dilbert describes how he would secretly outsource the job to internet strangers for a fraction of his pay and do nothing. The designer's tense, gritted-teeth expression reveals Dilbert has described exactly what he is already doing.
punchline: Dilbert unwittingly describes the new hire's secret scheme of subcontracting his work cheaply and slacking off, then sarcastically apologizes for exposing it.
summary: A newly introduced designer is caught out when Dilbert lays out a lazy outsourcing racket that the newcomer is evidently already running.

title: Answering Reorganization Rumors With Questions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I heard a rumor of a reorganization. Is it true?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who told you that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Answering a question with a question means yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you accusing me of being a deceptive weasel?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would you ask that?

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss whether the rumored reorganization is real. The Boss dodges by replying with a question, and Dilbert points out that answering a question with a question amounts to a yes. The Boss keeps deflecting with another question, and Dilbert answers in kind.
punchline: Dilbert turns the Boss's evasive tactic back on him by answering the Boss's question with a question, confirming the reorganization is real while showing the Boss is being deceptive.
summary: A worker catches his evasive manager dodging a rumor by only responding with questions, then mirrors the trick right back at him.

title: Matching Outfits, Violent Threat

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, it's the first day of our new dress code and we wore exactly the same outfits!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If you ever say that again I will rip out your tongue and use it to slap you to death.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it because I wore it better?

situation: On the first day of a new company dress code, Dilbert cheerfully points out that he and Alice are wearing identical outfits (red shirts and black pants). Alice responds with a graphically violent threat if he ever mentions it again. Dilbert replies by asking whether she's angry because he wore the outfit better.
punchline: Dilbert turns Alice's extreme threat into a fashion joke, implying her rage comes from being outdressed, which borrows the red-carpet 'who wore it better' trope and ignores the fact that they are wearing a mandatory uniform.
summary: A coworker's cheerful remark about identical clothes draws a gruesome threat, which he answers with a vain fashion quip.

title: Proud of Misleading the Analysts

transcript.speaker: Bald Executive
transcript.text: You should be proud that we beat the earnings that analysts expected.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why should we be proud that analysts are bad at making estimates?

transcript.speaker: Bald Executive
transcript.text: Those bad estimates don't happen on their own. I had to mislead them.

transcript.speaker: Dark-Haired Executive
transcript.text: I'm proud of you.

setting: Conference room at a meeting table
situation: At a meeting, a bald executive tells the group they should be proud of beating the earnings analysts expected. Dilbert questions why that is something to celebrate, and the executive admits he deliberately misled the analysts to lower their estimates. Another executive praises him for it.
punchline: Beating analyst expectations is presented as an achievement, but it was only possible because the executive deliberately deceived the analysts, and his colleague applauds the deception.
summary: A manager boasts about topping market forecasts, then cheerfully confesses he rigged those forecasts himself, earning a colleague's praise.

file: 2014/2014-03-12_competition (psychology)_mobile (cell) phones_money_tiny screen_enormous phone_expensive_paid mortgage_phone with tiny screen.gif
title: Giant Phone Mines Bitcoins, Pays Mortgage

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Topper

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: I see you have a phone with a tiny screen.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: That must be embarrassing compared to my enormous phone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it expensive?

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: It paid off my mortgage by mining bitcoins.

situation: Topper, Dilbert's smug rival, mocks Dilbert's small phone and holds up his own enormous phone. When Dilbert asks if it was expensive, Topper replies that it mined bitcoins and paid off his mortgage.
punchline: Topper's one-upmanship backfires on Dilbert's question, because the giant phone turns out to be a money-making asset that makes Topper look even more successful.
summary: A boastful coworker waves a comically huge phone at a colleague with a small one, then trumps any price concern by claiming it earned enough cryptocurrency to clear his home loan.

file: 2014/2014-02-26_public speaking_stress_10 thousand attendees_don't be stressed_nervous_fall apart_speech_large audience.gif
title: Boss Slaps Stress Out of Ted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I want you to give a speech to ten thousand conference attendees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll be great. Don't get stressed.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Slap

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I said, "Don't."

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Pow!

situation: The Boss tells a visibly nervous Ted that he must give a speech to ten thousand conference attendees. When Ted looks stressed, the Boss slaps him on the arm and tells him not to be stressed. Ted shatters into pieces from the blow, and the Boss says he said "don't".
punchline: The Boss treats Ted's stress as a personal disobedience of his order, so Ted is physically broken by the Boss's heavy-handed attempt at reassurance.
summary: A manager springs a huge speaking gig on a nervous employee, then clumsily "reassures" him so hard that the employee falls to pieces.

title: Succeeding Only If We Succeed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can only succeed if we execute.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How is that different from saying we can only succeed if we succeed?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's also the strategy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Does the strategy create itself?

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss declares that the company can only succeed if it executes. Wally points out that this is just a circular way of saying they can only succeed if they succeed. The Boss tries to rescue the claim by adding that strategy matters too, and Wally asks whether the strategy creates itself.
punchline: Wally sarcastically exposes the Boss's business platitude as meaningless circular logic, and the Boss's attempt to add strategy to the equation leaves him no better off.
summary: A manager's grand statement about success is dismantled by a skeptical coworker who spots the empty logic and keeps pushing back on every follow-up.

file: 2014/2014-10-05_cruelty_leadership_managers_managers & supervisors_choices_bullying_60 hour week_fatique_lower quality_enlightened leader_work fewer hours_better outcome_illusion_created by underlings_abuse_pian_enforcement_business.gif
title: Leadership Is Abusing Your Underlings

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have an interesting choice today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can continue bullying me into working sixty hours per week...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: While knowing that fatigue will lower the quality of my work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or you can be an enlightened leader and encourage me to work fewer hours for a better net outcome.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not supposed to tell you this, but...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Leadership is an illusion created by the abuse of underlings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The more pain I force you to endure, the more of a leader I appear to be.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's the truth feel?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ouch! Ouch! Ouch!

situation: Dilbert presents his boss with a choice: keep forcing him to work sixty-hour weeks and get worse work, or be an enlightened leader and let him work fewer hours. The boss confesses that leadership is really an illusion built on abusing subordinates. He then asks how the truth feels as Dilbert doubles over in pain.
punchline: The boss admits that appearing to be a leader depends on inflicting pain on employees, then literally hurts Dilbert to demonstrate the point.
summary: A boss responds to a plea for saner work hours by revealing that his authority depends on making his staff suffer.

title: Boss Has Troll DNA, Therapist Suggests

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: None of my subordinates are supportive. I don't know why.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Perhaps they're sensing that you have troll DNA.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um... What?

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Did your mom ever live under a bridge?

setting: Therapist's office, with the patient lying on a couch
situation: The Boss lies on a therapist's couch and complains that none of his subordinates are supportive and he can't work out why. The therapist, taking notes on a pad, suggests his employees may be sensing that he has troll DNA. When he reacts with confusion, she asks whether his mother ever lived under a bridge.
punchline: The therapist's deadpan diagnosis implies the Boss is so unpleasant that his staff instinctively see him as a literal troll, rather than as someone with a management problem.
summary: A boss seeks therapy over his team's lack of loyalty and is told, with a straight face, that his workers can smell the troll in him.

file: 2014/2014-12-16_financial advisor_investing_money_stock market_swindling_convertible notes_preferred stock_call options_career ambition_ginat mosquito.gif
title: Financial Advisor Admits Draining Accounts

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Financial advisor

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: Convertible notes... Preferred stock... Municipal bonds... Covered call options.

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: These are things you can never hope to understand. So trust me and try to forget that my only career ambition is to drain your account like a giant mosquito.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds reasonable.

transcript.speaker: Financial Advisor
transcript.text: I'm always surprised at how easy this is.

situation: Dilbert sits across the desk from a financial advisor who rattles off investment jargon. The advisor then openly admits that his only goal is to drain Dilbert's account like a giant mosquito and tells him to trust him anyway. Dilbert calmly agrees, and the advisor remarks on how easy his job is.
punchline: Even when a financial advisor openly confesses he intends to bleed his client dry, the client still trusts him, because jargon and perceived expertise make people gullible.
summary: A money manager bluntly confesses his predatory intentions, and his client accepts it without objection.

file: 2014/2014-05-19_electronic mail_internet & world wide web_scams_enter bank acct_employee_boss.gif
title: Why Phishing Scams Keep Working

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Why phishing scams keep working

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Enter your bank account number.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Scam.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Wait for it

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Enter your bank account number.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Scam.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: There it is

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Enter your bank account number.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okey-dokey.

situation: Three people each see a computer message demanding their bank account number. Dilbert and Alice both think 'scam' and refuse. The Boss, however, cheerfully thinks 'okey-dokey' and is ready to comply.
punchline: Phishing scams keep working because it only takes one gullible person like the Boss to fall for them, no matter how many others spot the fraud.
summary: Two sharp employees spot a phishing attempt instantly, but the naive boss happily agrees to hand over his banking details.

title: Alpha Dominance Puffer Fish Showdown

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Studies say I can increase my alpha dominance by using lots of space in the room.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Topper

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That's nothing. I can inflate my body like a puffer fish!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: At times like this, you must be glad you're barely male.

situation: Dilbert stretches his arms wide to take up space, citing studies that this boosts alpha dominance. Asok tops him by announcing he can inflate his body like a puffer fish, and then does so, ballooning into a red sphere. Alice, standing nearby with Wally, remarks on how glad Dilbert must be that he's barely male.
punchline: Alice sarcastically suggests that being barely male is what spares Dilbert from joining the ridiculous posturing contest, while also insulting his masculinity.
summary: Two coworkers compete in absurd displays of dominance until a bystander dryly points out the one benefit of not being very manly.

title: Seated Next to the Hated VP

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have you seated next to our senior vice president at the technology awards banquet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because you hate me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, it's because I hate him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is making me very unhappy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't peak too soon. Wait for the banquet.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has been seated next to the senior vice president at the technology awards banquet. Dilbert assumes it is a punishment from the Boss, but the Boss explains he is using Dilbert to inflict misery on someone he dislikes. When Dilbert complains about being unhappy already, the Boss tells him the worst is yet to come at the banquet.
punchline: The Boss uses Dilbert as a weapon against a person he hates, and warns that Dilbert's present unhappiness is nothing compared to how miserable the banquet will be.
summary: A manager reveals he put an employee beside an executive he despises, then advises the employee to save his misery for the actual event.

file: 2014/2014-02-28_frustration_work ethic_drink lots of coffee_disrespect authority_reading my goals_before signing_accomplish stuff_feels good.gif
title: Employee Goals: Coffee and Disrespect

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Maybe next year YOUR goal should be something about reading MY goals before you sign them.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Accomplishing stuff feels good. You should try it.

setting: Office, during a performance review at a desk
situation: The boss, holding a tablet, complains that an employee's written goals for the year were to drink lots of coffee and disrespect authority. The employee, holding a coffee mug, points out that the boss signed off on those goals without reading them. The employee then sips coffee and tells the boss that accomplishing things feels good.
punchline: The boss criticizes the employee's absurd goals but is the one who approved them unread, and the employee sarcastically suggests the boss try actually accomplishing something.
summary: A manager scolds a worker over ridiculous annual goals, only to be reminded that he rubber-stamped them without reading a word.

title: Ignoring Email Lowers the Boss's IQ

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That's the sort of question that one asks after checking email too often.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you just insult me?

transcript.speaker: Employee

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What were we talking about?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You were complimenting me on my efficiency.

setting: Office hallway with coffee mugs in hand
situation: An employee tells the Boss that constantly checking email lowers IQ, and the Boss vows to ignore the employee's email. When the Boss asks whether he's been insulted, the employee says the answer is in an email. The Boss gets distracted by six new important-looking emails and forgets the whole conversation, so the employee tricks him into believing he was complimented.
punchline: The Boss is so addicted to checking email that he is easily distracted and manipulated, proving the employee's point about reduced functional intelligence.
summary: A worker exploits his boss's inbox obsession to dodge an insult by redirecting him to email and then rewriting the conversation.

title: Pellet of Attention Texting Power Play

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hold on, I have a text message that is probably more important than you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I will demonstrate my power over you by handling a text message while you sit there, waiting for a pellet of my attention.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Stop texting me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mmm... pellet.

situation: The Boss interrupts a conversation with Dilbert to read a text message, announcing it is more important than Dilbert. He explains that he is demonstrating his power by making Dilbert wait for a pellet of his attention. Dilbert quietly texts the Boss repeatedly, and when the Boss complains, Dilbert treats the interruption as a pellet of attention.
punchline: Dilbert turns the Boss's power play against him by texting him nonstop, then mockingly accepts the Boss's irritated reply as the 'pellet' of attention he was promised, like a lab animal being rewarded.
summary: A boss flaunts his dominance by answering his phone mid-conversation, but his employee subverts the stunt by flooding him with messages and gleefully accepting the scolding as a reward.

file: 2014/2014-05-01_managers & supervisors_investor meeting_emailed_powerpoint slide_dumbed down_technical stuff_non engineers_it be good_no questions_business.gif

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: Dilbert tells his seated boss that he emailed a PowerPoint slide for an upcoming investor meeting, simplified because the boss isn't an engineer. The boss reads the slide aloud and it consists of a single crude sentence. Dilbert advises him not to take questions.
punchline: Dilbert has simplified the technical content so far, treating his boss as unintelligent, that the slide says nothing of substance and could not survive any investor questions.
summary: An engineer simplifies a presentation for his clueless manager so thoroughly that it reduces a whole technology pitch to a childlike slogan.

file: 2014/2014-04-06_bodily fluids_buggy_ceo reputation_competitors_death_medical_misleading ads_not selling_overriced_owls_pal costume_product failure_product name_super yacht_vaguely racist.gif
title: Owl Costume Fixes Everything

transcript.text: It's buggy and overpriced.

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does anyone have an idea to fix all of that?

transcript.speaker: Wally

situation: The Boss convenes a meeting to find out why a new product is not selling. Dilbert, Wally and Alice, plus a fourth attendee, list a damning series of problems: it's buggy, overpriced, outclassed by competitors, advertised misleadingly and racistly, badly named, and tied to a CEO with an owl shooting range. The Boss asks for a fix for all of it, and Wally answers by asking if he owns an owl costume.
punchline: After a devastating list of fundamental failures, Wally offers an absurd, useless suggestion, implying the problems are so hopeless that a ridiculous idea is as good as any.
summary: A product post-mortem uncovers an avalanche of fatal flaws, and the only remedy proposed is a bizarre costume.

file: 2014/2014-06-19_lying_non disclosure agreement_disbelief_wrong person_mighty judgy_so many secrets.gif

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: A man in a suit asks the Pointy-Haired Boss to sign a non-disclosure agreement before they begin a meeting. The Boss declines, saying it's unnecessary because nobody believes anything he says. The visitor doubts he has the right person, and the Boss fires back that the visitor is judgmental for someone with so many secrets.
punchline: The Boss's admission that he's too untrustworthy to be believed makes him a useless confidant, and he deflects the visitor's doubt by turning it into an accusation about the visitor's own secrecy.
summary: A cautious visitor wants legal protection for a confidential chat, but the boss shrugs it off because his word carries no credibility anyway.

title: Lawyer Delivers Flaming Contract Mess

transcript.text: Company lawyer

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: Look what just landed in your back-yard.

setting: Outdoors near the office, then Dilbert's cubicle
situation: The company lawyer, holding a coffee mug, tells an employee pushing a wheelbarrow that he has turned a simple business deal into a flaming pile of excrement. He proudly calls it some of his best work, admitting he doesn't understand it himself. He then dumps the burning mess onto Dilbert's desk, telling him it has landed in his backyard.
punchline: The lawyer takes pride in making a contract so convoluted that even he can't understand it, then cheerfully dumps the resulting disaster on Dilbert as someone else's problem.
summary: A smug in-house attorney boasts about wrecking a straightforward agreement with legalese and then hands the blazing wreckage to an unsuspecting engineer.

file: 2014/2014-04-29_business people_business plan_corporate dysfunction_dishonesty_incompetence_longer_lumbering monument_seeking feedback_more of the same.gif
title: Longer Business Plan, Brutal Feedback

situation: A woman with big curly hair approaches Dilbert to ask about the feedback he gave on her business plan. Dilbert, reading from his phone, recites his own scathing critique calling it a lumbering monument to incompetence, dishonesty and corporate dysfunction. She ignores the insult and asks only whether the plan should be longer.
punchline: She is so unfazed by the devastating critique that her only concern is whether to make the plan longer, suggesting that more of the same is her instinct.
summary: A woman seeking input on her business plan responds to a brutal takedown by wondering if the document should simply be expanded.

title: Sexiest Engineer Title, Weak Competition

situation: A woman with big dark hair tells Dilbert he has been named one of the sexiest engineers in the world, then snaps his photo while admitting the competition was weak. Later Dilbert repeats the news to Wally, who is holding a coffee mug and welcomes him to the club.

summary: Dilbert is crowned a top sexy engineer, but the honor is undercut by the lack of rivals and by a fellow slacker who claims membership too.

title: Boss Checks In, Then Stops Caring

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... how's your job going?

transcript.text: How long will it take you to fix everything?

situation: The Boss stops by Dilbert's cubicle holding a coffee mug and casually asks how his job is going. Dilbert answers with a gruesome, vivid description of how awful it is. The Boss thinks to himself that he is back to not caring and walks away, while an off-panel voice asks how long it will take Dilbert to fix everything.
punchline: The Boss only asks out of token politeness and instantly returns to indifference when he hears the job is miserable, while someone else immediately expects Dilbert to fix all the problems.
summary: A manager makes small talk about an employee's job, gets a horrifying answer, and mentally shrugs it off as someone else demands a total fix.

title: Billionaire Who Quits Working Paradox

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If you made a billion dollars, would you stop working?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How would I make a billion dollars?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You would have to start working.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It seems sort of self-defeating.

situation: Two coworkers stand holding coffee mugs while one asks the other whether he would stop working if he became a billionaire. Dilbert asks how he would get that much money, and the coworker points out he would have to start working. The coworker then sips his coffee and concludes the whole idea is self-defeating.
punchline: The only way to earn enough money to quit working is to work, which makes the dream of retiring through work a circular, self-defeating idea.
summary: A hypothetical about getting rich enough to quit working collapses when the colleagues realize that getting rich would require working.

title: Wally Explains Competence Is a Trap

transcript.text: Can you teach me to be useless like you?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's better if I don't so you learn by example.

situation: Asok tells Wally he is constantly tense and doesn't know why. Wally, holding his coffee mug, explains that being competent leads to ever-higher expectations. Asok asks to be taught to be useless, and Wally declines to teach him directly, saying Asok will learn by watching him.
punchline: Wally's refusal to give lessons in uselessness is itself a display of his own laziness, since teaching would require effort, so he claims watching him is the better lesson.
summary: Wally convinces a stressed Asok that doing good work only invites more demands, then dodges the effort of mentoring him in slacking.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, remarks to Alice at her cubicle that every employee seems to be complaining today. Alice replies that his leadership has turned the workplace into a 'skunk opera.' She says it's lucky he doesn't understand analogies, and he confidently declares the analogy is about singing.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that he takes the insulting 'skunk opera' analogy literally as being about singing, proving Alice's point that he doesn't understand analogies and missing that he is the cause of the complaints.
summary: A manager puzzled by widespread employee grumbling is told his leadership created a stinking, chaotic mess, but he misses the insult entirely.

punchline: Alan's marketing job of making bad products smell nice is shown literally, as he sprays perfume on Dilbert, the skunk in this case, while Dilbert's restraint from violence goes unrewarded.
summary: A marketer and an engineer trade pointed job descriptions, and the marketer demonstrates his craft by dousing the engineer in scent.

setting: Dilbert's living room, then an unspecified location where two women look at a phone

He explains that he only listed being six feet tall, having hair and having a job. A 'Meanwhile, everywhere' panel shows two excited women looking at a phone and gushing about the 'triple threat'.
punchline: Dilbert's basic, minimal qualities of height, hair and employment are so rare among eligible men that they make him wildly sought after, implying very low standards or a scarcity of such men.
summary: A man gets thousands of dating site replies just for listing three ordinary traits, while women elsewhere swoon over his combination of qualities.

punchline: The Boss's own ghostwritten book contains sensible advice he never read, so he is bound by wisdom he didn't write, and Dilbert slyly credits the unnamed ghostwriter.
summary: A manager gets barred from a crowded meeting by a rule from his own book, which he admits he never bothered to read.

title: Marketing Discovered, Hidden From Boss

punchline: Dilbert has innocently reinvented marketing and thinks it's an evil weapon, while management deliberately kept him ignorant of what marketing is.
summary: An engineer fears he has invented a dangerous mind-control technique, unaware that it is simply the everyday practice of advertising.

transcript.text: You have offended Bixtappa, the deity of unseasonably warm weather and twice-baked potatoes.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Our tradition says I must now strangle you with a mud adder.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Luckily, I brought one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do Elbonians have a lot of deities?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: No, just the one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He seems easily offended.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Grab the head and yank!

situation: The Boss explains that their product name is an insult in Elbonian, so he hired an Elbonian to vet new name choices. The Elbonian reacts in horror to one of the options, declares that the company has offended his deity, and pulls out a mud adder to strangle the Boss according to tradition. Dilbert looks on and comments while the Boss is being strangled.
punchline: The hired Elbonian reviewer turns out to be so easily offended by a product name that he tries to ritually strangle the Boss, who is supposedly the one he was hired to help.
summary: A consultant brought in to screen product names for cultural offense instead takes such offense himself that he attacks the manager who hired him.

title: Skipping Conference Call While Holding Coffee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't look productive.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm on a conference call.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you should be in your cubicle listening to it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Nah. They aren't saying anything important.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe they will.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Optimism sounds exhausting.

situation: The Boss sees Wally wandering the hallway with a coffee mug and complains that he doesn't look productive. Wally says he is on a conference call, and when the Boss suggests he listen from his cubicle, Wally explains the call is not worth his attention. The Boss hopes the call may eventually become important, and Wally dismisses that hope as too tiring.
punchline: Wally declines to pay attention to a pointless conference call and mocks the Boss's hope that it might become useful by calling optimism exhausting.
summary: A manager catches an employee idling with coffee during a meeting call, and the employee brushes off the manager's hopeful view with a lazy quip.

title: Initiative Review Already Written

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My projects are winding down and I'd like to take on more responsibility.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh. That's a problem because I just finished your performance review and it says you don't take initiative.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess you need to redo that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That would be one way to play it.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that his projects are finishing and he wants more responsibility. The Boss replies that he has just completed a performance review saying Dilbert lacks initiative. When Dilbert suggests the review be redone, the Boss only says that would be one way to handle it, with no intention of changing it.
punchline: The Boss won't revise his review even when Dilbert demonstrates the initiative it says he lacks, showing that management cares more about paperwork than reality.
summary: An employee shows initiative the very moment after his boss has formally written that he has none, and the boss refuses to budge.

file: 2014/2014-08-05_discrimination_women_simple interface_ruby on rails_someone else mother_sexist imbecile.gif
title: Your Mother Could Use It

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The interface needs to be so simple that your mother could use it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My mother taught herself Ruby on Rails over a weekend.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then imagine someone else's mother.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I imagine a sexist imbecile?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that a software interface must be so simple that his mother could use it. Dilbert replies that his mother taught herself Ruby on Rails in a weekend. The Boss tells him to imagine someone else's mother instead, and Dilbert asks if he can imagine a sexist imbecile.
punchline: Dilbert turns the Boss's condescending assumption that mothers are technically incompetent back on him by implying that the Boss is a sexist imbecile.
summary: A manager's stereotype about clueless mothers using software backfires when the programmer's mom turns out to be a skilled coder, leaving the manager exposed as a sexist fool.

title: Defending the Boss Isn't Supportive

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Did you read the article I forwarded about the ten things every leader should be doing?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I defended your honor by writing a blog post saying you don't do any of those things and you still get paid.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why doesn't this feel supportive?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: That's one of life's little mysteries.

situation: Carol asks the Boss whether he read an article she forwarded about the ten things every leader should be doing. She then explains that she 'defended his honor' by writing a blog post saying he does none of those things and still gets paid. The Boss wonders why this doesn't feel supportive, and Carol feigns innocence.
punchline: Carol's 'defense' is actually a public insult confirming the Boss is a lazy, incompetent leader who is overpaid, and she sarcastically pretends not to understand why he doesn't feel supported.
summary: A secretary claims to have stood up for her manager by publicly announcing that he ignores every leadership rule yet still collects a salary.

title: Co-CEO Wants Authority to Fire

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I decided to hire a co-CEO to share the job with me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I assume you know that having a co-CEO does not mean you get paid the same while working half as much.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can I fire you?

transcript.speaker: Co-CEO
transcript.text: No, we need a third CEO to break the tie.

situation: The Boss tells his staff he has hired a co-CEO to share his job, with the new executive standing beside him. Dilbert warns that sharing the role does not mean he will keep full pay for half the work. The Boss then asks the new co-CEO if he can fire him, and is told a third CEO would be needed to break the tie.
punchline: The Boss has thought of the co-CEO arrangement only as a way to work less, and when he realizes the new peer has equal power, he immediately asks to fire him, only to be blocked by the deadlock of a two-person leadership.
summary: A lazy executive brings in a partner to halve his workload, then discovers he lacks the power to remove the person he hired.

title: Drunken Retreat Produces Slurred Slogan

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our officers came up with a new company slogan after two weeks at a retreat.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The new slogan is "Shtop spitting ahn me when you talk!"

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We believe alcohol was involved.

setting: Office exterior and hallway, with a shot of the company building
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Dilbert and a coworker that the company's officers invented a new slogan during a two-week retreat. The slogan is shown over the company building and is written in slurred, drunken speech. The Boss then casually admits they suspect alcohol played a role.
punchline: The company's official slogan is clearly a drunken slur, and management's only explanation is that alcohol was probably involved in the executive retreat.
summary: After a lengthy executive getaway, leadership unveils a motto that reads like a drunk person's complaint, and the boss shrugs off the obvious cause.

title: Cynical Or Just Accurate Worldview

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm getting reports that you're being cynical.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's called an accurate worldview. You should try it sometime.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If it's accurate, why are people upset?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Said the angry guy to the one who isn't.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that people have reported him being cynical. Dilbert insists he simply has an accurate worldview and suggests the Boss try it. The Boss asks why people are upset if the view is accurate, and Dilbert points out that the angry person is the one asking the question.
punchline: Dilbert turns the Boss's argument around by noting that the person claiming upset proves inaccuracy is himself the angry one, while Dilbert remains calm.
summary: A manager complains about an employee's negativity, but the employee calmly reframes his pessimism as realism and flips the accusation of upset onto the manager.

file: 2014/2014-04-12_cruelty_executives_work ethic_acting ceo_murder employees_start up_unprofitable_ridiculous jargon_wishful thinking_luck_show off_management fad.gif
title: Acting CEO Blames Luck

transcript.speaker: Bald Executive
transcript.text: I heard that while you were acting CEO you ...

transcript.speaker: Bald Executive
transcript.text: ... murdered nine employees, bought an unprofitable start-up and embraced a new management fad that is nothing but ridiculous jargon and wishful thinking.

transcript.speaker: Bald Executive
transcript.text: No one likes a show-off.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I swear it was just luck.

situation: A bald executive with a bandage around his head confronts the Boss, who sat in as acting CEO. He lists the awful things the Boss did, including killing nine employees, buying an unprofitable start-up and adopting a jargon-filled management fad. The executive then accuses him of showing off, and the Boss insists it was just luck.
punchline: The executive treats the Boss's catastrophic decisions as impressive achievements, and the Boss modestly credits luck, so terrible management is mistaken for success.
summary: A grim list of an interim boss's disastrous decisions is met with an accusation of bragging and a humble claim of fluke.

file: 2014/2014-03-22_anxiety_employees_hiring and budget problem_perfromance review_three people_will resign_slightest criticism_pre google thinking_business.gif
title: Alice Threatens Boss Before Review

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Before we start my performance review, I should remind you that it would take three people to replace me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And I will resign at the slightest criticism, leaving you with a huge hiring and budget problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This was supposed to make YOU nervous, not me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That thinking is so pre-Google.

setting: Boss's office during a performance review
situation: Alice sits across from the Boss at the start of her performance review and preemptively warns him that replacing her would take three people. She adds that she will quit at the slightest criticism, saddling him with a hiring and budget headache. The Boss, holding the review paper, protests that the review is supposed to make her nervous, not him.
punchline: Alice dismisses the Boss's expectation that a review intimidates the employee as outdated, implying modern employees hold the leverage and managers fear losing them.
summary: An employee turns her own evaluation into a power play by promising to walk out if she is criticized, leaving her manager rattled.

file: 2014/2014-06-01_choosing_electronic mail_successful habits_eight things_inspirational links_emails_change subject_huge success.gif
title: Eight Habits of Successful People

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you see my email about the eight things that successful people do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes. I did all eight things and now I'm a huge success.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No you're not.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's that possible? I did all of the things that successful people do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This only makes sense if the inspirational links you send me every day are a complete waste of time!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So which one is it? Am I a huge success or do you email me worthless things?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe we should just change the subject.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that what successful people do?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether he read his email listing eight things successful people do. Dilbert says he did all eight and is now a huge success, but the Boss insists he isn't. Dilbert argues that either he is a success or the Boss's daily inspirational emails are worthless.
punchline: Dilbert's logic exposes that the boss's inspirational advice can't be valid if following it doesn't produce success, and the boss dodging the question by changing the subject is itself mocked as a supposed habit of successful people.
summary: A manager's motivational email advice gets turned against him when his employee points out the contradiction in it.

title: Dinosaur Clings to Obsolete Technology

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: All I need is my flip phone, my Windows XP, and my basic cable television.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Did I sound like a big, dumb dinosaur that time?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Pretty much.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Wow... there is no cool way to describe my life.

setting: Office, with Dogbert seated on a desk
situation: A green dinosaur announces that all he needs is a flip phone, Windows XP, and basic cable TV. He then asks Dogbert whether he sounded like a big, dumb dinosaur. Dogbert confirms it, and the dinosaur glumly admits his life can't be described in a cool way.
punchline: The dinosaur literally is a dinosaur clinging to outdated technology, so his lifestyle is exactly as uncool and obsolete as he fears.
summary: A literal dinosaur praises his outdated gadgets, then discovers that his dusty tastes make him sound exactly like the relic he is.

title: Prince of Insufficient Light's Cereal Pitchspoon

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I am Phil, the Prince of Insufficient Light. I got a report that you wished bad karma upon your co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You would put off a more menacing vibe if you didn't have leftover cereal in your pitchspoon.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I was really hungry and I didn't feel like emptying the dishwasher.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We've all been there.

situation: Phil, dressed in a red devil costume and carrying a pitchfork-like utensil, confronts Dilbert about wishing bad karma on his co-workers. Dilbert points out that the leftover cereal on Phil's pitchspoon ruins his menacing image. Phil explains he used it as a spoon because he was hungry and didn't want to empty the dishwasher.
punchline: The fearsome devil figure is undermined by a mundane, lazy household habit, and Dilbert sympathetically relates to it, deflating the threat entirely.
summary: A would-be intimidating devil is brought down to earth when his pronged utensil turns out to be doubling as a breakfast spoon because chores were too much effort.

file: 2014/2014-06-23_career_success_who you know_know losers_promising career_holding me back.gif
title: Networking Advice Blames Dilbert's Connections

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Success depends on who you know.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I only know losers such as you, so thanks for nothing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm sorry I ruined your promising career.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're holding me back.

setting: Office break area, both holding coffee mugs
situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells Dilbert that success depends on who you know. Dilbert replies that the only people he knows are losers like Wally, so the advice is useless to him. Dilbert then sarcastically apologizes for ruining Wally's promising career, and Wally retorts that Dilbert is holding him back.
punchline: Each man blames the other for dragging his career down, and Wally's calm insistence that Dilbert is the one holding him back turns Dilbert's insult into a mutual insult, since each treats the other as a networking liability.
summary: Two coworkers over coffee trade insults about whose lousy connections are sabotaging their careers.

title: Overeating to Save Willpower for Work

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I took your advice to start overeating so I could save all of my willpower for work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only downside is a twenty-year reduction in my life expectancy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you okay with that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who would want twenty extra years of my life?

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he followed his advice to overeat so that he could conserve his willpower for his job. He admits the cost is a twenty-year drop in life expectancy, and the Boss asks if he is fine with that. Dilbert replies that he sees no value in having those extra years.
punchline: Dilbert is so miserable at work and in life that losing twenty years of it seems like a bargain rather than a downside.
summary: A worn-down engineer happily trades two decades of lifespan for the energy to endure his job, since he finds his own life not worth extending.

file: 2014/2014-02-16_public speaking_slides tell a story_status of project_clown_broken watch_eagle_technology_old shoe_storm drain_pie chart_dcitionary_images_offcie_cubicle.gif
title: Dilbert's Honest Slide Images Rejected

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Experts say your slides should tell a story in pictures.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Start with an image that captures the status of your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about this image of a clown with a broken watch?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was thinking eagle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fine. Eagle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now find an image that shows our technology strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about this image of an old shoe in a storm drain?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was thinking pie chart.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fine.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now for the words.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about this image of a dictionary?

situation: The Boss coaches Dilbert on building presentation slides that tell a story in pictures. Dilbert keeps proposing brutally honest images for his project status and technology strategy, and the Boss overrides each with a clichéd stock image like an eagle or pie chart. When asked for the words, Dilbert suggests a picture of a dictionary.
punchline: Dilbert's images honestly depict a failing project and a disastrous technology strategy, but the Boss wants generic, impressive-looking visuals, and Dilbert's literal-minded dictionary suggestion shows he's sarcastically mocking the whole exercise.
summary: A manager demands picture-based slides, and the employee's candid, unflattering images are replaced by empty corporate clichés.

file: 2014/2014-03-15_internet & world wide web_power (social sciences)_slaves_a-b testing_manipulate humans_orange button_mindless puppets_legality.gif
title: Dogbert's A/B Testing Mind Control

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Buwhahaha!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm using A-B testing to manipulate irrational humans!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bend to my will and choose the orange button, you mindless click-puppets!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And this is legal?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I own you now!

setting: Dilbert's office, at Dogbert's computer desk
situation: Dilbert walks up holding a coffee mug and finds Dogbert gleefully announcing that he is using A-B testing to manipulate irrational humans. Dogbert shouts at his screen, commanding website visitors to pick the orange button. Dilbert asks whether this is legal, and Dogbert replies that he owns the users now.
punchline: Dogbert treats routine website A-B testing as a sinister mind-control scheme, and when Dilbert asks about legality he ignores the question and gloats about ownership, implying that the practice of manipulating users is both common and ethically murky.
summary: Dogbert cackles over his website experiment, ordering visitors to click the orange button and declaring them his property when questioned about its legality.

title: Networking Book Meets Loser Avoidance

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm reading a book that says the key to success is networking with successful people.

transcript.speaker: Bald Executive
transcript.text: Did you get to the chapter where it says successful people should avoid all contact with losers?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It seems we have a stand-off.

transcript.speaker: Bald Executive
transcript.text: Security.

situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells a bald executive seated at a table that he is reading a book about networking with successful people. The executive replies that the book also says successful people should avoid losers. Wally notes a stand-off, and the executive calls security to remove him.
punchline: Wally's attempt to network with a successful person backfires because the executive treats him as exactly the kind of loser the same book says to avoid, and has him thrown out.
summary: A slacker's bid to rub shoulders with a successful executive ends with the executive summoning guards to get rid of him.

title: Workaholic Rehab Means Paid Idleness

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If I become a workaholic, will the company pay for rehab?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What would workaholics rehab look like?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hope it involves getting paid while doing no work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's what you do now.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: At rehab I think they do your laundry for you.

situation: Wally sits across the desk from The Boss and asks whether the company would pay for rehab if he became a workaholic. The Boss asks what that rehab would look like, and Wally says he hopes it means being paid to do no work. The Boss points out that's already what Wally does, and Wally replies that rehab might also include free laundry service.
punchline: Wally's idea of a cure for overwork is exactly his current lazy routine, and he isn't even embarrassed by the Boss's accusation, instead asking for a perk on top.
summary: Wally eyes a hypothetical addiction treatment as a chance to loaf on the company's dime, and doesn't mind being called out for already doing so.

title: Zig When Others Zag Leadership

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The secret to being a great leader is to zig when others zag.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Coincidentally, that is the same strategy used by the insane.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I should fire you for your insubordination.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or you could zig.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss shares his leadership wisdom about zigging when others zag. Dilbert dryly points out that the same strategy is used by insane people. The Boss threatens to fire him for insubordination, and Dilbert replies that he could instead zig, turning the Boss's own advice against him.
punchline: Dilbert uses the Boss's own 'zig when others zag' maxim to suggest he should do the unexpected thing and not fire him, exposing the advice as hollow while escaping punishment.
summary: A manager's contrarian leadership slogan is mocked as madness by an employee, who then uses the same slogan to dodge being fired.

file: 2014/2014-01-30_frustration_negative_good communicator_terrible ideas_be more positive_fixed now_good job_leadership.gif
title: Negative Employee Or Good Communicator

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're being too negative lately.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Am I negative or am I a good communicator surrounded by terrible ideas?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just try to be more positive!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, I'm all fixed now. Good job on the leadership.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has been too negative lately. Dilbert questions whether he is really negative or simply an effective communicator reacting to bad ideas. The Boss ignores the point and tells him to be more positive, so Dilbert sarcastically praises the Boss's leadership.
punchline: Dilbert fakes positivity by giving the Boss sarcastic praise, showing that demands for positivity just encourage insincere flattery rather than addressing the terrible ideas behind the criticism.
summary: Told to stop being so negative, an employee wonders if he is merely honest about bad ideas, then complies with hollow compliments for his boss.

title: CEO Works Harder Than Other CEOs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can only succeed if we work harder than our competitors!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oops, gotta go. My helicopter is here to take me to my massage appointment on my superyacht.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop staring at me. I only have to work harder than the other CEOs.

setting: Office, shown against a plain green background
situation: The Boss gives a motivational speech telling employees they must work harder than the competition to succeed. He then announces he has to leave because his helicopter is waiting to take him to a massage on his superyacht. When he notices people staring, he defensively says he only needs to work harder than other CEOs.
punchline: The executive demands extreme effort from his staff while living a life of luxury, justifying it by comparing himself only to other pampered CEOs.
summary: A boss preaches relentless hard work to his team, then jets off for a yacht massage and brushes off the hypocrisy with a self-serving standard.

file: 2014/2014-02-01_basket cases_bottom dollar_dysfunction_mentor_new hire_office equipment_office robot_human life_less important.gif
