transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need someone to mentor our new hire, but every one of you is dysfunctional.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I'm having our office robot do the mentoring. It can't be worse than you basket cases.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: So... human life is less important than office equipment?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Far less. It's not even close.

situation: At a team meeting, the Boss announces that he needs a mentor for the new hire but considers all the employees too dysfunctional. He assigns the office robot to do the mentoring instead. The new hire, Asok, asks whether this means human life is less important than office equipment, and the robot cheerfully confirms it.
punchline: The robot agrees that human life is far less important than office equipment, confirming the company's values and the Boss's low opinion of his employees.
summary: Deciding his staff is too flawed to guide a newcomer, a manager hands the job to a machine that then confirms people matter less than gadgets.

title: Typing In All Caps For Hearing Aid

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll just send a quick text to Paul.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Paul has a hearing aid, so type in all caps.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good idea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's messed up.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: A little.

setting: Office break area, while the characters stand around holding coffee mugs
situation: The Boss says he will text a coworker named Paul. Wally advises him to type in all capital letters because Paul wears a hearing aid, and the Boss agrees it is a good idea. Dilbert points out how nonsensical that is, and Wally concedes it a little.
punchline: Wally's advice is absurd because a hearing aid has no bearing on how a written text message is read, and the Boss believes it anyway, with Wally only grudgingly admitting it is a bit messed up.
summary: A gullible manager follows a coworker's bogus tip that shouting in capital letters will help a hard-of-hearing recipient read a text.

title: New Hire Punished for Questions

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Inexperienced guy

transcript.speaker: Inexperienced Guy
transcript.text: Put together a deck showing the minimum viable product feature list.

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: What is a deck? What is a minimum viable product? How would I know what the features are?

transcript.speaker: Inexperienced Guy
transcript.text: I have no respect for people who ask questions.

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: First day, not good.

situation: A manager labelled 'Inexperienced Guy' hands a new employee on his first day an assignment full of jargon: a deck showing the minimum viable product feature list. The newcomer, understandably confused, asks what a deck and a minimum viable product are and how he would know the features. The manager responds that he has no respect for people who ask questions, leaving the new hire thinking his first day is going badly.
punchline: The inexperienced manager gives vague, jargon-laden instructions and then punishes the new hire for asking the very questions needed to do the job.
summary: A clueless supervisor assigns buzzword-heavy work to a rookie and then scorns him for seeking clarification.

title: Boss's Wisdom Wrecks the Company

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Our sales dropped to zero because you told the media we have a better product coming soon.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And 95% of the staff resigned because you announced plans to fire 50% of them.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Maybe it would be better if you never spoke to anyone again.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How would people get my wisdom?

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, sits across from the Boss and lists the damage caused by his public statements. Announcing a better product coming soon killed current sales, and announcing layoffs made nearly all the staff quit. Catbert suggests he stop talking to anyone.
punchline: The Boss, oblivious to the disasters his remarks caused, worries only about how people will benefit from his supposed wisdom.
summary: After a pair of ruinous public announcements, an HR chief proposes muzzling the executive, who thinks his pronouncements are a gift to the world.

file: 2014/2014-03-29_miserliness_wages_good work_saves billons_no raise_personal item_on desk_insoubordination_abuse of power_boss_money.gif
title: No Raise Over Desk Item

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, your good work has saved the company over a billion dollars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I can't give you a raise because you once had a personal item on your desk.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How are those things equal?!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And here comes the insubordination.

situation: The Boss praises Alice for saving the company over a billion dollars, then tells her he cannot give her a raise because she once kept a personal item on her desk. When Alice angrily objects to the absurd comparison, the Boss calmly labels her protest insubordination.
punchline: The Boss uses a trivial rule violation to justify denying a deserved raise, then pre-emptively frames any complaint as insubordination so that Alice has no legitimate way to object.
summary: A manager acknowledges an employee's enormous financial contribution yet refuses to reward it over a petty desk violation, then brands her outrage as defiance.

title: Dogbert's News: Look In Mirror

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In today's news, people all over the world continued to act like idiots.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Most of the time it didn't turn out well.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For details, look in your mirror.

setting: Dogbert News Network anchor desk, with Dilbert watching at home
situation: Dogbert, seated at the Dogbert News Network desk, delivers a newscast stating that people everywhere kept acting like idiots and mostly suffered for it. In the last panel, Dilbert watches the broadcast on his computer screen as Dogbert tells viewers to look in their mirror for details.
punchline: The news anchor ends the report by pointing out that the idiots in the story include the viewer, delivering an insult disguised as a news tip.
summary: A canine news anchor wraps up his broadcast by sending viewers to their own reflections to learn who has been behaving foolishly.

file: 2014/2014-06-28_wounds & injuries_work related injury_year off_with pay_drinking coffee_listening to podcast_personal_butt hurts_kill_murder_surfing internet.gif
title: Sitting Injury Demands Paid Year Off

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have a work-related injury, so I need a year off with pay.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: What happened?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I was drinking coffee and listening to a podcast while surfing the Internet for personal reasons.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now my buttocks hurt.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I think I'm within my rights to kill you.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells Catbert, the evil HR director, that he needs a year off with pay for a work-related injury. He explains that he hurt himself by sitting, drinking coffee, listening to a podcast and browsing the web for personal reasons. Catbert responds by saying he is within his rights to kill Wally.
punchline: Wally's claim of a work injury is really just sore buttocks from slacking off all day, which is so absurd that the HR director threatens to murder him.
summary: A lazy employee tries to claim a year of paid leave because his backside aches from idle sitting, and the HR cat answers with a murder threat.

file: 2014/2014-01-21_career scuccess_babbling jargon_special gift_paid for nothing_lead by example.gif
title: Special Gift: Babbling Jargon

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The key to career success is finding your special gift.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My special gift is getting paid for doing nothing but babbling jargon.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I should lead by example.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you already did.

situation: The Boss lectures Dilbert that career success comes from finding your special gift. Dilbert replies that his gift is being paid for nothing but babbling jargon. The Boss thinks he should lead by example, and Dilbert points out that he already has.
punchline: Dilbert implies that the Boss himself gets paid for doing nothing but spouting jargon, so he has already been leading by example without realizing it.
summary: A manager's pep talk about finding a talent backfires when his employee describes the manager's own job as meaningless buzzword chatter.

file: 2014/2014-04-09_acting ceo_rolex accident_power crazed_obliterated human decency_abuse of power_furry friend.gif
title: Acting CEO Power Goes to Head

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The board wants you to be our acting CEO until our regular CEO recovers from his Rolex accident.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (thought) Buwhahaha!!! The power has gone to my head and obliterated my last crumb of human decency!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're creeping me out.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (thought) I'm going to buff my shoes with you, my furry friend.

setting: The Boss's office, at his desk
situation: Catbert tells the Boss that the board wants him to serve as acting CEO while the regular CEO recovers from a Rolex accident. The Boss, in thought bubbles, gleefully admits that power has corrupted him and he starts grinning maniacally. Catbert notices his creepy expression, and the Boss privately plans to use Catbert to polish his shoes.
punchline: Even before taking the job, the Boss's mind instantly turns to abusing power, and he plans to treat the already-sinister Catbert as a shoe rag, so that the person who wields cruelty for a living becomes its victim.
summary: A sudden promotion to interim chief executive instantly turns a clueless manager into a gleeful tyrant who eyes his subordinate as footwear polish.

title: Boring Stories Kill Office Plants

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hey, Plantkiller, do you have the data I asked for?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Plantkiller? Who calls me that?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Everyone does. Your stories are so boring that you kill all office plants within earshot.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Give me a hand signal when you're done.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This reminds me of the time I took the stairs.

situation: Alice asks a coworker for data and calls him 'Plantkiller', explaining that his stories are so dull they kill office plants nearby. She tells him to signal when he's finished talking. Rather than getting the hint, he launches into yet another dull story about taking the stairs.
punchline: The coworker proves Alice's point by immediately starting another boring anecdote, oblivious to the insult.
summary: A woman mocks a colleague's tedious storytelling as lethal to houseplants, and he responds by beginning a pointless tale about climbing stairs.

file: 2014/2014-12-28_arguing_email_expectations_logic_sleep_winning_work ethic_promptly respond_employees_necessary_brain function_succumbs to leadership_dysfunctional moron_confsuion_win converstions_ceo_health_business.gif
title: Sleep Deprivation Wins The Argument

transcript.text: You didn't promptly respond to my email last night.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You sent that email at 1 a.m.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I expect my employees to be checking email at all times.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sleep is necessary for normal brain function.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anyone who succumbs to your leadership on this topic will turn into a dysfunctional moron in 48 hours.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't see where you're going with this. It's all so confusing in my brain.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So tired... can't stay awake...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't usually win conversations this decisively.

setting: Office hallway and doorway, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: The Boss scolds Dilbert for not answering an email sent at 1 a.m., insisting employees should check email around the clock. Dilbert points out that sleep is necessary for brain function, and the Boss's own reasoning begins to fall apart from exhaustion until he collapses asleep in the doorway.
punchline: The Boss's own sleep deprivation proves Dilbert's point, as he becomes confused and passes out while arguing against sleep, handing Dilbert an easy victory.
summary: A boss who demands round-the-clock email vigilance is undone by his own lack of sleep and keels over mid-argument.

title: Naked Vacuuming Accident Delays Dilbert

transcript.text: He said something about having a freak accident while vacuuming naked.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you tell him traffic was bad?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: More or less.

setting: Office cubicle area at a receptionist's desk
situation: A pointy-haired man in a blue shirt is told by a cubicle-dwelling coworker that Dilbert called to say he would be late for a meeting. The coworker reveals Dilbert's actual excuse was a freak accident while vacuuming naked. When Dilbert finally arrives and asks if the coworker told them traffic was bad, the coworker deadpans that they more or less did.
punchline: The coworker's claim of passing along 'traffic was bad' is a flat, sarcastic understatement, since they actually reported the embarrassing naked vacuuming accident instead of the cover story.
summary: A coworker relays a late colleague's mortifying real excuse to the boss, then deadpans that it was basically the same as blaming traffic.

title: Career Advice From Dilbert: Don't Decide

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I brought my son to work. Do you have any career advice for him?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All boys your age are idiots. If you make any career decisions today, your life will forever be determined by an idiot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are we expecting any unforeseen problems today?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But you get used to it.

setting: Office cubicle area on take-your-son-to-work day
situation: A coworker brings his young son to work and asks Dilbert for career advice for the boy. Dilbert bluntly tells the kid that boys his age are idiots, so any career decision he makes now will be made by an idiot. The Boss then walks up asking about unforeseen problems, and Dilbert's remark about getting used to it lands as a jab at the Boss.
punchline: Dilbert implies that being stuck with decisions made by an idiot is something you simply get used to, a dig at the Boss who is an idiot making decisions for everyone.
summary: Asked to mentor a visiting kid, Dilbert warns him that youthful decisions are made by idiots, then hints that his own boss is proof you eventually adapt to that.
themes: take your child to work day

file: 2014/2014-12-27_customer retention_death_immersive technology_moratlity_technology_virtual reality_immersive 3d head gear_starved_bliss point_medical.gif
title: Customers Too Immersed to Eat

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We found the "bliss point" for immersive 3-D headgear.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The product is so good that 87% of our customers starved to death while using it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We never get the customer retention part right.

setting: Conference room during a product presentation
situation: Dilbert presents a product demo showing a man wearing immersive 3-D headgear, claiming they have found the perfect 'bliss point.' He reveals that 87% of customers starved to death while using it. He then remarks to the executives at the table that they never get customer retention right.
punchline: The product is so addictive that users die of starvation, which Dilbert treats as merely a customer retention failure rather than a catastrophe.
summary: A presenter proudly explains that his virtual reality headset is so engrossing that most users die of hunger, then calls it a retention shortfall.

file: 2014/2014-09-11_complimenting people_flattery_indirect_made car_make his own car_new car_parking lot.gif
title: Complimenting The Car's Makers, Not You

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I saw your new car in the parking lot. It's nice.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm complimenting the people who made your car, not you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well, I guess only one of us knows how to make his own car.

setting: Office hallway or break area, both holding or near coffee
situation: Dilbert compliments a coworker on his new car, and the coworker thanks him. Dilbert then clarifies that the praise is for the car's manufacturers rather than the owner. The coworker retorts that Dilbert can't make his own car either, so neither of them deserves credit.
punchline: Dilbert's backhanded clarification that the credit belongs to the car makers is turned back on him, since he is just as unable to build a car and so has no standing to be smug.
summary: A grudging compliment about a colleague's new vehicle turns into a tit-for-tat over who can claim credit for something neither of them built.

file: 2014/2014-05-09_studies_healthy exercise_healthier lifestyle_poor health_ruin meeting_attend stupid meetings.gif
title: Reversing Causation, Then Ruining Meetings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Studies show that people who exercise are healthier.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's because people who are in poor health don't exercise.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why does it seem as if you ruin every meeting?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is it because I only attend the ones that are stupid?

situation: The Boss cites a study claiming that exercisers are healthier, and Wally points out that the causation may run the other way, since unhealthy people don't exercise. The annoyed Boss then asks why Wally seems to ruin every meeting, and Wally replies that he only goes to the stupid ones.
punchline: Wally applies the same reversed-causation logic to himself: meetings aren't ruined because he attends, he attends only the meetings that are already stupid.
summary: A manager's health statistic gets flipped on its head by a coworker who then uses the same trick to deflect blame for spoiling meetings.

title: Declining Constructive Criticism, Requesting Ignorant Opinions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you want some constructive criticism?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, but I would love some under-informed opinions about things you don't understand.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That took a lot of the fun out of it.

situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert's desk and offers him some constructive criticism. Dilbert declines and instead sarcastically asks for uninformed opinions about things the Boss doesn't understand. The Boss walks away thinking that Dilbert has spoiled his fun.
punchline: Dilbert bluntly admits that the Boss's feedback is really just uninformed opinion, so the Boss loses the enjoyment of delivering it.
summary: A manager offers feedback, but his employee preempts it by naming it for what it is: ignorant meddling, which leaves the manager deflated.

file: 2014/2014-07-15_business ethics_takes picture_flash spot_vision_place ads_little spot_huge personal violation_your privacy.gif
title: Advertising on the Camera Flash Spot

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would be a huge personal violation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bah! You said the same thing when we took your privacy.

setting: Office, standing in a hallway or workspace
situation: Dilbert holding a coffee mug mentions that a camera flash leaves a bright spot in your vision for a few seconds. The Boss immediately wants to sell advertising on that spot. When Dilbert objects that it would be a personal violation, the Boss dismisses him, noting Dilbert made the same complaint when the company took his privacy.
punchline: The Boss shrugs off the ethical objection because the company has already stripped Dilbert of his privacy, implying that no invasion is too much once the first one has been accepted.
summary: Upon hearing about a harmless visual quirk, the Boss spots a chance to monetize it and waves away objections by pointing to past intrusions.

file: 2014/2014-05-17_efficiency experts_friendship_money_you won't quit_friends at work_pay less_relationships.gif

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.text: So this guy is costing me money?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and Wally that experts say employees are more engaged when they have a friend at work. He then reveals that engagement lets him pay people less because they won't quit. Dilbert concludes that Wally, his supposed work friend, is costing him money, and Wally brushes off the idea of any friendship.
punchline: The boss's real motive for encouraging workplace friendships is to justify lower pay, and Wally sarcastically denies he is Dilbert's friend at all.
summary: A manager pitches workplace friendships as a way to keep staff cheaply loyal, and the supposed friend wants nothing to do with it.

file: 2014/2014-12-21_anger_criticism_perfection_psychological disorder_psychological evaluation_perfectionist_warning_not a problem_cognitive dissonance_unrealistic optimism_projection bias_jerk_anger issues.gif

situation: A woman hands Dilbert a paper, warning him she is a perfectionist. Dilbert reads her writing and starts diagnosing a string of psychological biases, delivering them as insults. When she finally calls him a jerk, he cheerfully declares that her anger issues have appeared.
punchline: Dilbert insults her with armchair psychology, then treats her justified angry reaction as further proof of her disorders, so she can't win.
summary: After a self-described perfectionist hands over her writing, Dilbert rattles off a list of her supposed mental flaws and then labels her annoyed response as one more symptom.

file: 2014/2014-06-25_celestial bodies_managers & supervisors_black hole_management style_dangerous_importnat emails_employee named ted_business.gif

punchline: The Boss is relieved that the black hole only swallows employee emails, but it has also swallowed Ted, and nobody treats that as a real problem.
summary: A hole in the office floor swallows the staff's messages to their manager, and eventually one unlucky worker as well.

title: Winning Contest for Fridge Cleaning

The Boss walks up and says he needs one of his underlings to clean the mold out of the office fridge, then tells Dilbert it's his top priority. Wally, having avoided the task, asks what this 'winning' is that he keeps hearing about.
punchline: Dilbert gets stuck with the disgusting chore, leaving Wally the 'winner' in a way that is ironic since Wally's win is simply escaping work, and he doesn't even know what winning means.
summary: A coworker's chat about the benefits of winning is followed by the boss assigning one worker an unpleasant moldy-fridge cleanup while another dodges it.

situation: A coworker delivers a requested analysis, and the gray-haired colleague who asked for it admits they forgot to say it's no longer needed. title: Robot Boss Learns Why Employees Lie

situation: A temporary robot boss wonders whether the employees are lying to him constantly. Catbert, the HR director, explains that management trained them to lie by punishing honesty. The robot then asks Alice about her project and she cheerfully claims it is perfect, proving the point.

summary: A mechanical stand-in manager suspects his staff of dishonesty and learns that the company's own habits taught them to fib.

file: 2014/2014-07-11_engineers_work ethic_personal lifestley engineer_career advice_work and leisure_hours per week_ideal means.gif

punchline: The employee's agreement that he can take orders from a soulless, unintelligent creature is a dig at the Boss himself, who misses the insult and congratulates him on his good attitude.
summary: A manager leaving on holiday names a mindless machine as his stand-in, and a worker's deadpan reply slips a jab past him unnoticed.

situation: Dilbert stands beside Dogbert, who is typing at his computer. transcript.text: It's like that but with less attendance.

setting: The Boss's office, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: An employee wearing glasses and a tie asks the boss if he can shift his workday to 4 a.m. through noon, citing studies that successful people start early. The boss asks how he would verify the employee is actually working in the early hours, and the employee points out the boss has no way of knowing now either. The boss admits he doesn't know, and the employee says it would be the same, just with less attendance.
punchline: The employee reveals that the boss never actually knows whether staff are working, so unsupervised early hours would simply be the status quo with fewer people in the building.
summary: A worker proposes an ultra-early schedule and cleverly argues that management's ignorance of what employees do makes oversight irrelevant.

file: 2014/2014-05-18_electronic mail_mobile (cell) phones_instant message_emailed_texted_personal phone_called_inperson_negate_ignore_push away_no answer_excuses.gif
title: Every Channel Is The Wrong One

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You never answered my I.M.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You should have emailed me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I did. You didn't answer my email.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If it was so important, you should have texted me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You didn't answer my texts.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You have to text my personal phone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You didn't answer those texts either.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Had it been important, you would have called me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I did. You don't answer your phone and you don't return calls.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So here I am.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's premature to get your hopes up.

situation: Dilbert tells Alice she never answered his instant message, and she replies that he should have used a different channel. Each time he shows he already tried email, texts, her personal phone and a call, she names yet another method he should have used. Out of options, he finally confronts her in person, and she still brushes him off.
punchline: Alice will always claim the request should have come through some other channel, so no method of reaching her will ever count, even face to face.
summary: A coworker who refuses to be reached keeps moving the goalposts on how she should have been contacted until he simply walks up to her desk.

file: 2014/2014-10-22_deception_investor_investors_pick up lines_start up idea_funding_saturday night drinks_date.gif
title: Angel Investor Wants Drinks Saturday

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: An angel investor agreed to meet with me about my start-up idea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You need to be careful because he might be...

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: We're meeting for drinks at his house on Saturday night.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm socially inept and even I know that sounds wrong.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: He keeps texting to say he can't wait to fund me.

situation: A coworker tells Dilbert that an angel investor has agreed to hear her start-up idea. Dilbert starts to warn her to be careful, and she explains the meeting is for drinks at the investor's house on Saturday night. She admits that even she, being socially inept, can tell that sounds wrong, and the investor keeps texting that he can't wait to fund her.
punchline: The investor's eagerness to "fund" her and his insistence on a late-night meeting at his home strongly suggest he's after a date, not a business deal, and she is aware of how suspicious it looks.
summary: A woman who's hoping to land funding for her business idea realizes the wealthy backer's invitation may have less to do with investing than with romance.

file: 2014/2014-09-01_cruelty_work ethic_human resources_feeling of inadequency_boost company profits_all weekedn_adequate temporary basis_business.gif
title: HR Offers Temporary Adequacy For Weekend Work

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: My job in Human Resources is to instill in you a permanent feeling of inadequacy.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your only hope for feeling good about yourself is to work feverishly to boost company profits.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If you work all weekend for free, I am willing to call you adequate on a temporary basis.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll take it.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, sits behind a desk and tells Dilbert that his job is to make employees feel permanently inadequate. He explains that the only way Dilbert can feel good about himself is by working hard to boost company profits. He then offers to call Dilbert adequate, but only temporarily and only if he works all weekend for free, and Dilbert accepts.
punchline: Dilbert is so desperate for a moment of validation that he gladly accepts a temporary label of adequacy in exchange for unpaid weekend labor, showing how companies exploit employees' insecurity.
summary: A malicious HR boss admits he exists to undermine staff confidence, then dangles a short-lived compliment as payment for free overtime, and the worker eagerly agrees.

title: Third CEO Fires the Executives

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a co-CEO, but it isn't working because we disagree on everything.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We want to hire you as our third CEO so we always have a tiebreaker.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I accept. The new guy and I have decided to fire you and split the CEO spot two ways.

setting: Executive office, with Dogbert sitting on a desk
situation: The Boss explains that his co-CEO arrangement is failing because the two disagree on everything. Together they offer Dogbert a third CEO position to act as a tiebreaker. Dogbert accepts and promptly announces that he and the new co-CEO will fire the Boss and share the top job between them.
punchline: Hiring a tiebreaker backfires because the two other parties immediately agree on something, which is to get rid of the one who hired them.
summary: Two bickering chief executives recruit a third to settle their arguments, only to be undercut when the newcomer forms an alliance against one of them.

title: Catbert's Pharaoh Policy Fact-Check

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Egyptian pharaohs killed the engineers who built their pyramids so they would never share their secrets.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No . . . I don't think they did.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Really? Dang!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Can we reschedule this meeting until I find a historically accurate explanation of our new policy?

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, with Catbert perched on a desk
situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, tells Dilbert that Egyptian pharaohs killed the engineers who built their pyramids to keep their secrets safe. Dilbert corrects him, saying he doesn't think that actually happened. Catbert, disappointed, asks to reschedule the meeting until he can find a historically accurate justification for the company's new policy.
punchline: The new policy is evidently to kill engineers to protect company secrets, and Catbert's only concern is that his historical precedent for it was factually wrong, not that the policy is monstrous.
summary: An HR villain tries to justify a sinister new rule with ancient history, and when the history turns out to be false, he simply postpones the meeting to find better cover.

file: 2014/2014-08-30_executives_how-to_snobbishness_book on success_hard work_wise decisions_being lucky_lazy and dumb.gif
title: Co-Authoring a Book on Success

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to co-author a book on success with me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The goal is to make readers believe success comes from hard work and wise decisions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So instead of hating me for being lucky, they will hate themselves for being lazy and dumb.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And for buying your book?

setting: Office, with Dogbert standing on a desk
situation: The Boss asks Dogbert to co-author a book on success with him. He explains the book's purpose is to convince readers that success comes from hard work and wise decisions, so they will blame themselves rather than resent him for being lucky. Dogbert adds that readers will also hate themselves for buying the book.
punchline: The book is designed to make readers feel inadequate for not succeeding, and Dogbert points out they will also regret paying for it.
summary: A lucky executive wants a self-help book that shifts resentment onto readers, and his cynical co-author notes that it profits from their regret too.

file: 2014/2014-06-14_chocolate_obliviousness_dark chocolate_brain works better_magical thinking_fad chasing_eating_three pounds.gif
title: Chocolate Reveals Career of Fads

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I ate three pounds of dark chocolate and it made my brain work better.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I realize that everything I've done in my career up to this point has been magical thinking and fad-chasing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What should I do?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Stop eating chocolate.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Catbert that eating three pounds of dark chocolate made his brain work better. With his improved thinking he admits his whole career has been magical thinking and fad-chasing, then asks Catbert what he should do. Catbert advises him to stop eating chocolate.
punchline: Catbert implies that the Boss's only moment of clear thinking was a chocolate-induced state, and that he is better off returning to his usual oblivious self than realizing how misguided his career has been.
summary: After a chocolate binge gives the boss a flash of self-awareness about his foolish career, his cat advisor tells him to quit the sweets.

title: Everything Is a Top Priority

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I can't do my budget projections until you tell me your priorities for the coming year.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Then you say, "Everything is a top priority. Fuh-fuh-fuh-fuh-fuh."

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I hope this is what you meant by "bring me solutions, not problems."

situation: Carol, standing in front of the Boss's desk, says she needs his priorities for the coming year before she can prepare budget projections. She then acts out the answer she expects from him, that everything is a top priority, and finishes by pointing out she is bringing him a solution as he demanded. The Boss sits silently at his desk throughout.
punchline: Carol pre-empts the Boss's predictable non-answer and sarcastically presents her own scripted version of the conversation as the 'solution, not problem' he always asks for.
summary: A manager's assistant saves everyone time by scripting her boss's evasive reply herself and then sarcastically claims it as the solution he keeps demanding.

title: Boss Knows Nothing, Needs One Slide

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to make a PowerPoint deck for my meeting with investors.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll be telling them everything I know about technology, competition, and the industry.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... just the one slide?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Huh?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How big do these fonts go?

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, asks Dilbert to build a PowerPoint deck for an investor meeting, saying he'll cover everything he knows about technology, competition and the industry. Dilbert asks if that means just one slide, and the confused Boss doesn't catch the insult. Dilbert then asks how big the fonts can go, implying the content will be tiny.
punchline: Dilbert implies the Boss knows so little that his entire knowledge fits on one slide in giant font, and the oblivious Boss doesn't realize he's been insulted.
summary: A manager prepping for an investor pitch is subtly mocked by his employee, who suggests his expertise would barely fill a single slide.

title: Optimist Wants To Die Younger

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What a great day!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What's all this nonsense?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm trying to be an optimist.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Studies show that optimists die younger.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So this optimism thing just makes you look ignorant.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And because my happiness is based on a comparison to my peers, I don't want your future to be too bright.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop thinking you're better than me in the future!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is exactly why I want to die younger.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You already knew that optimists die young?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yup! How's your plan working?

situation: Dilbert cheerfully announces it's a great day and explains he is trying to be an optimist. Alice, an irritable coworker, lectures him that optimists die younger and that she resents anyone whose future might be brighter than hers. Dilbert reveals he already knew optimists die young and that being around Alice makes him want that outcome.
punchline: Dilbert's apparent optimism was a ploy: he wants to die younger to escape Alice's negativity, and he sarcastically asks how her plan to discourage him is working.
summary: A man's sunny attitude draws a bitter coworker's scorn, but he turns her warning about early death into a jab at her own misery.

file: 2014/2014-07-26_surveillance_outsourced micromanaging_amazons mechanical turk_other countries_computer cameras_criticize_resisting change.gif
title: Outsourced Micromanaging Via Mechanical Turk

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I outsourced my micromanaging to Amazon's Mechanical Turk.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: People in other countries will watch you on your computer cameras and criticize every move you make.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That feels like a terrible idea.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop resisting change.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces to his team that he has outsourced his micromanaging to Amazon's Mechanical Turk. Remote workers in other countries will watch employees through their computer cameras and criticize everything they do. When Dilbert objects, the Boss dismisses the concern by accusing him of resisting change.
punchline: The Boss uses 'resisting change' as a catch-all dismissal to shut down a legitimate objection to invasive, crowdsourced surveillance of employees.
summary: A manager hands off his nagging to anonymous overseas gig workers who will spy on staff through webcams, and brushes off complaints as mere reluctance to adapt.

title: Lawyers Complicate Simple Three-Point Proposal

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your proposal with the three bullet points looks good to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll ask my lawyers to turn it into an incomprehensible nine-page document that introduces complexity risks for... no... reason.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can I get back to you in the year 2018?

transcript.speaker: Businessman
transcript.text: Stop making me cry!

setting: Conference table in an office meeting room
situation: A boss reviews a simple three-bullet-point proposal from a visitor and says it looks good. He then explains that his lawyers will inflate it into an incomprehensible nine-page document that adds risk for no reason, and that he can respond in 2018. The proposer breaks down in tears at the prospect of the delay.
punchline: A simple, workable deal gets buried in needless legal complexity and years of delay, enough to make the proposer weep.
summary: A manager praises a short proposal, then cheerfully promises that legal review will bloat it and delay any answer for years, reducing the presenter to tears.

title: No Winners in Intern Promotion

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Is it my imagination or is there no career path here from intern to anything else?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If we promote you, we just have to find another intern. No one wins in that scenario.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Actually, I would be the winner in that scenario.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I've never thought of it that way and I don't like it.

setting: Catbert's office in the human resources department
situation: An intern asks Catbert, the evil HR director, why there seems to be no career path from intern to any other position. Catbert explains that promoting the intern would only force the company to find a replacement intern, so nobody benefits. The intern points out that he would benefit, which Catbert had not considered.
punchline: Catbert's HR logic ignores the promoted employee as a beneficiary, and when he realizes the intern would win, he dislikes the idea rather than reconsidering.
summary: The company's cat-shaped HR chief rejects an intern's hope of advancement because it would merely create another vacancy to fill, overlooking that the intern himself would gain.

file: 2014/2014-10-11_business casual_clothing_dorks_dress code_fashion_business dorky_unstylish_tan colored_dumb name_new order.gif
title: Business Dorky Dress Code

transcript.text: Our new dress code is "business dorky."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your clothes must be dorky, unstylish, and 50% tan colored.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... business casual?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's a dumb name for it.

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, announces a new dress code called "business dorky" to Dilbert and the Boss seated at a conference table. He describes the required clothing as dorky, unstylish, and half tan. Dilbert points out that this is just business casual, and Catbert agrees that business casual is a dumb name for it.
punchline: Catbert's absurdly honest description of the dress code is simply business casual, which he admits is a dumb name, mocking how drab and unfashionable office casual wear really is.
summary: The company's HR chief unveils a mock-honest clothing policy that turns out to be the familiar office dress standard under a blunter name.

title: Lonely Leader Needs Less Jerkiness

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Being a leader is a lonely job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Try being less of a #!@*. Then people might want to spend time with you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't see how that could work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can we get back to you manipulating my emotions for financial gain?

situation: The Boss complains to Dilbert that leadership is a lonely job. Dilbert suggests he could fix that by being less of a jerk so people would want his company. The Boss dismisses the idea, and Dilbert sarcastically asks to return to the Boss's attempt to manipulate his emotions for money.
punchline: The Boss's self-pity was really a manipulation tactic, and he is so oblivious that he rejects the obvious solution of being nicer, leaving Dilbert to point out the scheme.
summary: A boss fishing for sympathy gets blunt advice about his personality and brushes it off, revealing his sympathy-seeking was a calculated ploy.

title: Air Bags Prevent Accidental Work Assignments

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I added air bags to my underpants to avoid accidental assignments.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, Wally, I need you to...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: BAM!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I'll ask someone else.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The system works!

situation: Wally tells Dilbert he has installed air bags in his underpants to avoid being handed work by accident. When the Boss walks up and starts to ask him for something, the air bags inflate with a bam and bury Wally in padding. The Boss gives up and decides to ask someone else.
punchline: Wally's absurd air bag contraption works exactly as intended, since being inflated into an obstacle is enough to make a manager pick another victim, which Wally treats as a triumph of his lazy engineering.
summary: A slacker engineers a ridiculous inflatable defense that bounces management away whenever work comes near him.

file: 2014/2014-04-28_business people_work ethic_new line_products_business plan_good track record_useful_accurate_make up numbers.gif
title: Business Plan With Invented Numbers

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that because business plans have a good track record of being useful and accurate?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, it's nothing like that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good, because I plan to make up all of the numbers.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to write a business plan for a new product line. Dilbert sarcastically asks whether business plans are known for being useful and accurate, and the Boss denies that is the reason. Dilbert replies that he will simply invent all the figures.
punchline: Business plans are widely understood to be fiction, so Dilbert cheerfully admits he will fabricate the numbers, and the Boss's denial confirms the exercise is meaningless.
summary: Asked to produce a business plan for upcoming products, an engineer cheerfully reveals he will fabricate every figure in it.

title: Consultant Is a Hungover Travel Wreck

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: My life is a nightmare of business travel, loneliness, and sleep deprivation.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I'm only 25 years old!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a travel day. He'll calm down after he drinks lunch.

situation: The Boss introduces a consultant he hired from a firm called Booze Muhkidney while Dilbert sits listening. The consultant, a gray-suited man with glasses, laments his miserable life of constant travel, loneliness and sleep deprivation, adding that he is only 25. The Boss shrugs it off, saying the consultant will settle down once he drinks his lunch.
punchline: The consultant's bleak, burned-out state is brushed aside by the Boss, who casually implies the man is a heavy drinker whose mood improves with alcohol, echoing the firm's name Booze Muhkidney.
summary: A young, exhausted consultant from a firm with a boozy name complains about his wretched travelling life, and the boss dismisses it by noting he'll feel better after a liquid lunch.

title: Work Is Escape From Home

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know how you juggle work plus a family.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Spending time with my family is like fighting porcupines in a salt mine. I come here just to get away from them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So ... you like your job?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No, but at least I can go home to get away from it.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker seated at her computer that he doesn't know how she balances work and family. She replies that family life is so unpleasant she comes to work to escape it. When Dilbert asks if that means she likes her job, she says no, but she can go home to escape it.
punchline: She is miserable at both work and home, and each place only serves as relief from the other.
summary: A woman reveals that she dreads both her family and her job, using each as a refuge from the other.

file: 2014/2014-06-02_hypocrisy_managers & supervisors_wages_world records set_best employee_job performance_no raise_drug enhancing drugs_injected against will_leadership_business_money.gif

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.text: You injected me against my will.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: The Boss praises an employee for setting world records in job performance, then refuses him a raise because he used performance-enhancing drugs. The employee protests that the Boss injected him against his will, and the Boss replies that this is how leadership works.
punchline: The Boss forced the drugs on the employee himself, then punishes him for them and defines leadership as making people do things they wouldn't choose to do.
summary: A manager lauds a record-setting worker, withholds his raise over drug use, and shrugs off the fact that he drugged the man himself.

file: 2014/2014-06-20_gadgets_beat up_strangers_new glasses_with camera_less creepy_defenseless_user error_photoshopped_head on donkey.gif

punchline: The Boss blames the victim for a product's obvious privacy flaw, and Dilbert responds with a petty, passive-aggressive act of revenge, announcing he has doctored a picture of the Boss as a donkey.
summary: After being roughed up by strangers over a wearable camera gadget, an employee is told by his manager that it's his own fault, and he retaliates with a mocking edited photo.

Dilbert replies that he has already requested, installed and thoroughly tested the patch in production. The Boss, having contributed nothing, says he will go add value somewhere else, and Dilbert agrees that is a good place to do it.
punchline: The Boss's input was entirely unnecessary, and Dilbert sarcastically agrees that the Boss adds value anywhere other than where he is.
summary: A manager issues an instruction that the employee finished long ago, then wanders off to be useful elsewhere, to the employee's sarcastic approval.

file: 2014/2014-07-08_frustration_mental health_work ethic_bad attitude_70 hr. wk.week_hire insane_whistle_happy tune.gif

file: 2014/2014-02-24_costumes_deception_downtrodden employee_awesome person in disguise_spider eggs_bosses coffee_survive_learned_knowledge is over rated.gif

summary: A manager in a flimsy disguise as a regular worker boasts about a macabre prank and then dismisses the idea of learning anything.

file: 2014/2014-01-06_managers & supervisors_suspicion_startegic engineer group_worst in one group_insightful_business.gif
title: Dumping Worst Employees Into Doomed Group

transcript.speaker: The Boss

situation: The Boss tells Ted he is being transferred to a newly created strategic engineering group. Ted shrewdly guesses that the group is a dumping ground for underperformers, to be shut down later so nobody has to be fired individually. The Boss replies that Ted's insight comes at a bad time, implicitly confirming the scheme.
punchline: The Boss's reply implicitly confirms Ted's suspicion, and shows that being perceptive about management's tricks will not save Ted.
summary: A manager's quiet plan to quietly dispose of his weakest staff is exposed by the very employee he is reassigning, and he does not deny it.

title: Wally's Quantum Excuse for Missing Work

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The universe is full of dark matter, quantum strangeness, and hidden dimensions.

transcript.text: In such a universe, can we really know whether or not I did my assignment?

transcript.text: How'd the new excuse work out?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It did well in the A-B test against "You never told me to do that."

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway
situation: Wally stands in front of the seated Boss holding his coffee mug and offers a pseudo-scientific argument that nobody can truly know whether he completed his assignment. Afterward Dilbert asks how the new excuse worked, and Wally says he tested it against his old excuse.
punchline: Wally treats dodging work like a product experiment, A-B testing his excuses to find the most effective way to avoid responsibility.
summary: Wally tries out a physics-flavored excuse to dodge an assignment and then reports on its performance like a marketing experiment.

title: Ghostwriting Boss's Boring Leadership Book

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, I want you to ghostwrite a book of my leadership advice.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Do you plan to read it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, it sounds boring.

situation: The Boss, seated at his desk, orders Tina to ghostwrite a book containing his leadership advice. Tina asks whether he intends to read the finished book. He admits he won't, because it sounds boring to him.
punchline: The Boss wants the credit for a leadership book but finds his own leadership advice so dull that he won't even read it, implying his advice has no real value.
summary: A manager commissions a ghostwritten book of his own wisdom, then admits he would never bother reading something so tedious.

file: 2014/2014-06-18_obstinacy_prove wrong_never work_reflex_worst idea_last day of life_jump off roof.gif
title: Jeff Contradicts Everyone Until Death

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Jeff had to prove everyone wrong.

transcript.speaker: Jeff
transcript.text: That will never work.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: It was like a reflex. He couldn't stop it.

transcript.speaker: Jeff
transcript.text: That's the worst idea I have ever heard.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: This was his last day of life.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You can't jump off the roof right now.

transcript.speaker: Jeff
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

situation: In a meeting, a coworker named Jeff reflexively shoots down every idea, saying it will never work and is the worst idea he has heard. A narrator explains he compulsively has to prove everyone wrong and that this is his last day alive. Alice then says that he can't jump off the roof right now, and Jeff realizes his contrarian habit has trapped him.
punchline: Jeff's compulsive need to contradict everyone means that when Alice tells him he can't jump off the roof, his reflex will force him to do exactly that and die.
summary: A knee-jerk naysayer's habit of contradicting anything said to him seals his fate when someone makes the wrong remark about a rooftop.

title: Keeping Simple Gets Complicated Fast

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The secret to success is keeping things simple.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mean simple in an absolute sense or relative to the alternatives?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It depends on the situation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sounds complicated.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, ending with an exterior shot of an office building
situation: At a meeting table, the Boss declares that the secret to success is keeping things simple. Dilbert asks whether he means simple in an absolute sense or relative to the alternatives. The Boss answers that it depends on the situation, and Dilbert remarks that this sounds complicated, with the speech shown over an exterior view of the office building.
punchline: A simple maxim about simplicity immediately becomes complicated once Dilbert asks a clarifying question, and the Boss's vague answer proves his advice isn't simple at all.
summary: A manager's neat piece of wisdom about simplicity collapses into hedging when an engineer asks him to define it.

file: 2014/2014-02-22_costumes_deception_employees_ordinary workers_new employee_best way_kill boss_kindness_strangling w intestines_business.gif
title: Undercover Boss Hears Murder Plans

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hello, ordinary workers. I am a new employee just like you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We're discussing the best way to kill our boss.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You could kill him with kindness.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm leaning toward strangling him with his own intestines.

situation: The Boss shows up in a disguise with a fake mustache and glasses, introducing himself to two employees as a new coworker. Alice, seeing through the lame disguise, announces they are discussing the best way to kill their boss. The Boss nervously suggests killing him with kindness, and Alice counters with a gruesome preference for strangling him with his own intestines.
punchline: Alice plays along with the Boss's obviously fake disguise while pointedly letting him hear how much his employees hate him, and he gets no gentle response to his suggestion.
summary: A disguised manager poses as a fellow worker and gets an earful of violent fantasies about himself from the staff who clearly recognise him.

title: Boss Offers to Trash-Talk Carol's Family

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I know it isn't easy balancing your work duties and your family.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I thought it would help if I trash-talk your family. That way you won't feel so guilty when you ignore them to do my busywork.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll start with your husband.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Don't bother. I got that one covered.

situation: The Boss pretends to sympathize with Carol's struggle to balance work and family, then offers to insult her family so she will feel less guilty about neglecting them for his busywork. When he proposes starting with her husband, Carol deadpans that she has already handled that one herself.
punchline: The Boss's 'helpful' offer is really a way to get more work out of Carol, and her reply reveals she already has a low opinion of her husband, so his insults are unnecessary.
summary: A manager kindly offers to badmouth an employee's relatives so she can ignore them guilt-free, only to learn she has already got her spouse covered.

title: Garbage Man Debunks Good Days

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I had a great day yesterday!

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: No you didn't.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Good and bad days are only in your mind. The environment is largely the same as the day before.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're ticking me off.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Or am I?

setting: Outdoors on a grassy area beside a blue garbage bin
situation: Dilbert cheerfully tells a garbage man that he had a great day yesterday, and the garbage man flatly contradicts him. He then lectures that good and bad days exist only in one's mind because the environment barely changes. When Dilbert says the man is annoying him, the garbage man turns the same logic back on him.
punchline: The garbage man's claim that moods are purely subjective is undercut when he is asked whether he is actually irritating Dilbert, since by his own logic Dilbert's annoyance is just in his head too.
summary: A trash collector insists that happy and miserable days are mental inventions, then smugly uses that idea to dodge blame for annoying Dilbert.

title: Immersive Goggles Tester Is Dead

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, Ted, how do you like our new 3-D immersive goggles you've been testing for two weeks?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Some people say the experience is so good that you forget to eat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're dead, aren't you...

situation: Dilbert asks Ted, who sits motionless at his desk wearing new 3-D immersive goggles he has been testing for two weeks, how he likes them. Getting no reply, Dilbert remarks that the experience is so good people forget to eat. In the last panel Ted is slumped in his chair and Dilbert concludes he has died.
punchline: Ted was so absorbed in the goggles that he forgot to eat and starved to death, and Dilbert's reaction is calm and matter-of-fact rather than alarmed.
summary: A coworker who has worn experimental goggles for two weeks without responding turns out to have perished at his desk.

file: 2014/2014-09-13_optimism_work ethic_career advancement_asking advice_pet kangaroo_marry one_time lag_promotion.gif
title: Asking The Boss About Kangaroos

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Research says that asking for advice doubles your odds of career advancement.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you think I should get a pet kangaroo?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't care if you marry one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder how long the time lag is until my promotion.

setting: Office break area and conference room
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert that research shows asking for advice doubles your odds of career advancement. Dilbert then asks his boss a ridiculous question about getting a pet kangaroo, and the boss dismissively says he doesn't care if Dilbert marries one. Walking away, Dilbert wonders how long until his promotion arrives.
punchline: Dilbert technically asks for advice to boost his promotion odds, but he deliberately asks a meaningless question, and he still expects the promotion to follow.
summary: Armed with a statistic about seeking advice, Dilbert pesters his indifferent boss with a silly question and then waits for his reward.

file: 2014/2014-02-17_managers & supervisors_sleeping & waking up_get up at 4am_successful people do_power nap_sound sbetter_than looks_business.gif
title: Power Nap After 4 A.M. Wake-Up

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I got up at 4 a.m. because I heard it's what successful people do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Power nap!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This sort of thing always sounds better than it looks.

setting: Office break area with coffee mugs
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and Wally he woke at 4 a.m. because successful people supposedly do that. He then abruptly announces a power nap and collapses onto the floor, while Wally calmly comments on the sight as Dilbert looks on.
punchline: The boss's attempt to imitate the habits of successful people ends with him passed out on the floor, showing that such trendy habits look much worse in practice than they sound in theory.
summary: A manager copies a trendy early-rising habit and ends up flat on the office floor while his coworkers sip coffee and watch.

file: 2014/2014-05-05_managers & supervisors_mathematics_work ethic_work time_donate_1% work time_charitable cause_110% to job_learn math_asking employess_business.gif
title: 110 Percent Plus One Percent

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO has asked each of us to donate 1% of our work time to a charitable cause.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Last week you told us to give 110% to our work. Does this mean we can back off to 109%?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, you should give 110% to everything you do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe my charitable cause could be helping you learn math.

setting: Conference room meeting, with an office building shown in the final panel
situation: The Boss announces that the CEO wants everyone to donate 1% of their work time to charity. Dilbert points out that the Boss recently demanded 110% effort and asks if that can now drop to 109%. The Boss, speaking from offstage over a view of the building, insists on 110% for everything and suggests teaching Dilbert math as his charity.
punchline: The Boss's insistence that employees give 110% of everything is mathematically absurd, and he responds to Dilbert's valid arithmetic by insulting his math skills rather than admitting the contradiction.
summary: A manager's request for charitable time collides with his own impossible demand for extra effort, and he deflects the logic with an insult.

title: Both Partners Blame Each Other

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You two have failed to meet your project milestones.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because you paired me with a toxic moron who is incapable of having an original thought.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That happened to me, too.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and a coworker that they have missed their project milestones. Dilbert blames the failure on having been paired with a toxic moron who cannot come up with an original thought. His partner cheerfully replies that the same thing happened to him, not realizing Dilbert means him.
punchline: The partner agrees with Dilbert's insult without realizing he is the toxic moron being described, proving Dilbert's point about his lack of original thought and self-awareness.
summary: Two teammates called out for late work each blame the other, but one is oblivious that the insult describes him.

file: 2014/2014-08-29_laziness_not caring what others think_total uslessness_key to success_discussion_employees_hoping it goes_business.gif
title: Success Through Not Caring, Or Uselessness

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Asok, the key to success is not caring what others think of you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Coincidentally, that is also the key to being totally useless.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The important thing is that other people can't tell which way you're hoping it goes.

setting: Office break area, coworkers holding coffee mugs
situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, lectures Asok and Dilbert that success comes from not caring what others think. He then admits the same trait is also the key to being useless. He concludes that the trick is keeping others from knowing which outcome you are hoping for.
punchline: Wally, a famously lazy slacker, admits that his philosophy of not caring works equally well for success or failure, so he benefits by hiding his true intent.
summary: A coffee-sipping Wally offers Asok career advice that conveniently doubles as a defense of his own uselessness.

file: 2014/2014-02-23_ignorance (knowledge)_thinking_objection to plan_potential problems_works fine_system used_non zero chance_get rid of hospitals_idiot_normal life.gif
title: Realizing You're an Idiot Mid-Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does anyone have an objection to this plan?

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: In my opinion, there are too many potential problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This system has been used for years in other places and works fine.

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: There is still a non-zero chance of problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By that logic, we should get rid of hospitals because sometimes they make mistakes.

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! I just realized I'm an idiot!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can still lead a normal life.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It only stings for a minute.

situation: Dilbert presents a plan and asks for objections. A coworker objects that there could be problems, even though the system has worked elsewhere for years. Dilbert counters that by this logic hospitals should be abolished, which makes the coworker suddenly realize his own foolishness.
punchline: The coworker is so thoroughly defeated by an analogy that he realizes he's an idiot, and Dilbert and another attendee offer deadpan, backhanded comfort that he can still live a normal life.
summary: A coworker's reflexive fear of any risk is dismantled by a hospital comparison, leaving him shaken by his own foolishness while others coolly console him.

title: Insincere Compliments Don't Make Wally Likeable

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't feel any different.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe the problem is on your end.

situation: Dilbert tells Wally he read that using people's names and handing out insincere compliments makes a person likeable. He then tries it by praising Wally for pouring coffee without spilling. Dilbert says he doesn't feel any different, and Wally suggests the problem is on Dilbert's end.
punchline: Wally implies that Dilbert's unlikeability is a personal flaw that no flattery technique can fix, and his own lack of reaction to the compliment is Dilbert's failing, not his.
summary: After trying a self-help trick of flattering a coworker over trivial coffee pouring, a man finds it changes nothing and gets blamed for it instead.

transcript.text: We need to talk.

setting: A seminar or training class in an office
situation: Dogbert stands on a stool teaching a class, with Dilbert and Alice seen from behind as students. He advises that the only way to handle difficult co-workers is to murder them untraceably. The Boss, holding a coffee mug, steps in to say they need to talk, and Dogbert responds by reminding the class that everyone received a jar of polonium at registration.
punchline: Dogbert's seminar on dealing with jerks is a murder tutorial, and when the Boss tries to confront him he casually reveals he has already supplied everyone with a poison, which doubles as a veiled threat.
summary: A canine instructor teaches his class that the sole answer to obnoxious colleagues is undetectable homicide, then answers his supervisor's confrontation with a hint about the radioactive poison already handed out.

title: Strategic Planning Means Hallucinating the Future

transcript.speaker: Wally

transcript.text: You also have to pretend it's useful.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really? That sounds hard.

situation: A coworker holding a coffee mug says he is considering a career in strategic planning. Dilbert summarizes the job as imagining the future and then watching reality turn out differently. The coworker adds that you must also pretend the planning is useful, and Dilbert remarks that this sounds hard.
punchline: Strategic planning is mocked as inventing fictional futures that never come true, with the real challenge being the pretense that the exercise has value.
summary: Two coworkers cynically define strategic planning as confidently imagining a future that never arrives while acting as if the effort matters.

punchline: The therapist gives up on treating Dilbert's real problem and plants absurd false memories instead, and Dilbert is so suggestible that he immediately accepts that he was a robot.
summary: A counselor facing an unfixable social-media complaint decides to manufacture bogus memories, and her patient happily adopts them.

situation: Dilbert and Ratbert walk along a path while Ratbert daydreams about going to Google after he dies, listing perks like free food, bus service and massages. Dilbert points out the downside, that he would be surrounded by smart, ambitious people, and Ratbert says he will just bring earplugs.
punchline: Ratbert treats Google as an afterlife paradise of perks and sarcastically dismisses the drawback of being surrounded by relentlessly smart, ambitious colleagues by planning to tune them out.
summary: A small rodent fantasizes that the tech giant's employee benefits make it a perfect afterlife, then shrugs off its overachieving crowd with a simple fix.

summary: A boss's harsh assessment evaporates the moment his employee mentions he will be reviewing the boss's own performance.

title: CEO Kills Sales, Then Fires Staff

punchline: After sabotaging sales through his own careless public announcement, the boss plans to scapegoat employees with layoffs, and an employee implies a menacing response by asking where he lives.
summary: A manager who tanked his company's revenue with a television comment plans to cut half the workforce to cover himself, prompting a veiled threat from the audience.

title: Cultural Fit Hire Admits Incompetence

transcript.speaker: Larry
transcript.text: But I don't know how to do that.

situation: A new employee named Larry introduces himself to Alice, saying he was hired for being a good cultural fit. He hopes to overcome the stigma that such hires are incompetent, then admits he has no idea how to do that. Alice dryly suggests he ask a competent person for help.
punchline: Larry's helplessness confirms the very stigma he wants to escape, and Alice's sarcastic reply implies that he is incompetent and that she is the one who is not.
summary: A newly hired colleague unwittingly proves that hiring for cultural fit can bring in people who cannot do the job.

title: Camera Glasses Flamethrower Defense

punchline: The wearable-tech glasses turn out to hold a hidden flamethrower, so the bullies who expected an easy target get burned down to skeletons.
summary: Bullies who pick on a nerd over his high-tech eyewear get an unexpectedly fiery lesson in why that was a mistake.

title: Deep Thinking Costs Social Awareness

situation: Dilbert stands in front of the seated Boss and warns him that he will be concentrating hard on a technology problem. He explains that doing so will use up the brain resources he normally devotes to social awareness. The Boss replies that this sounds like a radical change, and Dilbert can't tell if he was being sarcastic.
punchline: Dilbert's demonstration of lost social awareness is that he can't detect the Boss's obvious sarcasm, implying he normally has little social awareness anyway.
summary: An engineer cautions his manager that intense concentration will dull his social skills, then immediately fails to catch an obvious jab.

title: Battery Recycling Ends in Landfill

transcript.text: Maybe we could ask him not to.
