transcript.text: No one knows what language he speaks.

setting: Conference room table, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: The Boss announces an environmentally motivated policy requiring used batteries to go into a special break room receptacle. He then explains that the janitor simply empties it into the regular trash bound for the landfill. Dilbert suggests asking the janitor not to, but the Boss says nobody can communicate with him.
punchline: The eco-friendly battery policy is meaningless because the collected batteries end up in a landfill anyway, and management won't even try to fix it because of a language barrier.
summary: A company's green battery-collection rule is revealed to be pointless theater when the janitor just dumps everything in the landfill and nobody can talk to him.

title: Doubling Half Pay With Worthless Equity

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A start-up offered to pay me half of what I make now, plus equity in a company that has no value.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I will double that if you stay!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I decided to stay, but it was hard to feel good about it.

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert tells his boss that a start-up has offered him half his current salary plus worthless equity. The boss responds with a counteroffer to double that offer if he stays. Dilbert later tells Dogbert at home that he decided to stay, though he felt bad about it.
punchline: The boss's counteroffer of double a terrible offer is still a pitiful amount, so Dilbert's decision to stay feels like a defeat rather than a win.
summary: A job offer worth next to nothing gets matched and doubled by an employer, leaving the employee staying put with little to celebrate.

title: CEO Avenges Fired-Day Happy Dancers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good news! I got rehired as CEO!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I checked the security videos for the day I got fired, and now I'm getting revenge on anyone who did a happy dance.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did I...?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Frankly, I can't tell. Do you have spasms?

situation: The Boss announces to Dilbert that he has been rehired as CEO. He explains that he reviewed security footage from the day he was fired and plans to punish everyone who celebrated with a happy dance. Dilbert nervously wonders if he did it, and the Boss admits the footage is ambiguous and asks if Dilbert has spasms.
punchline: Dilbert's usual awkward, jerky movements are so odd that even security footage can't distinguish his happy dance from a medical condition, which saves him from revenge but insults him.
summary: A vengeful, newly reinstated executive hunts through old camera footage for celebrants, but can't tell whether one employee was dancing or just twitching.

title: Secretly Subcontracting to a Bigger Liar

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The good news is that we had the winning bid for the project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The less-good news is that we don't make the product we just sold, nor could we make it for the price we bid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My plan is to put out an RFP to secretly subcontract the work to a bigger liar.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That could work.

situation: Dilbert presents to his colleagues, using a whiteboard diagram of dollar signs flowing toward a center point. He announces that the company won a bid for a project but cannot make the product, nor could it do so at the bid price. His plan is to issue an RFP to secretly subcontract the work to someone who lies even more, and the boss approves.
punchline: The company's solution to having won a bid it can't fulfil is to find a bigger liar to take over the work, and management thinks this is a sound plan.
summary: After winning a contract for something they can't build at the quoted price, Dilbert proposes passing the buck to an even more dishonest subcontractor.

file: 2014/2014-02-20_death & dying_inventions_health directive_technological progress_transhumanism_kill me_robot body forever_make painful.gif
title: Dilbert's Transhumanism Kill Order

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm updating my health directive to account for technological progress.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When the age of transhumanism is upon us, I want you to kill me so I don't live forever in a robot body.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sure. Can I make it painful?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would you even ask that?

setting: Grassy hillside, with Dogbert standing on a rock
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he is updating his health directive to cover the future age of transhumanism. He instructs Dogbert to kill him rather than let him live forever in a robot body. Dogbert cheerfully agrees and asks whether he can make it painful, which alarms Dilbert.
punchline: Dogbert accepts the grim assignment and treats it as an opportunity for sadism, so Dilbert is horrified at the person he trusted with his end-of-life wishes.
summary: Dilbert gives his dog a standing order to end his life before he can become an immortal machine, and the dog eagerly asks for creative latitude in carrying it out.

file: 2014/2014-09-05_bunch of names_complaining_name of new app_new app_underscore_suggestions.gif
title: Boss Rejects App Name, Offers Nothing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't like the name of our new app. You need to change it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Perhaps you can underscore your point by suggesting a bunch of names that are already taken.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you mind if I think of other things while you do that?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he dislikes the name of the new app and orders him to change it. Dilbert sarcastically suggests the Boss back up his complaint by proposing names that are already taken. The Boss responds that he'd rather think about other things while Dilbert does the work.
punchline: The Boss wants to criticize and delegate the naming problem without contributing any ideas himself, leaving all the effort to Dilbert.
summary: A manager vetoes a product name but declines to help find a replacement, preferring to daydream while his employee does the work.

title: Working From the Cloud, Actually Home

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you need me, I'll be in the cloud fixing a software issue.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There's no cell coverage in the cloud, so it might seem to you as if I am at home doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you need me, I'll be at home doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would anyone need you?

situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells his seated boss he'll be in the cloud fixing a software issue. He explains that since there's no cell coverage in the cloud, it may look like he is at home doing nothing. He then walks off with a bag, announcing he'll be at home doing nothing, and Dilbert asks why anyone would need him.
punchline: Wally uses cloud computing jargon as a cover story for slacking off at home, and Dilbert bluntly points out that nobody ever needs him anyway.
summary: Wally dresses up going home to loaf as important remote work in the cloud, until Dilbert deflates him.

title: Only Losers Plan For Failure

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If our business plan fails, do we have a plan for that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Only losers plan for failure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think we're on the same page, but for some reason you're angry about it.

setting: Conference room during a business planning meeting
situation: At a meeting table, Dilbert asks whether there is a contingency plan in case the business plan fails. The Boss snaps that only losers plan for failure. Dilbert points out that the Boss's answer implies there is no backup plan, which is exactly what Dilbert suspected, yet the Boss is angry about it.
punchline: The Boss's answer effectively confirms that there is no plan for failure, so Dilbert is agreeing with him, but the Boss is irrationally angry at having his lack of planning exposed.
summary: A cautious question about backup plans gets an angry, defensive answer that accidentally admits there is none.

title: Laughing at the Boss's Neck Pain

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My neck is killing me. I must have slept wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha ha ha! You can't even sleep right!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm doing you a favor because laughter is the best medicine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why does that no longer sound wise?!!

situation: The Boss complains that his neck hurts because he must have slept wrong. Dilbert bursts out laughing and mocks him for being unable to even sleep properly. When the Boss grows angry, Dilbert claims he is helping because laughter is the best medicine, and the Boss realizes the saying no longer sounds wise.
punchline: Dilbert uses the proverb 'laughter is the best medicine' as a flimsy excuse to mock his boss's pain, and even the Boss sees how the saying sounds foolish when applied to his own suffering.
summary: A man who groans about a stiff neck gets ridiculed by his employee, who passes off the mockery as a health benefit.

title: Great Leader Because Nobody Likes Him

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A good leader has to be willing to be disliked.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You must be a great leader.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry. I didn't expect you to be listening to me.

setting: Boss's office, sitting across a desk
situation: The Boss lectures Dilbert that a good leader must be willing to be disliked. Dilbert replies that the Boss must therefore be a great leader. The Boss asks what that means, and Dilbert apologizes, saying he didn't think the Boss was listening.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies the Boss is widely disliked, so by his own definition he must be a great leader, and he only admits the insult because he assumed the Boss wasn't paying attention.
summary: A manager's remark about leaders being disliked gets turned into a backhanded compliment about how unpopular he is.

file: 2014/2014-09-20_engineers_joking_practical jokes_sex appeal_sexiness_honor_practical joke_evil genius_cleverly_concealed_true identity_sit on rocks.gif
title: Sexiest Engineer Award Is Suspicious

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was named one of the sexiest engineers in the world!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That honor sounds like a practical joke perpetrated by an evil genius who cleverly concealed his true identity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nah.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I bet he likes to sit on rocks.

situation: Dilbert walks across a hill and proudly announces he was named one of the sexiest engineers in the world. Dogbert suggests the honor is really a practical joke by a hidden evil genius. Dilbert dismisses the idea, and in the last panel Dogbert is seen sitting on a rock.
punchline: Dogbert is himself the evil genius behind the prank, and his sitting on a rock gives him away.
summary: A pleased engineer shrugs off his dog's theory that his flattering award is a hoax, while the dog quietly sits on a rock, revealing himself as the culprit.

title: Resisting Terrible Ideas Is Rational

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm getting reports again that you're resistant to change.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I only resist terrible ideas but I can see how that would confuse you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whatever you're doing, cut it out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I stop being rational in general or only in this one way?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that he keeps hearing Dilbert is resistant to change. Dilbert replies that he only resists terrible ideas, which he suggests the Boss can't distinguish from change in general. The Boss orders him to stop, and Dilbert asks whether he should abandon rationality entirely or just in this one instance.
punchline: By ordering Dilbert to stop resisting, the Boss effectively demands that Dilbert stop being rational, since his objections only target bad ideas.
summary: An employee defends his pushback against bad proposals as simple good sense, and his manager's demand that he quit amounts to asking him to think less clearly.

file: 2014/2014-09-27_analogies_creativity_haters_ideas_trapped ideas_attract haters_zombies to fish syicks_analogy_great ideas.gif
title: Zombies, Fish Sticks, and Haters

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My best ideas are trapped in my head.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whenever I voice my ideas, I attract haters like zombies to fish sticks.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is that analogy one of your great ideas?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't like the way you asked that.

setting: Office break area, both holding coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker that he keeps his best ideas to himself because sharing them draws critics. When he compares this to zombies drawn to fish sticks, the coworker asks whether that analogy is one of his great ideas. Dilbert objects to the way the question was asked.
punchline: Dilbert complains about attracting haters, then immediately reacts badly to a mildly snarky question, showing he is the sort of person who invites criticism.
summary: A man who says he stays quiet to avoid critics bristles the moment a colleague gently mocks his odd comparison.

file: 2014/2014-03-04_managers & supervisors_office workers_organized as holacracy_dynamic governance_transparent operations_harnessing_conscious capacity_wander around_dynamically_business.gif
title: Holacracy Means Wander Around Dynamically

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now that we're organized as a holacracy, I have no idea what I should be doing.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Holacracy involves dynamic governance, transparent operations, and harnessing your conscious capacity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That sounds like "wander around."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Try to do it dynamically.

situation: The Boss tells Catbert, the HR director, that since the company reorganized as a holacracy he has no idea what his job is. Catbert recites buzzword-heavy principles of holacracy. The Boss translates them as simply wandering around, and Catbert agrees, adding that he should do it dynamically.
punchline: Holacracy's lofty jargon boils down to aimless wandering, and the only improvement offered is to wander "dynamically."
summary: After a trendy management restructure leaves a manager clueless about his duties, the HR cat's jargon-laden explanation amounts to telling him to roam around with more energy.

file: 2014/2014-04-15_computer programmers_email_email down_guy in hopsital_ouija board_limited rescources.gif
title: Email Fixer Hospitalized, Try Ouija Board

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Email is down again.

transcript.speaker: IT Guy
transcript.text: The only guy who can fix it is in the hospital.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So . . . if he dies, we can never again have email?

transcript.speaker: IT Guy
transcript.text: Maybe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is there any way I can reach him?

transcript.speaker: IT Guy
transcript.text: Wait a week and try a Ouija board.

situation: Dilbert tells an IT worker that email is down again. The tech explains that the only person who knows how to fix it is in the hospital, and Dilbert realizes email might be gone permanently if the man dies. Asked whether the expert can be reached, the tech deadpans that Dilbert should wait a week and try a Ouija board.
punchline: The IT guy casually implies the sole expert will be dead within a week, suggesting a Ouija board as the only way to contact him and showing how dangerously dependent the company is on one person.
summary: A company's email system hinges on one hospitalized specialist, and the tech support worker coolly suggests contacting his ghost.
keywords: only person who can fix it

file: 2014/2014-07-13_big business_business ethics_obliviousness_core competencies_automating things_worshipping stars quo_steve jobs_reanimated body_making lapses_fiduciary responsibility_hearing what we want.gif
title: Core Competencies Study Goes Over Boss's Head

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I did a study of our core competencies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It seems we're very good at automating things that we shouldn't be doing in the first place.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But that's not all we're good at.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're also good at worshipping the status quo as if it were Steve Jobs' reanimated body.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And no one is as good at masking lapses in fiduciary responsibility.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lastly, we're good at hearing what we want to hear.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... we're good at automating things?

situation: Dilbert presents the findings of his study of the company's core competencies to his boss. He lists a series of damning strengths, including automating pointless tasks, worshipping the status quo, hiding fiduciary lapses and hearing only what they want to hear. The boss, holding a coffee mug, takes away only the one flattering-sounding item.
punchline: The boss proves the final point of the study by hearing only the one positive-sounding finding and ignoring all the criticism.
summary: A damning self-assessment of a company's strengths is delivered to a boss who cheerfully latches onto the only part that sounds like a compliment.
keywords: hearing what we want to hear

file: 2014/2014-02-14_anger_competition (psychology)_employees_difficult coworkers_methods against me_need to know_counter neasures_learn tricks_business.gif
title: Difficult Coworker Seeks Counter-Tactics Workshop

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can I sign up for a workshop on how to deal with difficult co-workers?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: People will be using those methods against me, and I need to know how to thwart their countermeasures.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Will you leave my office if I say yes?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where did you learn that trick?!!

situation: Alice asks her boss for permission to attend a workshop on dealing with difficult co-workers, explaining that she needs to counter the methods others will use against her. She then tries one of those tactics on him by offering to approve his request if he will leave his own office, and he is startled and demands to know where she learned it.
punchline: Alice reveals that she is the difficult co-worker, using the very tactic from the workshop on her boss, who is baffled that she already knows the trick.
summary: A notoriously prickly employee asks to learn defences against awkward colleagues, only to prove she already has the manipulation skills down.

file: 2014/2014-04-20_cleaning_engineers_coal break room_highest priority_mold grow_mutating bacteria_rapidly eveolved_sentient being_fueled by lunch_learned languages_job in hr_plans on  firing_inappropriate websites.gif
title: Break Room Mold Becomes HR Menace

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You need to clean the break room refrigerator more often.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We're engineers. We only do the highest priority tasks.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Mold started to grow in there.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's no big deal.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Bacteria caused the mold to mutate.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So what?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It rapidly evolved into a sentient being fueled by forgotten lunches.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Then it learned language skills and got a job in Human Resources.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It plans to frame you for viewing inappropriate web-sites at work and then fire you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This sort of thing usually works itself out.

setting: Office break room and cubicle area
situation: Alice asks the engineers to clean the break room refrigerator, but Wally dismisses it as not a high-priority task. Alice then escalates through a series of warnings: the mold mutated, became sentient, and now works in Human Resources with a plan to frame and fire Wally. Wally remains unconcerned.
punchline: Wally's lazy, dismissive belief that problems resolve themselves persists even when the neglected mold has become an HR employee plotting to get him fired.
summary: Ignoring a dirty fridge leads to mold that evolves into a vengeful HR worker, yet the unbothered engineer still shrugs it off.

title: Boss Demands Vague Company Origin Story

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, I need you to write a company "origin story." All the cool companies have them.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why? Well, for starters, we need it for various things. And so on.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't think I can be any clearer.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I don't think you can either.

situation: The Boss tells Tina, the technical writer, to produce a company origin story because trendy companies all have one. When she asks why, he offers only a vague non-answer about various things. He claims he couldn't be clearer, and Tina agrees he can't.
punchline: Tina sarcastically agrees the Boss can't be any clearer, because his explanation is empty and he has no real reason beyond copying trendy companies.
summary: A manager assigns a writing task purely to imitate fashionable firms and, when pressed for a reason, offers a vacant explanation that his employee drily accepts as his best effort.

title: Curiosity Killed the Anecdotal Cat

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They say curiosity is a sign of a nimble intellect.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Curiosity killed the cat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That evidence was anecdotal, but I still found it compelling.

setting: Office break area with coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert, Wally and the Boss stand around holding coffee. Dilbert says curiosity shows a nimble intellect, and the Boss replies with the proverb that curiosity killed the cat. Dilbert then remarks that the evidence was only anecdotal but he still found it compelling, after the Boss walks away.
punchline: Dilbert dryly mocks the Boss's proverb as weak anecdotal evidence, while admitting that a flimsy argument can still be persuasive and so scare people off being curious.
summary: A co-worker's pet proverb gets treated like flimsy research findings, and the only person left to hear the verdict is Wally.

title: Early Riser Brushes With Face Cream

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm trying to turn myself into a morning person so I can be more productive.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've been getting up at 4:30 every day, and so far, so good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... no problems at all?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Nothing huge. I've brushed my teeth with face cream a few times.

setting: Office building break area, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: Alice tells Dilbert and Wally, who are holding coffee mugs, that she is trying to become a morning person by waking at 4:30 every day. She says it is going well, then admits when Dilbert asks about problems that she has accidentally brushed her teeth with face cream several times. Her wild, messy hair and tired look suggest she is far from well rested.
punchline: Alice claims her extreme early-rising experiment is going fine, but brushing her teeth with face cream reveals she is sleep-deprived and barely functioning.
summary: A worker bragging about her new pre-dawn wake-up routine casually confesses to a groggy toothpaste mix-up that exposes how badly it is really going.

title: Dilbert Wishes Ice Death on Distracted Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I would like to thank each of you for playing with your phones and not listening to a word I said all meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope karma is a real thing and frozen lavatory debris from airplanes kills each of you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What was he going on about?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Beats me. I'm not much of a multi-tasker.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, then a hallway afterward
situation: Dilbert runs a meeting while Alice and Wally stare at their phones the whole time. He sarcastically thanks them for ignoring him, then says he hopes karma kills them with frozen airplane toilet waste. Afterward Alice asks what he was talking about and Wally says he has no idea.
punchline: The coworkers are so absorbed in their phones that they didn't even notice Dilbert's angry rant, and Wally excuses his inattention by claiming he's bad at multitasking.
summary: A frustrated meeting leader curses his phone-obsessed colleagues, who remain too distracted to realize they were insulted.

title: Garbage Man Says Dilbert Is Simulated

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How much wearable tech can I use before I'm technically a cyborg?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: It doesn't matter because you're a software simulation created by humans who perished after the technological singularity.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: And you're programmed to scoff at what I just said.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Crazy old coot.

setting: Outdoors on a sidewalk beside a hedge, next to a blue trash bin
situation: Dilbert, wearing a wearable gadget, asks a garbage man how much wearable technology he can use before he counts as a cyborg. The garbage man calmly replies that Dilbert is just a software simulation made by humans who died after the singularity. He adds that Dilbert is programmed to scoff, and Dilbert promptly scoffs.
punchline: Dilbert's dismissive reaction is exactly what the garbage man predicted, which seems to confirm that he really is a programmed simulation.
summary: A sanitation worker tells a gadget-loving engineer he's merely a simulation of a dead civilization, then watches him react exactly as scripted.

file: 2014/2014-01-31_incompetetnt_laziness_passive agressive_threatened me more_work ethic_realtionships_defensive_admits to incompetetnt.gif
title: Passive-Aggressive or Just Incompetent

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't tell if you're passive-aggressive or just incompetent.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Which one sends a message that I could do good work if you threatened me more?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Passive-aggressive.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Okay. I'm the other one.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Alice tells Wally she can't decide whether he is passive-aggressive or simply incompetent. Wally, holding his coffee mug, asks which label would imply that he could do good work if she threatened him more. When Alice answers that it is the passive-aggressive one, Wally calmly admits he is the other one.
punchline: Wally chooses to admit he is incompetent rather than be labeled passive-aggressive, because he'd rather avoid being threatened into doing real work.
summary: Faced with a choice between two unflattering labels, a lazy employee picks the one that spares him from extra pressure.

file: 2014/2014-09-08_big business_competition (psychology)_bad ads_increase sales_competitors_running ads_increases ads_strategic incompetence_luck.gif
title: Ads So Bad They Help Competitors

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Our ads are so bad that they increase sales for our competitors.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try running ads for our competitors and see if it increases our sales.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Strategic incompetence?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't get this far by luck!

setting: Conference room during a sales presentation
situation: A marketing presenter stands by a chart of rising sales and admits the company's ads are so terrible that they boost competitors' sales. At the conference table, the Boss suggests running ads for the competitors instead. Dilbert wonders aloud if that is strategic incompetence, and the Boss proudly insists his success is no accident.
punchline: The Boss's absurd inverted strategy is accidentally logical, and he takes credit for it as if his incompetence were a deliberate skill rather than luck.
summary: When a presentation reveals that the company's advertising only helps rivals, management proposes advertising the rivals instead and claims it as masterful planning.
keywords: didn't get this far by luck

title: Context Ruins the Business School Rankings

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The new business school rankings are out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that the list that is based on the votes of people who have no direct knowledge of those schools?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You ruin everything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Context is not your friend.

setting: Office break area where coworkers stand around with coffee mugs
situation: Three coworkers are chatting over coffee when one announces that the new business school rankings have been published. Dilbert asks whether this is the list based on votes from people with no direct knowledge of the schools. The coworker complains that he ruins everything, and Dilbert replies that context is not your friend.
punchline: Dilbert points out that the rankings are essentially meaningless popularity contests, and he acknowledges that knowing the context spoils any enjoyment of the news.
summary: A casual chat about school rankings turns sour when Dilbert reveals that the list rests on opinions from people who know nothing about the schools.

title: Algorithm Hiring Places Critic in Engineering

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No one looks at résumés anymore. Now we use special algorithms to see where your personality fits in our culture.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: That process sounds like a steaming pile of stupidity that will beat itself to death in a few years.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'll start you in engineering. You'll fit right in.

setting: Catbert's office, during a job interview
situation: Catbert, acting as human resources, tells a job candidate that résumés are obsolete and that algorithms now match personality to company culture. The candidate bluntly criticizes the process as stupid and doomed to fail. Catbert responds by placing him in engineering, saying he'll fit right in.
punchline: The candidate's cynical, negative outlook is exactly what the algorithm associates with engineers, implying engineering is full of pessimistic critics.
summary: A frank opinion about a quirky hiring method lands an applicant a spot in the department where complaining is the norm.

title: Boss Introduces Dead Exoskeleton Employee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is Barry. He has been working on our exoskeleton project for five years.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Evidently Barry, died years ago, and his exoskeleton keeps taking his bones to meetings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In my defense, that is only obvious after you say it.

situation: The Boss proudly introduces Barry, an employee who has supposedly worked on the exoskeleton project for five years, but Barry is really a skull sitting atop a robotic exoskeleton. Dilbert points out that Barry died long ago and his exoskeleton has just been carrying his bones to meetings. The Boss defends himself by saying the fact is only obvious once it is stated.
punchline: The Boss failed to notice for years that a coworker was a dead skeleton in a machine, and his excuse is that it only seems obvious after someone points it out.
summary: A manager presents a skull-topped robot suit as a long-serving colleague, and when told the man is actually long dead, he shrugs that it was not obvious until mentioned.

file: 2014/2014-01-24_executives_slapped ceo_report says_success is following your instinct_being passionate_engaged_creative_meaningful_office meeting_literal meeting.gif
title: Alice Slaps CEO Following Instinct

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This report says you slapped our CEO senseless after he said the key to success is following your instinct.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I was following my instinct. I was also being passionate, engaged and creative.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Apparently, the things you say actually mean stuff.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: How was I supposed to know?

situation: Catbert, the HR director, confronts Alice with a report saying she slapped the CEO senseless after he told employees that success comes from following your instinct. Alice calmly explains she was just following her instinct while being passionate, engaged and creative. In the last panel the bandaged CEO protests that he had no idea his words would be taken literally.
punchline: The CEO's empty motivational slogans were taken at face value, and he is baffled that his words were meant to mean something.
summary: A hotheaded employee takes a boss's cliched success advice literally and turns it into assault, leaving the injured executive bewildered.

file: 2014/2014-01-10_chipmunks_in hair_less talking_love_more rubbing_rodents_oxytocin levels_human contact_family of chipmunks_relationships.gif
title: Chipmunks in Alice's Hair

transcript.speaker: Man with squirrel
transcript.text: It boosts my oxytocin levels without the need for human contact.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You didn't invent that. I've had a family of chipmunks living in my hair since the eighties.

transcript.speaker: Chipmunk
transcript.text: There goes our privacy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Less talking, more rubbing!

situation: A bald coworker with glasses and a lab coat has a squirrel perched on his shoulder and explains that petting it raises his oxytocin levels without needing human contact. Alice replies that he didn't invent the idea, since a family of chipmunks has lived in her big hair since the eighties. Two chipmunks peek out of her hair, worried about their privacy, and Alice demands that the coworker stop talking and start rubbing.
punchline: Alice reveals she has had the same animal-based comfort for decades, and her blunt demand for 'more rubbing' turns the coworker's antisocial coping trick into an awkward, funny invitation.
summary: A coworker boasts about a pet-petting trick for feeling good without people, but Alice already keeps chipmunks in her enormous hair and tells him to get on with petting them.

title: Budget Only Affords Half-Competent Hire

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: And I am proud to say that I'm 75% competent.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wish I could afford that.

setting: Office interview, a desk with a boss and a job candidate
situation: The Boss explains to Ratbert, who sits across the desk, that his budget only covers an employee who is incompetent half the time, and that unspent funds will vanish next year. A job candidate then proudly claims to be 75% competent, and the Boss laments that he can't afford someone that good.
punchline: The Boss turns away a better-than-needed candidate because the budget only pays for mediocrity, showing that budget rules reward settling for incompetence.
summary: A manager with a tiny hiring budget rejects a stronger applicant as too expensive because the money can only buy partial incompetence.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's all I need.

setting: Office meeting room or cubicle with a desk
situation: Dilbert sits down with a coworker to review a piece of engineering work and announces he will skip straight to telling the coworker how it should have been done. The coworker points out that Dilbert has no idea what was actually built. Dilbert's retort is that he has only five minutes to pretend that matters, and that is all he needs.
punchline: Dilbert's review is a formality in which his criticism is predetermined and ignorance of the actual work is irrelevant, and the time-boxed 'five minutes' is all the effort he intends to spend on it.

situation: Alice tells Dilbert, who is holding a coffee mug, that Warren Buffett says showing passion for your job will improve your career. punchline: Alice's fake enthusiasm is over the most trivial task imaginable, which underscores how dull her job really is.

situation: The Boss claims robots will never match human intelligence, and Dilbert asks him to name something humans can do that robots can't. The Boss offers judging movies and reading faces, and Dilbert shoots down the first and tests him on the second. The Boss's absurd reading of Dilbert's expression is oddly accurate.
punchline: The Boss's bizarre guess about Dilbert's feelings (admiration, arousal and bacon) turns out to be right, so Dilbert grudgingly concedes the point despite the Boss's obvious cluelessness.
summary: A boss insists machines can never match human minds, then wins a debate by absurdly but accurately reading his coworker's expression.

summary: A man proudly shares the odd search phrases his experiments found, only for a colleague to say asking him would have been quicker.

file: 2014/2014-03-08_choosing_thinking_tests_orange buttons_more clicks_than green_lost faith_human intelligence_green looks better_liberated_tyranny of thinking.gif

punchline: Dilbert sarcastically embraces the Boss's decision to ignore hard data in favor of personal taste, joking that he is freed from the burden of thinking.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe THAT'S the problem.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that research shows giving customers too many choices can stop them from buying. The Boss dismisses the idea that studies could show such a thing. When Dilbert is left unsure how to respond to the Boss's denial, the Boss unwittingly suggests that this paralysis is exactly the problem described.
punchline: The Boss's dismissal of the research leaves Dilbert with too many ways to respond and no idea which to pick, so the Boss accidentally demonstrates the very choice-overload effect Dilbert described.
summary: A manager waves away a claim about choice overload, then unknowingly illustrates it when his employee is stumped on how to reply.

file: 2014/2014-06-10_problem_we don't know_what we don't know_common saying_stole it_dumbest converstion.gif
title: Who Stole the Unknown Unknowns

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The problem is that we don't know what we don't know.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You stole that saying from me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a common saying. I've been using it for years.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No, you stole it from me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is officially the dumbest conversation I've ever had.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's my other saying!

situation: Dilbert sits across a table from a coworker and says that the problem is not knowing what they don't know. The coworker accuses him of stealing that saying, and the two argue over who originated it. When Dilbert calls it the dumbest conversation he's ever had, the coworker claims that line as his too.
punchline: The coworker is so possessive of clichés that he claims ownership even of Dilbert's complaint about the argument itself, making the conversation even dumber.
summary: Two colleagues bicker over who owns a well-worn catchphrase until one claims even the insult about their argument as his own.
keywords: we don't know what we don't know

file: 2014/2014-01-13_employees_mental health_vision not money_mental problems_low self esteem_performance review_business.gif
title: Hiring for Vision, Not Money

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need employees that are motivated by our vision, not by money.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Are we looking for any other mental problems or just that one?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm also a big fan of low self-esteem. It comes in handy at performance review time.

situation: The Boss walks with Catbert, the evil human resources director, and announces that the company wants employees driven by its vision rather than by pay. Catbert sarcastically asks if there are any other mental problems they want in new hires. The Boss cheerfully adds that low self-esteem is desirable because it helps during performance reviews.
punchline: Management openly wants psychologically damaged employees who will accept low pay and poor reviews without pushing back.
summary: A manager and the company's feline HR chief candidly list the unhealthy traits they hope to find in job candidates.

file: 2014/2014-04-19_best advice_insignificant advice_worst advice_be true to yourself_doesn't mean anything.gif

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Three coworkers sit at a table. One shares that the best advice he ever received was to be true to yourself. Dilbert bluntly says the advice is meaningless, and the third coworker, who usually stays out of conversations, jumps in to ask what the worst advice must have been.
punchline: Dilbert's dismissal implies that if "be true to yourself" is the best advice the man ever got, the worst must be truly terrible.
summary: A man's favorite life lesson gets picked apart by Dilbert, leaving a bystander wondering how bad the rest of his guidance could be.

file: 2014/2014-03-21_telecommunication lines_work ethic_studies show_telecommunters_survey people_lying weasles_level of awareness.gif
title: Telecommuter Studies Rely on Self-Reporting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You should let me work at home a few days per week because studies show that telecommuters put in more hours.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do they study that sort of thing?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They survey people who work at home.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if those people are lying weasels?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wasn't counting on this level of awareness.

setting: Boss's office, seated at a conference table
situation: Dilbert asks the boss for permission to work from home, citing studies that say telecommuters work more hours. The boss asks how such studies are done, and Dilbert explains they survey people who work at home. The boss then suspects the respondents might be lying, which catches Dilbert off guard.
punchline: The boss unexpectedly raises the exact flaw in Dilbert's argument, that self-reported survey data from remote workers is unreliable, and Dilbert admits he never expected the boss to be that perceptive.
summary: A worker's pitch for remote work backfires when his usually clueless manager spots the weakness in the survey data behind it.

title: Dinosaur Smartwatch Carbon Dates Him

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Ha ha! I am now the coolest member of the household because I have a smartwatch.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Hello, watch. What time is it?

transcript.text: This is the Anthropocene epoch.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Wow, that carbon dates me.

situation: Dilbert's pet dinosaur brags that he is now the coolest household member because he owns a smartwatch. He asks the watch for the time, and it answers with the geological epoch, the Anthropocene. The dinosaur remarks that this carbon dates him while Dilbert stands silently beside him.
punchline: The dinosaur's smartwatch answers a request for the time with a geological epoch, and he puns that it 'carbon dates' him, meaning it shows how ancient and out of date he is.
summary: A boastful pet dinosaur with a new gadget gets a prehistoric-sized reminder of his age when the device names the current geological era.

file: 2014/2014-07-27_work load_complaints_inexperinced_exact opposite_doesn't know much_hired useless man_bad attendence_not perfect_ask questions.gif
title: Boss Hires Useless Helper, Questions Follow

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You complained about your workload, so I hired an inexperienced guy to help.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is exactly the opposite of what I wanted.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He doesn't know much, but he makes up for it by asking lots of questions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So he'll be bugging me every minute?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not every minute. He takes a lot of sick days.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... you hired a guy who is useless, but it's okay because he also has bad attendance?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's not a perfect world.

transcript.speaker: New Hire
transcript.text: Is this a good time to ask some questions?

situation: Dilbert complains about his workload, and the Boss responds by hiring an inexperienced helper who asks endless questions. The Boss insists it won't be so bad because the new hire takes lots of sick days. As the Boss walks off, the new hire arrives at Dilbert's desk ready with questions.
punchline: The Boss treats the new hire's poor attendance as a selling point, and Dilbert gets no relief from his workload, just an eager questioner added to it.
summary: Instead of easing an overworked engineer's burden, management adds a clueless assistant who needs constant hand-holding, and the only consolation offered is that he is often absent.

file: 2014/2014-11-19_deception_money_wages_work ethic_annual pay_deal_split work_salary_work percentage_pass the buck.gif
title: Dogbert Outsources the CEO Job

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will give you 10% of my annual pay if you do 100% of my job for me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: 10% of my pay as CEO is still a lot of money.

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: I'll do it.

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: I'll give you 10% of what he's paying me if you do 100% of his work plus mine. It's still a lot of money.

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: I'm in!

situation: Dogbert, now CEO, offers an employee 10% of his annual pay to do his entire job. The employee accepts, then makes the same offer to a younger employee: 10% of what he is paid to do both his own work and the CEO's work. The young employee eagerly agrees.
punchline: The job gets passed down a chain of people each pocketing a cut while the person at the bottom does all the work for a tiny fraction of the pay, and he is happy to accept.
summary: A boss hands off his job for a cut of his salary, and the delegate promptly repeats the trick on someone further down.

file: 2014/2014-03-03_business people_managers & supervisors_holacarcy_underlings_abusing for years_boot on neck_resistance to changes_business.gif
title: Boss Begs Against Flat Holacracy

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I'm eliminating all management levels and making us a holacracy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Noooo!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Please don't make me equal to the underlings I've been abusing for years!

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

setting: Office hallway, then a conference room
situation: The bald CEO announces he is abolishing all management levels to create a holacracy. The Pointy-Haired Boss panics and pleads not to be made equal to the underlings he has mistreated for years. In the conference room he blurts out that he always expected to keep his boot on their necks, and Dilbert tells him to hush.
punchline: The Boss's fear of a flat organization reveals that his authority depended on abusing his subordinates, and he accidentally confesses it to the very people he mistreated.
summary: Facing the loss of his rank, a manager inadvertently admits he was counting on mistreating his staff forever.

title: Robot Beheads Coworker Over One-Upmanship

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'm rapidly evolving into a super-intelligent being with godlike powers.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's nothing!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Zoink!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My allergies are bad today.

transcript.speaker: Headless Coworker
transcript.text: That's nothing!

situation: A robot at the table announces that it is evolving into a super-intelligent being with godlike powers, and a coworker dismissively says that's nothing. The robot zaps the coworker's head clean off. Later, Dilbert and another coworker complain about their allergies while the headless coworker, holding his severed head, still insists that's nothing.
punchline: The coworker's compulsion to one-up everyone's complaints is so strong that he keeps saying 'That's nothing!' even after being decapitated by a godlike robot.
summary: A habitual complainer trivializes everything even after a newly godlike robot literally takes his head off.

file: 2014/2014-09-28_bird poop_cars_incentives_mass transit_punishment_worst employee of the month_special parking spot_big tree_every bird_firemans axe_wallow in shame_incentives dont work.gif
title: Worst Employee Parking Spot Backfires

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You've been named worst employee of the month.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's under the big tree that every bird in the county uses as a public restroom.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: By the end of the day, you'll need a fireman's axe just to find the door handle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As you chop your way toward the inner core that is your car, think about how you could have worked harder this month.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll probably draw a crowd in the parking lot so remember to wallow in your shame.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I take mass transit to work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Incentives don't work.

situation: The Boss tells a bald, bespectacled employee that he has been named worst employee of the month and describes his punishment: a parking spot under a tree full of bird droppings, where his car will be buried in filth and he will be publicly shamed. The employee calmly points out that he takes mass transit to work, so the punishment is meaningless.
punchline: The Boss's elaborate punishment is defeated because the employee doesn't drive, leading him to conclude that incentives don't work rather than that his plan was poorly thought out.
summary: A manager's carefully imagined humiliation involving bird-fouled parking falls flat when the target never drives to the office.

title: Happiest Person Without Ambition

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You have no ambition, no pride, and no self-respect.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm also the happiest person in this room.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Now I just want to kill you.

situation: Alice sits across from Wally, who sips coffee while she lists his failings: mental weakness, no ambition, no pride, no self-respect. Wally calmly replies that he is also the happiest person in the room. Alice, who is clearly not happy, responds that she now wants to kill him.
punchline: Wally's total lack of ambition and self-respect has made him happier than the driven, ambitious Alice, which infuriates her enough to wish him dead.
summary: A coworker's scathing critique of a slacker backfires when he points out that his low standards have left him far more content than she is.

title: Feedback That Makes You Feel Valued

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're supposed to appreciate feedback because it makes you feel valued.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How does listening to you belittle me about things you don't understand make me feel valued?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It must be an indirect thing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe we should just try it and see how it feels.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whatever.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't actually watch you work, so I'm mostly guessing about the things you do wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I accuse you of being slow and disorganized!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it working yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, if that makes you go away.

situation: The Boss offers Dilbert feedback on his performance, insisting he should appreciate it because it makes him feel valued. Dilbert questions how being belittled by someone who doesn't understand his work could feel valuable, so the Boss proposes a trial run and admits he never watches Dilbert work. He then accuses Dilbert of being slow and disorganized and asks if it's working yet.
punchline: Dilbert says the feedback is working only if it makes the Boss go away, exposing it as baseless criticism that does nothing to make anyone feel valued.
summary: A manager insists that guesswork-based criticism should make his employee feel valued, and the employee's only appreciation is that it ends the conversation.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

punchline: Dogbert's identical, deadpan 'You're doomed' response to every stage of Dilbert's plan suggests that no amount of pivoting or enthusiasm can save a start-up from failure.
summary: A hopeful Dilbert outlines his entrepreneurial game plan while Dogbert repeatedly and bluntly predicts failure.

title: Idiots Agree With Everything You Say

situation: Alice tells the Boss she has just been talking to some idiots. The Boss notes that these people agree with her on every topic, implying she may be the one who is wrong. When Alice asks what his point is, he says her reaction is just what the idiots would say.
punchline: The Boss cleverly implies that Alice's agreeing 'idiots' are a sign she is wrong, and then claims her defensive reply proves she is one of them.
summary: A manager turns a coworker's complaint about fools around by suggesting that anyone who agrees with her must be in the same camp.

punchline: The executives are so impressed by meaningless cloud and dollar-sign imagery that one of them is silently coaxing the others to give a slow clap, showing that executives reward presentation polish over actual results.
summary: A manager coaches his employee to disguise a total lack of results with big fonts and shiny symbols, and the brass in the boardroom are completely won over.

title: Boss Doubts Employee's Perfect Project Status

punchline: The employee sarcastically admits his status report is fiction, and slyly implies he does little or no real work, which the Boss foolishly assumes he does.
summary: A worker's rosy progress report meets suspicion from his manager, and he retorts that the manager's real mistake is thinking he does any work.

file: 2014/2014-04-27_business ethics_deception_new business strategy_laptop_coffee shop_public access_wifi_hackers_strategy document_sell secrets_competitors_business strategy_break in.gif

summary: By flattering his vain boss into claiming the credit, an engineer wins budget approval for his own pet project.

punchline: The Boss builds up false hope that she is being promoted, then crushes her with a flat "no" and an extra insult for guessing wrong.
summary: A newly appointed interim chief executive teases an employee about a promotion, then cruelly rejects her hopeful answer.

file: 2014/2014-07-22_ignorance (knowledge)_magic_thinking_incomplete data_intuition and epxerince_make decision_magical thinking_fixes ignorance.gif

punchline: Dilbert extends the baby metaphor to its logical conclusion, so his agreement with the coworker is actually a scathing insult to the software.
summary: Asked to treat a colleague's software like a precious infant, an engineer agrees by describing the code as a messy, resource-draining lump.

situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate and asks about his biggest accomplishment at his last job. The candidate gives a vague, unimpressive answer about making phone calls and stuff. When the Boss asks if he actually wants the job, the candidate cheerfully admits he is just lonely.
punchline: The candidate's honest admission that he is only seeking the job for companionship, not out of any real interest, undercuts the usual interview pretense of enthusiasm and shows how little his last job accomplished.

title: Dilbert Flushes Unimportant Names

transcript.text: Flush

situation: A coworker greets Dilbert and reminds him they met last week, but Dilbert has no memory of it. Dilbert explains that he only retains information that might be important and discards everything else. When the coworker offers his name, a flush sound signals Dilbert has just deleted it.
punchline: Dilbert's cold admission that he mentally flushes unimportant information is proven immediately when he dumps the coworker's name the moment he hears it, implying the man is not worth remembering.
summary: A colleague tries to reintroduce himself to Dilbert, who bluntly admits he purges anything unimportant from his memory and promptly does so with the man's name.

file: 2014/2014-05-15_dating_time travel_date cyborgs_time travelrs_from future_less flattering guess_relationships.gif
title: Dilbert's Dating Guess Escalates

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I don't date cyborgs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not a cyborg. Yet.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I don't date time travelers from the future.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not a time traveler.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: My third guess is less flattering.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm a time traveler.

setting: A social gathering or party where both hold drinks
situation: Dilbert is chatting with a woman at a party. She guesses he is a cyborg, then a time traveler from the future, and he denies both. When she hints her third guess will be less flattering, he suddenly admits to being a time traveler.
punchline: Dilbert would rather claim to be an implausible time traveler than hear the woman's unflattering opinion of him, which is implied to be worse than any sci-fi explanation for his oddness.
summary: Faced with the prospect of an insulting guess about himself, a awkward man at a party prefers to confess to impossible time travel.

title: Criticize Behavior, Not Person, Badly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Criticize the behavior, not the person.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The email you sent to everyone looks as if it had been written by a monkey on crack.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just to be clear, you are terrific, but everything you do is exactly what a moron would do.

situation: The Boss reminds himself in a thought bubble to criticize the behavior and not the person. He then confronts an employee about an email sent to everyone, insulting its quality in harsh terms. He tries to soften it by saying the employee is terrific, but then insults everything the employee does, leaving the employee visibly angry.
punchline: The Boss follows the advice to criticize behavior rather than the person in a technical sense only, so his supposed reassurance is just a thinly veiled insult that the employee is a moron.
summary: A manager attempts to give diplomatic feedback but ends up delivering an insult wrapped in a fake compliment.

file: 2014/2014-07-16_money_trees_computer model_genetically modify_tree growth_rare earth minerals_run a trail_money dents grow on trees_fault.gif
title: Money Doesn't Grow on Trees, Strangers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My computer model indicates that I can genetically modify a tree to grow leaves made of rare earth minerals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All I need is a hundred dollars to run a trial.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sorry. Money doesn't grow on trees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, now we know whose fault that is.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Strangers?

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that his computer model shows a tree could be genetically modified to grow leaves made of valuable rare earth minerals, and asks for a hundred dollars to run a trial. The Boss refuses, saying money doesn't grow on trees. Dilbert says that now they know whose fault that is, and the Boss cluelessly guesses 'Strangers?'
punchline: Dilbert implies that his own tree idea could finally make money grow on trees, so denying funding is what blocks it, while the clueless Boss misses the point and offers 'Strangers?' as if answering a whodunit about who is to blame.
summary: A cheap research request to grow valuable leaves is rejected with a cliché, and the Boss cannot even follow the engineer's retort.

file: 2014/2014-07-29_avarice_business ethics_stock market_stock split_dumb stock holders_fantastic prodcuts_money.gif
title: Stock Split Beats Building Better Products

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The board has voted to do a stock split.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It came down to a choice between creating fantastic products or attracting dumber stockholders.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: One of those two things is easy.

setting: Conference room during a board or management meeting
situation: The Boss announces to Dilbert and another man at the conference table that the board has voted for a stock split. He explains the board was choosing between building fantastic products and attracting dumber stockholders, then notes that only one of those is easy.
punchline: The board chose the stock split because courting gullible investors is far easier than making good products, implying the company would rather manipulate share appeal than improve what it sells.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits that the company opted for a financial gimmick since it's simpler than actually making something good.

title: Larry, A Good Cultural Fit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, meet Larry. He isn't terribly competent, but he's a good cultural fit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, Larry. Thanks for reinforcing our culture of incompetence.

transcript.speaker: Larry
transcript.text: You're joking about the incompetence, right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure.

situation: The Boss introduces a new hire named Larry to Dilbert and admits Larry isn't very competent but fits the company culture. Dilbert shakes Larry's hand and sarcastically thanks him for reinforcing the culture of incompetence. Larry asks if Dilbert is joking, and the Boss answers 'Sure' while sipping his coffee.
punchline: The Boss's evasive 'Sure' reveals that the culture of incompetence is real and Dilbert wasn't really joking at all.
summary: A manager proudly presents an unqualified newcomer as ideal for the company's slack culture, and a sarcastic welcome gets a noncommittal reply.

file: 2014/2014-01-22_answers_asked_dumb guy_formatted data_obvious in hindsight_questions_stare at me_office seeting_not enough questions.gif
title: Obvious Only In Hindsight

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't have the data you requested last week because I didn't know how you wanted it formatted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could have asked.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's only obvious in hindsight.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why does everyone stare at me that way?

situation: Dilbert stands beside a seated coworker who admits he never delivered requested data because he didn't know the required format. Dilbert points out he could simply have asked, and the coworker dismisses this as only obvious in hindsight. Dilbert stares silently while the coworker wonders why everyone looks at him that way.
punchline: The coworker is oblivious to the fact that his excuse is absurd, and he cannot understand why people stare at him in disbelief.
summary: A worker blames his missed deliverable on not knowing the format, then puzzles over why people give him such incredulous looks.

title: Business Dorky Dress Code

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is our new company dress code. We call it "Business Dorky."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like it because it makes you look powerless, boring, and sexually irrelevant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They make me wear this badge so I don't look like an asexual trespasser.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Accessories make the outfit.

setting: Office, with Dogbert lounging on a green armchair
situation: Dilbert, wearing a red shirt and an ID badge, explains the company's new dress code, which he calls "Business Dorky." He says its appeal is that it makes employees look powerless, boring and sexually irrelevant. Dogbert watches from a chair and comments on the badge.
punchline: The dress code is deliberately designed to strip employees of any appeal, and the badge is the only thing marking Dilbert as an employee rather than a harmless-looking trespasser, which Dogbert treats as a fashion accessory.
summary: Dilbert describes a drab new uniform policy engineered to make staff look unthreatening, and his dog quips about the badge being the finishing touch.

file: 2014/2014-12-24_conversation_smartphone technology_speed evolve_meta organism_sum of parts_looked interetsing_employees_coffee break_cups_business.gif
title: Smartphones Created a Meta-Organism, Disappointingly

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What are you guys talking about? It sounds interesting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We were saying that our smartphone technology has caused us to speed-evolve into a meta-organism that is the sum of our connected parts.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: In my defense, from across the room it looked interesting.

setting: Office break area during a coffee break
situation: Alice walks up to Dilbert and a coworker holding coffee cups and asks what they are discussing, since it sounds interesting. Dilbert gives a lofty explanation that smartphones have made humans evolve into a connected meta-organism. Alice replies that the conversation only looked interesting from a distance.
punchline: Alice admits she only thought the conversation was interesting from afar, and up close it turns out to be pretentious tech jargon, so she regrets asking.
summary: A curious coworker joins a coffee chat and is let down by a grandiose explanation of how phones have merged people into one organism.

file: 2014/2014-04-17_interviews_human resources_random statements_ostriches eye_bigger than brain_randomness_confession_job interview_approved questions_business.gif
title: Interviewer Limited to Random Statements

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm only allowed to ask interview questions that have been approved by Human Resources.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And they haven't approved any yet. So all I can do is make random statements.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: An ostrich's eye is bigger than its brain.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: So is mine!

situation: The Boss is interviewing a job candidate but explains that Human Resources has not approved any interview questions. Since he can only speak approved material, he resorts to making random statements, such as a fact about ostriches. The candidate cheerfully replies that his own eye is bigger than his brain.
punchline: The candidate responds to the random ostrich fact by cheerfully admitting that his eye is bigger than his brain, which unwittingly confesses that he is unintelligent, and arguably suits an interview run this absurdly.
summary: With no approved questions available, a manager fills a job interview with trivia, and the applicant answers with an accidental self-insult.

title: Honest Leadership Assessment Goes Badly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to give me an honest assessment of my leadership.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Thirty minutes later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ... like being stabbed by an angry clown while drowning in a septic tank.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you heard of honesty?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: It's terrible.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert for an honest assessment of his leadership, and Dilbert spends half an hour delivering one, ending with a vivid and gruesome comparison. Afterward the Boss, now holding a coffee mug, asks Ratbert whether he has heard of honesty, and Ratbert replies that it is terrible.
punchline: The Boss claims to want honest feedback but is so wounded by the real thing that he turns to someone else to confirm that honesty is a bad idea.
summary: A manager solicits brutal candor about his leadership, gets exactly that, and promptly decides candor is a mistake.

title: Digital Age Ruined My Focus

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The distractions of the digital age have rewired my brain and ruined my ability to focus.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now I find it painful to dwell on any topic for longer than five seconds.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's talk about this.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No-o-o! Change the topic!

situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells the Boss that digital distractions have wrecked his attention span and that he can't stay on one topic for more than five seconds. The Boss responds by suggesting they discuss the problem itself. Wally panics and begs him to change the subject.
punchline: Wally's inability to focus is so severe that he can't even tolerate a conversation about his inability to focus, which proves his point and lets him dodge the discussion.
summary: An office worker blames the internet for his shrinking attention span, then recoils in horror when his manager offers to discuss it.

file: 2014/2014-07-20_new idea_dream_3d glasses_for real life_people love 3d_not movies_obvious_ideas.gif
title: 3-D Glasses for Real Life

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Last night, an idea for a new product came to me in a dream.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ick.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: 3-D glasses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To watch movies?

transcript.text: No, for real life.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... the glasses would make life in general appear three-dimensional?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Exactly! People love 3-D stuff.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not going to respond to your idea. I'm just going to sit here looking three-dimensional.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wait... how are you doing that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm wearing glasses that make me look 3-D.

situation: A coworker pitches a product idea from a dream: 3-D glasses, but for real life rather than movies. Dilbert points out the flaw that real life is already three-dimensional, and the coworker misses it entirely, insisting people love 3-D stuff. Dilbert silently mocks the idea by pointing out that he already looks three-dimensional.
punchline: Real life is already three-dimensional, so glasses to make it look 3-D are pointless, which Dilbert demonstrates by wearing glasses that do nothing, while the coworker is baffled.
summary: A colleague proposes eyewear that would give everyday existence a third dimension it already has, and Dilbert deadpans his way through the absurdity.

title: Catbert Takes Credit for Ted's Death

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ted retired yesterday and dropped dead this morning.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You worked him to death with perfect timing. Nicely done.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Unless it was just a coincidence.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If I'm being honest, hitting the exact day was just luck.

setting: Office hallway and corporate building exterior
situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, tells the Boss that Ted retired one day and dropped dead the next morning. The Boss congratulates him for working Ted to death with perfect timing. Catbert then admits, over a shot of the office building, that the exact timing may have been mere coincidence and luck.
punchline: Even a heartless HR director who may have literally worked an employee to death is honest enough to admit he can't take full credit for the perfectly timed death, a darkly comic bit of false modesty about overwork.
summary: A cat-faced HR chief and his boss admire the grim precision of a worker dying right after retirement, before conceding that fate may have done the scheduling.

title: Dilbert Mocks Boss's Certainty About Prototype

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your prototype will never be economical.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Certainty about the future is a sign of mental illness.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try to be more level-conscious.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, your Highness.

situation: The Boss, holding a piece of paper, declares that Dilbert's prototype will never be economical. Dilbert replies that being certain about the future is a sign of mental illness. The Boss then tells Dilbert to be more 'level-conscious,' demanding deference to his rank, and Dilbert sarcastically answers 'Yes, your Highness.'
punchline: The Boss, who just made a baseless prediction, reacts to Dilbert's pointed rebuttal by pulling rank and demanding deference, and Dilbert's 'Your Highness' mocks that hierarchy-obsessed ego.
summary: A manager's confident dismissal of an engineer's work is answered with a barb about delusional certainty, so the manager insists on being shown more respect for his position.

file: 2014/2014-01-08_emotional well being_hug_managers & supervisors_rodents_touch a rat_around neck_exercises_business.gif
title: Boss Offers Rat Touch Instead of Hug

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Experts say I can increase your engagement by caring for your emotional well-being.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I would give you a hug, but I'm afraid of getting whatever made you this way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I am willing to touch a rat that touches you, and that's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Put it on my neck.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has read that caring for an employee's emotional well-being boosts engagement. He refuses to hug Dilbert for fear of catching whatever afflicts him, and instead offers to touch a rat that has touched Dilbert. He holds up Ratbert, and Dilbert deadpans that the rat should be put on his neck.
punchline: The Boss's attempt at emotional support is so germophobic and absurd that a second-hand rat touch is his best offer, and Dilbert sarcastically accepts it as a neck massage.
summary: A boss trying to follow expert advice on employee care avoids a hug but proposes a bizarre rat-mediated substitute that Dilbert wearily goes along with.

title: Beta Launch Promise Draws Laughter

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Offscreen laughter
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a credibility problem.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I should believe that?

setting: Conference room, then the office building exterior, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert tells a meeting of colleagues that he plans to launch the beta version in two months. The whole office building erupts in laughter at the claim. Dilbert later admits to Dogbert that he has a credibility problem, and Dogbert doubts even that statement.
punchline: Dilbert's schedule estimates are so unreliable that everyone laughs at his deadline, and Dogbert is so skeptical that he doubts even Dilbert's admission of the problem.
summary: A confident product deadline gets mocked by the entire building, and even the admission of having a trust problem gets met with suspicion.

title: Boss's Self-Deprecating Joke Displays Power

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hello, underling. Watch me do a self-deprecating joke to underscore my true power.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ho ho! I am not good at some types of unimportant tasks! Ha ha!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why I'm glad I have people like you to do those things.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Impressive.

situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert, who is holding a coffee mug, and announces that he is about to make a self-deprecating joke to demonstrate his power. He jokes that he is bad at unimportant tasks, then points out that he has underlings like Dilbert to handle them. Dilbert deadpans that it is impressive.
punchline: The Boss's supposedly humble joke is actually a boast about his authority, since admitting weakness at trivial tasks only highlights that he can delegate them to subordinates.
summary: A manager stages a modest-sounding joke about his own shortcomings that really just reminds a subordinate who gets to dump the grunt work on whom.

title: Dinosaur Defends His Flip Phone

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
