transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Why are you proud of being a big, dumb dinosaur with a terrible phone?

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: I'm sensing a lot of judgment in that question.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Wait until you hear my follow-ups.

setting: Office, in front of a plain gradient background
situation: A green dinosaur coworker announces that he uses a flip phone instead of a smartphone because it meets his needs. A woman coworker responds by insulting him as a big, dumb dinosaur with a terrible phone. When he points out her judgmental tone, she says she's only getting started.
punchline: The woman's question is openly insulting, and when called out on it she gleefully promises even harsher follow-up questions rather than backing down.
summary: A coworker mocks a dinosaur's outdated phone with a thinly veiled insult, then threatens to unleash more criticism.

title: Dogbert Withholds Negativity Under Duress

transcript.text: Don't ruin this day for me. I don't want to hear one word of negativity out of you. None.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want this to be a perfect day.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Once again you have grossly underestimated my self-control.

setting: Outside on a street or lawn, with Dogbert sitting on a green cushion
situation: Dilbert comes home happily humming and announces he had a great day at work for the first time ever. He warns Dogbert not to say anything negative so he can keep the day perfect. Dogbert responds with a deadpan comment that technically complies while hinting he is straining to hold back his usual cynicism.
punchline: Dogbert's remark about his own self-control implies he is barely restraining his negative commentary, and the very statement lets the sarcasm slip through anyway.
summary: After a rare good day, a cheerful man begs his sarcastic pet to keep his cynicism to himself, and the pet smugly boasts about his restraint.

title: Start-Up Without The Start-Up Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to act more like a start-up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You mean we can ask for funding for one thing and then pivot six times and build something entirely different?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is there a version where we don't do any of that and I can still call myself a hacker?

situation: The Boss tells his team the company should act more like a start-up. Dilbert spells out what start-up behavior really involves: raising funding for one idea and then repeatedly pivoting to build something completely different. The Boss asks if there is a version that skips all of that while still letting him call himself a hacker.
punchline: The Boss wants the cool image of a start-up and a hacker without any of the risky, chaotic work that actually defines them.
summary: A manager craves start-up credibility but balks at everything a start-up actually does.

file: 2014/2014-07-14_money_rich people_being rich_income inequality_happy_networth_thousand times_800 times_net worth.gif

summary: A wealthy Dogbert revels in how much richer he is than his friend until a small factual correction about the size of the gap spoils his fun.

punchline: Wally turns the Boss's request for honest pushback into a trap, refusing the advisor role and then getting thanked for the refusal, which the Boss finds oddly persuasive.
summary: Seeking a candid advisor, the boss is turned down flat by Wally, who then talks him into expressing gratitude for the rejection.

file: 2014/2014-05-10_electronic mail_obliviousness_business plan_email about plan_rambling and disjointed_no understanding of problem_proposed solution_havent sen email.gif

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Was it a rambling and disjointed email that showed no understanding of the problem or the proposed solution?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, asks Dilbert whether he saw the email about Dilbert's business plan. Dilbert asks if it was a rambling, disjointed email showing no grasp of the problem or solution. The Boss says no, so Dilbert concludes he hasn't seen it.
punchline: Dilbert insults the Boss's writing by describing his email accurately, and the Boss obliviously denies it matches, never realizing Dilbert is mocking him.
summary: A manager asks about an email, and the employee's description of it is so brutally accurate that the manager's denial is the funniest part.

file: 2014/2014-01-07_ironic_irony_statue crushed guard_too soon_word invention_iron sculpture_crushed security guard.gif
title: Iron Sculpture Crushes Guard: Ironic

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The iron sculpture in our lobby fell off its base and crushed a security guard.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And that's where we get the word "ironic."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It happened ten minutes ago.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh, so it's "too soon"?

The coworker immediately jokes that this is the origin of the word 'ironic', using air quotes. Dilbert points out the accident happened only ten minutes ago, and the coworker asks whether the joke is 'too soon'.
punchline: The coworker makes a pun on 'iron' and 'ironic' about a real tragedy and only realizes it might be inappropriate when told it just happened, treating the sensitivity as a matter of timing rather than basic decency.
summary: A colleague turns news of a deadly accident into a wordplay joke and only wonders about its timing once he learns how recent it was.

file: 2014/2014-03-02_obliviousness_thinking_judge them_chipmunk_judge algebra_complex and useful_innovative circuit design_engineer_office setting_desks_computers_engineering.gif

summary: A manager happily accepts being compared to a clueless rodent facing math, then confirms the comparison by weakly critiquing a circuit.

title: Nothing Going Right, Boss Regrets

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Guess what's going right for me today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Nothing!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I usually do a better job of avoiding them when they have problems.

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's office
situation: Alice approaches the Boss, who is holding a coffee mug, and asks him to guess what is going right for her today. He thinks 'uh-oh', and she screams 'Nothing!!!' in his face, blowing his hair and tie back and splattering his coffee. Afterward, he stands shirtless and mildly bewildered, remarking that he normally avoids employees when they are upset.
punchline: The Boss's only takeaway from Alice's furious outburst is that he failed at his usual strategy of dodging employees who have problems.
summary: A furious employee blasts her manager with a scream, and he reflects only that he slipped up on his habit of steering clear of troubled staff.

file: 2014/2014-01-29_cowardice_terrorists_international terrorist_cancel order_big hit earnings_decimate value_stock options_transfer_poor safety record.gif
title: Drone Customer Is A Terrorist

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I discovered that the customer for our fleet sale of commercial drones is an international terrorist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now we have to cancel the order, take a big hit to earnings, and decimate the value of your stock options in the company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Or . . . I could transfer you to a department that has a poor safety record and hope for the best.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that the buyer of a big commercial drone order is an international terrorist. He points out that cancelling the sale would hurt company earnings and wipe out the value of the boss's stock options. The boss considers it and proposes transferring Dilbert to a dangerous department instead of cancelling.
punchline: The boss would rather get rid of the employee who found the problem, possibly fatally, than lose money by refusing to sell drones to a terrorist.
summary: Faced with a whistleblower who uncovered a dangerous customer, a self-interested manager plots to silence him rather than lose his stock options.

file: 2014/2014-01-23_key to success_follow instinct_slap you_stop babbling_relax_good feelings_slap.gif
title: Following Your Instinct To Slap

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: The key to success is to follow your instinct.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My instinct tells me to slap you until you stop babbling nonsense.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Please don't do that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Relax. I have a good feeling about it.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: At a meeting, a bald coworker offers the platitude that success comes from following your instinct. Alice replies that her instinct is to slap him until he stops babbling. When he nervously objects, she calmly tells him to relax because she has a good feeling about it.
punchline: Alice turns the coworker's own motivational advice against him, showing that blindly following instinct can mean violence, while she is happily confident about it.
summary: A coworker's glib self-help advice about trusting your gut is taken literally by a short-tempered colleague with painful intentions.

file: 2014/2014-02-02_engineers_managers & supervisors_questioning_jeff bezos rule_rule of meetings_two pizzas_feed a meeting_eat two pizzas_zeros paradox_feed everyone_cheese bread_business.gif
title: Engineers Overthink the Two-Pizza Rule

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to use the Jeff Bezos rule of meetings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bezos says you should never have a meeting that is so big you can't feed everyone with two pizzas.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can eat two pizzas by myself.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How do you count the people who have gluten sensitivity and don't eat pizza?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I apply Zeno's paradox to the slice size, can I have infinite attendees?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And what does it mean to "feed" everyone? Do they need to be totally full?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop being engineers!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How does cheese bread fit into this?

situation: The Boss announces that meetings will follow Jeff Bezos's two-pizza rule for limiting attendance. Wally, Alice and Dilbert respond with literal-minded objections about big eaters, gluten sensitivity, Zeno's paradox and the meaning of 'feed'. The Boss finally loses patience and shouts at them to stop being engineers.
punchline: The engineers nitpick a simple management heuristic with absurd technical rigor, and when the Boss yells at them to stop, Wally cheerfully continues with another pedantic question about cheese bread.
summary: A manager's attempt to adopt a famous pizza-based meeting guideline is derailed by employees who dissect it with pedantic, overly literal logic.

title: Networking Request Becomes Unread Email

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Would you mind if I network with you to help my career?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I would have said yes, but you made it feel all weird and creepy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Perhaps you could send me email that I won't read.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That makes you my best friend!

situation: A coworker holding a coffee mug asks The Boss if he can network with him to help his career. The Boss says the request felt weird and creepy, then suggests the coworker send emails that he will never read. The coworker happily declares that this makes The Boss his best friend.
punchline: The coworker is so delighted by any kind of connection that he treats being ignored by The Boss as friendship, showing how shallow and awkward corporate networking really is.
summary: A career-minded employee cheerfully turns a lukewarm brush-off from his boss into a new best friendship.

file: 2014/2014-09-06_big business_mergers & acquisitions_worry_short poition_cartoon cat_bloom county_comic strip_mantra_bill ackman_stocks_defective people.gif
title: Boss Unworried About Short Seller

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bill Ackman just took a huge short position in our stock.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not worried about a cartoon cat from an old "Bloom County" comic strip.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I care too much.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That is the mantra of all defective people.

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and a hallway
situation: Dilbert warns the Boss that a famous investor has taken a large short position against the company's stock. The Boss dismisses the threat, saying he is not worried about a cartoon cat from an old comic strip. Dilbert wonders aloud if he cares too much, and Wally, holding a coffee mug, tells him that attitude is the mantra of defective people.
punchline: Wally mocks Dilbert's concern by calling it the mantra of defective people, which makes the Boss's complete lack of worry sound like an enviable, even admirable, trait.
summary: A manager waves off an investor betting against the company by confusing him with a cartoon character, and a coworker sneers at the one employee who actually worries.

title: Chocolate Makes Boss Think Scientifically

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's some dark chocolate. Studies show it makes you think better.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why are you suddenly doing things that make scientific sense, instead of your usual magical thinking?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just ate three pounds of chocolate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow. It works fast.

situation: A speech bubble offers dark chocolate to a seated colleague, claiming studies show it improves thinking. The Boss then asks why the person is suddenly acting on scientific sense rather than his usual magical thinking. It turns out the boss ate three pounds of chocolate, and Dilbert is impressed at how quickly it worked.
punchline: The boss's sudden burst of rational behavior is credited to a huge binge of chocolate, implying that his normal state is so irrational that even a sugar overdose counts as an improvement.
summary: After gorging on chocolate said to boost brainpower, a manager abruptly starts making sensible decisions, and his employee marvels at the speed of the effect.

title: Sleepless Consultant Flatlines, Wants Graphs

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I haven't slept since October because the culture of consulting firms is anti-health.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I'm flat-lining!

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: False alarm. I'm back. Who wants to make some graphs?

situation: At a meeting table with Dilbert and the bald Boss, a consultant complains he hasn't slept since October because consulting firm culture is unhealthy. He then clutches his chest and announces he is flat-lining, only to recover moments later and cheerfully ask who wants to make graphs.
punchline: Even a near-death experience from overwork is treated as a minor interruption, and the consultant immediately returns to the grind of making graphs, proving the unhealthy culture he just described.
summary: A chronically sleep-deprived consultant fakes a fatal collapse, then bounces right back to eagerly crank out charts.

file: 2014/2014-07-03_friendship_internet & world wide web_facebook freinds_speed bumps_engineers_pictures of food_eat food_google_relationships.gif
title: Friends Are Engineering Speed Bumps

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can I be your friend on Facebook?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Friends are like speed bumps for engineers.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How will you see pictures of my food?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you eat food that Google doesn't know about?

situation: A coworker with a bowl-cut hairstyle asks Dilbert to accept her as a friend on Facebook. Dilbert replies that friends only slow engineers down, and when she points out he would miss her food photos, he retorts that Google already has pictures of any food worth seeing.
punchline: Dilbert dismisses social connection as an obstacle and implies that a search engine can supply everything a friend would, making her friendship pointless to him.
summary: A coworker's friendly social media request is brushed off by an engineer who trusts web search more than people.

title: Renounce Science For A Raise

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: According to scientific research, your happiness will not increase if you make more money.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Therefore, I can only authorize a raise for you if you renounce science.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Say it! Say you renounce science!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: El gato diablo!

situation: Catbert, acting as the evil HR director, tells Dilbert that research shows more money won't make him happier. He then offers a raise only if Dilbert publicly renounces science. Dilbert, cornered, responds by calling Catbert 'the devil cat' in Spanish rather than renouncing science.
punchline: Catbert twists scientific findings into a cruel loophole to withhold a raise, and Dilbert's reply cleverly sidesteps the demand by insulting Catbert in Spanish.
summary: An evil HR cat uses a happiness study as an excuse to demand an employee abandon science before getting any raise.

title: Software Passes Pointy-Haired Boss Test

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My software can't pass a standard Turing test yet, but it does pass the Pointy-Haired Boss test.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Computer, I have a question about our company strategy.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Try working smarter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't even make sense!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wasn't prepared to like it, but you won me over.

setting: Dilbert's office, around a small table with a software device
situation: Dilbert shows off his software, claiming it can't pass a real Turing test but can fool the Pointy-Haired Boss. When Dilbert asks the computer about company strategy, it replies with the empty advice 'Try working smarter.' Dilbert is frustrated by the nonsense, while the Boss and a coworker watch and the Boss is impressed.
punchline: The computer's meaningless management cliché is indistinguishable from what the Boss says, so the Boss is delighted by it, proving the software passes the Pointy-Haired Boss test.
summary: A programmer's chatbot fails at real intelligence but dazzles his boss by spouting a hollow buzzword-style platitude.

title: Engineers Versus Marketing Pay Dispute

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Marketing Guy

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: I don't see why engineers get paid more than marketing professionals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe because engineers designed and built every important part of modern civilization and all you did was misrepresent it.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: My point is that you need both.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You really don't.

situation: A marketing guy complains that engineers earn more than marketing professionals. Dilbert fires back that engineers built everything important in modern civilization while marketing only misrepresented it. When the marketer argues that both are needed, Dilbert flatly says they aren't.
punchline: Dilbert dismisses the marketer's claim of mutual necessity, implying that marketing adds no real value and engineers deserve higher pay.
summary: A marketer grumbles about engineers' higher salaries and gets a blunt lesson in who actually built the world.

title: Employee Loves Being Manipulated

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Happy Monday!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Thanks to your slavish pursuit of management fads, I feel engaged and motivated!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's sort of creepy.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I love being manipulated!

setting: Office hallway on a Monday morning
situation: An unusually cheerful employee greets the Boss, who is holding a coffee mug, with a happy Monday. He thanks the Boss for chasing management fads, claiming they have left him engaged and motivated. The Boss finds this creepy, and the employee enthusiastically says he loves being manipulated.
punchline: The employee is gleefully aware that management fads are just manipulation tactics, yet they work on him anyway, which unsettles even the Boss who uses them.
summary: A chipper worker praises his manager's trend-chasing for boosting his morale, then cheerfully admits he enjoys being manipulated.

file: 2014/2014-01-27_competition (psychology)_wages_big data_top perfromers_higher pay_average performance_average people say_money.gif
title: Still Here Means You're Average

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Our big data analysis tells us that only the top performers leave for higher pay.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Since you're still here, it means your performance is average at best.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not fair!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's what all the average people say.

setting: Catbert's office, across a desk from Dilbert
situation: Catbert, acting as the HR head, tells Dilbert that company data shows only top performers leave for better-paying jobs. He then concludes that since Dilbert hasn't left, he must be an average performer. Dilbert protests that this is unfair, and Catbert replies that average people always say that.
punchline: Catbert uses big data to turn an employee's loyalty into proof of mediocrity, and his protest is dismissed as exactly what mediocre people would say, so there is no way to win the argument.
summary: An HR executive twists workforce statistics to insult an employee who has stayed put, then waves off his objection as typical of the mediocre.

title: Catbert's High-Five Becomes a Slap

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm getting complaints that you've been trash-talking employees' families so they'll spend more time at work.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I stopped by to give you a high-five from Human Resources.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your aim is terrible.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The first one was practice!

setting: The Boss's office, with Catbert standing on his desk
situation: The Boss confronts Catbert, the evil HR director, about complaints that he trash-talks employees' families so they stay at work longer. Catbert says he came to deliver a high-five from Human Resources, and the Boss swings at him and knocks him flat on the desk. The Boss claims the first swing was only practice.
punchline: The Boss pretends to appreciate Catbert's cruelty but actually uses the 'high-five' as an excuse to slap him, then claims the first attempt was just practice, implying he'll try again.
summary: A manager reacts to word of the HR cat's family-wrecking schemes with a violent slap disguised as a congratulatory gesture, then promises a better attempt next time.

file: 2014/2014-08-10_any penalty_big trouble_idiotic plan_imperfect plan_leading by example_perfect plan.gif
title: Imperfect Plan, Zero Penalty Misunderstanding

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's better to execute an imperfect plan today than a perfect plan next week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yay! We're free from any penalty if we do things wrong!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um, no. Nothing like that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're still in big trouble if you do anything wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I'm also in big trouble if I take longer to do things right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Okay, I get it. Your plan is idiotic, but we should do it anyway and not wait for you to say something smarter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're leading by example. Nicely done.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What other dumb things should we do right away?

situation: The Boss tells his team it's better to execute an imperfect plan quickly than a perfect plan later. Dilbert cheerfully assumes mistakes will go unpunished, but the Boss clarifies that errors and slowness are both punishable. Dilbert concludes the plan is idiotic yet should be carried out anyway, and the Boss praises this as leading by example.
punchline: The Boss's no-win policy punishes both mistakes and delay, so Dilbert's sarcastic agreement to do an idiotic plan is mistaken for model leadership, prompting Wally to ask what other dumb things to do.
summary: A manager demanding fast action while penalizing both errors and delays gets sarcastic compliance that he mistakes for admirable initiative.
enterprise_concepts: perfect is the enemy of good

title: Adding Jeff Is Like Baby on Fire

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I'm adding Jeff to your project team.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's like trying to put out a forest fire by dropping a baby on it.

transcript.speaker: Jeff
transcript.text: I'm avail-able to help, too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, your job is to keep Jeff from doing anything.

situation: The Boss announces that he is adding a new person, Jeff, to Alice's project team. Alice responds with a sarcastic analogy about how useless that help will be. Jeff cheerfully offers to help, and the Boss responds by reassigning Alice's job to keeping Jeff from doing anything.
punchline: Instead of fixing the problem of an unhelpful team member, the Boss gives Alice the extra task of babysitting Jeff, making the 'help' actively counterproductive.
summary: A manager forces an unhelpful colleague onto a project, then tells the overworked engineer her new duty is to prevent him from accomplishing anything.

title: Boss Leans Toward Micromanaging Staff

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Experts say managers should hire great people and set clear expectations.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They don't say what to do when you get the first part wrong, but I'm leaning toward micromanaging.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My employee engagement just went down.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That was never a real thing.

situation: The Boss tells his team that experts advise hiring great people and setting clear expectations, then admits he doesn't know what to do when the hiring part goes wrong. He announces he will micromanage instead, and Alice says her engagement has dropped. The Boss dismisses employee engagement as something that was never real.
punchline: The Boss implicitly admits he hired poor performers and responds by micromanaging them, then waves away the resulting loss of morale by denying engagement ever existed.
summary: A manager who botched his hiring decides to hover over his staff, and shrugs off their sinking morale as imaginary.

title: Dilbert's Likability Plan Backfires Badly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Experts say I can improve my likeability by showing that I remember things that people have told me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For example, there was the time you said you always go to funerals dressed as a clown to keep things light.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I never said that!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you sure? I told everyone you did.

setting: Office desk or break table with coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert explains to a coworker that experts say remembering what people tell you makes you more likeable. He then cites an example of the coworker supposedly saying they dress as a clown at funerals. The coworker denies ever saying it, and Dilbert admits he has already told everyone that they did.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to seem likeable by recalling past conversations is undermined because he fabricated the memory and spread it around, ruining the coworker's reputation.
summary: A man trying to charm a colleague with his supposed memory instead reveals he invented a ridiculous story and has been spreading it as fact.

title: Solutions Not Unexpected Problems Demand

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you going to meet the launch deadline?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. There were unexpected problems.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need solutions, not unexpected problems!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did that mean anything?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Almost. Good try.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether he will meet the launch deadline, and Dilbert says no because of unexpected problems. The Boss responds with a demand for solutions rather than problems, then asks Dilbert if his own statement meant anything.
punchline: The Boss's demand for 'solutions, not unexpected problems' is a meaningless managerial slogan, and Dilbert politely grades it as nearly meaningful but a failed attempt.
summary: A manager barks a nonsensical demand at an employee who reports a missed deadline, then sincerely asks whether it made sense.

file: 2014/2014-07-31_mergers & acquisitions_start up_45 hours_mandatory online training_seven customers.gif
title: Acquired Founder Quits Over Training

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We got Randy by buying his start-up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Randy, Dilbert will show you how to access our 45 hours of mandatory online training.

transcript.speaker: Randy
transcript.text: I quit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, at least we still have his start-up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And all seven of its customers, too.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: The Boss announces that the company acquired Randy by buying his start-up, then tells him Dilbert will show him how to access 45 hours of mandatory online training. Randy immediately quits. The Boss consoles himself that they still own the start-up, and Dilbert dryly adds that they also got its seven customers.
punchline: The acquisition was so small and the training so awful that the new hire walks out instantly, leaving the company with a tiny start-up and just seven customers as its prize.
summary: A company buys a tiny start-up, and its founder resigns the moment he hears about the compulsory training, leaving management with a meagre consolation.

title: Finish Sooner By Dying Faster

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your project is behind schedule. Is there any way to finish sooner?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Well, in the long run, we all die, so you could die right now and get to your endpoint faster.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You went dark fast.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I had that one in the hopper.

situation: The Boss tells Alice her project is behind schedule and asks if she can finish sooner. Alice answers with a grim joke, telling him he could die right now to reach his own endpoint faster. The Boss remarks that she went dark quickly, and she admits she had that retort prepared.
punchline: Alice answers a pointless request to speed up the project with a morbid insult that she had ready and waiting for exactly this kind of demand.
summary: Pressed to speed up a late project, Alice offers her boss a deadly shortcut and admits she had the line saved up.
keywords: in the long run we all die

file: 2014/2014-05-08_personnel officers_hr approval_enjoying pain_new rule_interview qiuestions_awkward feelings_cat_desk_laughing at boss_animals.gif
title: Catbert Enjoys Boss's Interview Pain

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Interviews are getting awkward because of the new rule that Human Resources has to approve all questions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you haven't approved any yet.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Heh heh heh heh heh heh!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop enjoying my pain!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Stop making it so enjoyable!

setting: The Boss's office, with Catbert sitting on a desk
situation: The Boss complains to Catbert, the HR director, that interviews have become awkward because HR must approve every interview question, and Catbert hasn't approved any. Catbert responds by laughing gleefully at the Boss's frustration. The Boss demands that he stop enjoying his pain.
punchline: Catbert, the sadistic HR director, deliberately withholds approval of interview questions to cause the Boss misery, and he cheerfully blames the Boss for being too fun to torment.
summary: A manager grumbles that a new HR approval requirement is crippling his hiring interviews, only to find the HR cat is deliberately stalling and delighting in his suffering.

file: 2014/2014-02-13_deception_language_managers & supervisors_key to leadership_vague golas_jargon_wishful thinking_dumping work_whine about goals_better system_business.gif
title: Vague Goals Make Endless Work Dumping

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The key to leadership is setting vague goals that are a combination of jargon and wishful thinking.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That way, I can keep dumping work on you without hearing you whine that it doesn't fit with your goals.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have to admit, my system is better than whatever you're doing over there.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yup.

setting: Boss's office, sitting across a desk
situation: The Boss explains to Dilbert his leadership philosophy: setting vague goals made of jargon and wishful thinking. He says this lets him assign any work he likes without employees objecting that it falls outside their goals. He then asks Dilbert to concede that his system beats whatever Dilbert is doing, and Dilbert agrees.
punchline: Dilbert's flat 'Yup' concedes that the boss's cynical system really is better for the boss, since vague goals let him exploit employees without any pushback.
summary: A manager brags that fuzzy, buzzword-filled objectives are a clever way to pile on tasks without complaints, and his employee deadpans agreement.

title: Flat Organization Ends in Mug Fight

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our experiment with a flattened organization failed. I'm your boss again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think our best play here is to beat each other to death with our coffee mugs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one said the transition would be smooth.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Make the first one count.

setting: Office, coworkers standing around holding coffee mugs
situation: The Boss announces that the company's experiment with a flat organization has failed and he is back in charge. Dilbert suggests that the best response is for everyone to beat each other to death with coffee mugs. In the last panel the Boss shrugs off the rough transition while Dilbert encourages the angry coworker in yellow to make the first strike count.
punchline: Returning to a traditional hierarchy is treated as so dreadful that Dilbert proposes a coffee-mug brawl to the death, and the Boss only comments that nobody promised the transition would be smooth.
summary: After management abandons a failed no-hierarchy experiment and reclaims the top job, a deadpan employee proposes a deadly mug fight as the logical next step.

title: Ask My Opinion or Seem Idiotic

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need your opinion before I make a decision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Studies show that if you ask for my opinion before I make a decision, I will no longer perceive you as a leader.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And if I do not ask for your opinion?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I would perceive you as an idiot and a leader.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he wants his opinion before making a decision. Dilbert claims studies show that asking for input makes him stop seeing the boss as a leader. When the boss asks what happens if he doesn't ask, Dilbert says he'd see him as an idiot and a leader.
punchline: Dilbert sets up a no-win situation in which the boss is judged an idiot either way, with the label 'leader' attached only to the idiotic choice, implying that leaders are idiots.
summary: Dilbert tells his boss that seeking advice undermines his leadership, while ignoring advice merely makes him a foolish leader.

file: 2014/2014-07-10_deception_work ethic_growth hacker_web apps_perfect job_growth hackers_do nothing_work from home.gif
title: Growth Hacker: Perfect Do-Nothing Job

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We need a "growth hacker" for our web apps. I think I'd be perfect for that job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've heard of growth hackers, but I have no idea what they do all day.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You could do nothing and I wouldn't know the difference.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I could work from home.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells the seated Boss that the company needs a growth hacker for its web apps and that he'd be perfect for it. The Boss admits he has no idea what growth hackers actually do all day. Wally and the Boss each point out that the other could do nothing without being noticed, and the Boss adds that he could work from home.
punchline: Because nobody understands what a growth hacker does, the job is a perfect cover for doing nothing, and the Boss's reply shows he sees the same loophole for himself.
summary: A lazy employee pitches himself for a trendy job title nobody understands, and the clueless manager quickly sees how little oversight it would take.

file: 2014/2014-06-04_art education_engineers_inventions_humans do cretaive_robots_technology work_liberal arts majors_origami_game.gif
title: Robot Predicts Engineers' Creative Future

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Someday robots will do all of the technology work and humans will only do creative jobs.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: If you engineers work hard, someday the spoils will go to the liberal arts majors who partied while you studied.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I hear good things about origami. It's not too late to get into that game.

situation: A robot stands beside Dilbert while he works at his computer and cheerfully predicts that robots will take over all technology work, leaving humans only creative jobs. It then tells Dilbert, an engineer, that the rewards of automation will go to liberal arts majors who partied while engineers studied. Finally it suggests he take up origami as a new career.
punchline: The robot reveals that engineers are building the automation that will make their own skills obsolete, so it cheerfully advises Dilbert to retrain in a craft like origami.
summary: A chipper robot tells an engineer that automation will make his skills worthless while arts graduates reap the rewards, and recommends paper folding as a fallback career.

file: 2014/2014-06-29_computers & peripherals_cruelty_tech supprt_highly trained engineer_electrical engineer_most proabable_reinstalled software_rebooted_default_request.gif
title: Tech Support Insists On Rebooting

transcript.speaker: Tech Support
transcript.text: This is tech support. How may I help you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Before we start, I need to tell you that I'm a highly trained electrical engineer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have already eliminated all of the most probable causes of my issue.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have reinstalled the software and I have rebooted several times.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So please, if you have any respect for humanity, do not start this call by insisting that I reboot again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you do that? Can you not ask me to reboot as your first suggestion?

transcript.speaker: Tech Support
transcript.text: Try rebooting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: Tech Support
transcript.text: I kinda love my job.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle and a tech support call center
situation: Dilbert calls tech support and carefully explains that he is a trained engineer who has already reinstalled the software and rebooted several times. He begs the support agent not to open by telling him to reboot. The agent immediately says to try rebooting, and Dilbert screams in frustration.
punchline: The tech support agent gleefully does the one thing Dilbert pleaded against, revealing that he enjoys tormenting callers with the clichéd reboot advice.
summary: A desperate caller pre-empts the most overused support suggestion, and the technician cheerfully delivers it anyway, relishing the pain.

title: Productive Means Doing Useless Mandatory Tasks

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You didn't accomplish anything this month.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure I did.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I did the mandatory training that has no use, attended your mandatory meetings that don't help, and filled out regulatory paperwork for things we don't do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you trying to make a point?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nope. Just being productive.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dilbert seated across the desk
situation: The Boss accuses Dilbert of accomplishing nothing all month. Dilbert lists the useless mandatory training, pointless meetings and irrelevant regulatory paperwork that filled his time. When the Boss asks if he is making a point, Dilbert deadpans that he is just being productive.
punchline: Dilbert's feigned innocence shows that the useless tasks the company mandates are the only 'productive' work he was allowed to do, so the Boss's complaint indicts the company's own bureaucracy.
summary: An employee answers his manager's charge of idleness by itemizing the pointless obligations the company itself imposed on him.
